en: The Sūtra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna, Volume One.
Translated by Kumārajīva and others at the Xiaoyao Garden in Cháng'ān during the Hongshì era of the Later Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as five hundred virtuous śrāvakas,
including Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahākātyāyana.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the city of Rājagṛha named Mahākaṭhinanda, who was wise and possessed great knowledge. He came to where the Buddha was, prostrated before him, and circumambulated the Buddha seven times.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered a profound meditative concentration and remained silent without speaking.
When Kāṭhila-Nanda saw that the Buddha had entered concentration, he went at once to where Śāriputra was, prostrated himself with his head at Śāriputra’s feet, and said:
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
"I only pray that you will expound the essentials of the Dharma for me in detail.

Thereupon, Śāriputra immediately expounded the Four Noble Truths for him, analyzing their meanings and implications one time up to seven times; yet at that moment, Kāṭhila Nanda’s mind remained in doubt and he had not yet awakened.
In this manner, he proceeded until he had circumambulated and prostrated at the feet of all five hundred śrāvakas, requesting them to preach the essentials of the Dharma.
Each of the śrāvakas likewise turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths for him seven times, yet Kāṭhila-Nanda’s mind remained unawakened.
He returned once more to where the Buddha was and paid homage to him.

At that time, the World-Honored One arose from his meditative concentration and saw Kāṭhila-Nanda prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, his tears falling like heavy rain as he entreated the World-Honored One:
“I only pray that you will turn the Wheel of the True Dharma for me.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again expounded the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths extensively, from once up to seven times.
Yet Kāṭhila-nanda still did not understand.
However, five hundred devaputras, having heard what the Buddha taught, attained the pure Dharma-eye; they immediately took celestial flowers to make offerings to the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because of the bhikṣu Kāṭhila-Nanda, we have now swiftly attained the benefit of the Dharma; seeing the Dharma as it truly is, we have become stream-enterers.”

At that time, when Kāṭhila-Nanda heard the words of the devas, his heart was filled with shame and remorse; choked with sobs, he remained speechless. He cast his entire body to the ground like the collapse of a great mountain, and immediately prostrated himself before the Buddha with his four limbs spread out, confessing his transgressions to the Buddha.

At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions was this bhikṣu Kāṭhila Nanda born with such great wisdom,
such that he attained mastery in the four Vedas, the Viśvāmitra-kalpa, the movements of the sun, moon, and stars, and all arts and crafts?
Furthermore, what sin have I committed that, despite having been a renunciant for many years, I alone have not tasted the flavor of the Buddha-dharma?
Although the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, personally preached the Dharma for me, it was as if I were one born deaf—neither hearing nor attaining anything.

There have been five hundred great generals of the Buddha-dharma who, in accordance with the teachings, turned the wheel of Dharma; yet even when they preached the Dharma for me, there was likewise no benefit.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for me the past causes and conditions of this bhikṣu.
When Ānanda asked this, the Buddha immediately smiled; five-colored light issued from his mouth, circled the Buddha seven times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
He addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Long ago, countless eons in the past, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. This bhikṣu Kāśīrānanda was that very person.”
Within that Buddha’s Dharma, there was a bhikṣu named Acirajita Nanda, who was intelligent and possessed great wisdom.

Because of his great wisdom, he became arrogant and negligent, and failed to cultivate the dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness; consequently, when his body perished and his life ended, he fell into the Black Darkness Hell.

Emerging from hell, he was reborn among dragons and elephants; for five hundred lifetimes he constantly served as a dragon king, and for five hundred lifetimes he constantly served as an elephant king.
Shedding his animal body, by virtue of his previous power of renouncing the world and maintaining the precepts, he attained rebirth in the heavens.
Having ended his life in the heavens, he was reborn in the human realm.
Because he had recited the Tripitaka in his previous life, he has now encountered a Buddha;
yet, because he was negligent in his former life and did not cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, he is unable to awaken in this present body.
At that time, when Kāṭhila-Nanda heard these words of the Buddha, he immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will teach me how to fix my mindfulness.
At that time, the Buddha told Kāṭhila-Nanda:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."

Today you have skillfully questioned the Tathāgata regarding the nectar-like True Dharma that extinguishes the thieves of a distracted mind, the medicine for afflictions used by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, which shuts all doors of negligence and universally opens the Eightfold Noble Path for humans and devas.
“Observe this well and attentively; do not allow your minds to become distracted.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, fifty *mahallaka* bhikṣus among the assembly also said to Ānanda, “The World-Honored One now wishes to teach the Dharma for removing negligence; we wish to follow and study this matter.”
“I only pray that the Venerable One will inform the Buddha on my behalf.
When these words were spoken, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“It is not only for you, but also for the sake of those who will be heedless in the future, that I shall now, here in the Kalandakanivāpa at the Bamboo Grove, teach the Dharma of mindfulness to the bhikṣu Cīrānanda.”
The Buddha told Kāṭhila Nanda:
"Receive my words and be careful not to forget them.
From this day forward, you shall practice the dharma of a śramaṇa."

The dharma of a śramaṇa is as follows: one should spread out a sitting mat (niṣīdana) in a quiet place, sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), arrange one's robes neatly, sit upright with the body straight, bare the right shoulder, place the left hand upon the right hand, close the eyes, press the tongue against the palate, and concentrate the mind so that it remains fixed and does not become distracted.

First, one should fix the mind upon the big toe of the left foot and contemplate the half-joint of the toe with close attention, forming the mental image of a bubble arising; one should contemplate this until it is extremely clear.
Thereafter, one forms the mental image of the bubble bursting, seeing the half-joint of the toe as exceedingly white and pure, as if possessing a white radiance.
Having seen this, one next contemplates a single bone joint, causing the flesh to be split away, so that the single joint of the finger is seen with extreme clarity, as if there were a white light.
The Buddha told Kāṭhila-Nanda:
"This is called the method of binding the mindfulness."
Having heard what the Buddha had said, Kāṭhila-Nanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Having observed one joint, he next observed two joints.
Having observed two joints, he next observed three joints.
Having observed the three joints, the mind gradually expands; one should then observe the five joints.
Seeing the five joints of the feet as if they were white light, the white bones become distinct.
In this way, bind the mind and contemplate the five joints with precision, not allowing it to wander or scatter.
If the mind wanders and scatters, gather it and cause it to return.
When the visualization of half a verse is completed as before, the entire body becomes warm and the area below the heart feels hot.
When this visualization is attained, it is called "binding the mind in abiding."

Once the mind has become settled, one should further form a mental image, causing the flesh of the insteps to peel away in two directions, so that the bones of the insteps are seen with extreme clarity, appearing as white as jade or snow.
Once this visualization is accomplished, one next contemplates the ankle bones, causing the flesh to peel away on both sides so that the ankle bones are seen to be extremely bright white.
Next, one contemplates the shin bones, causing the flesh to fall away, until one sees the shin bones themselves as brilliantly and starkly white.
Next, contemplate the knee bones, making them likewise vivid and distinct.
Next, contemplate the hip bones, making them extremely white.

Next, contemplate the ribs; imagine the flesh peeling away from each rib in both directions until only the rib bones remain, white as jade or snow, even to the point that the vertebrae of the spine are seen with extreme clarity.

Next, one contemplates the bones of the shoulders, visualizing the shoulder flesh as if sliced away with a knife—from the shoulder to the elbow, from the elbow to the wrist, from the wrist to the palm, and from the palm to the tips of the fingers—causing the flesh to peel away on both sides until one sees the white bones of half the body.
Having seen the white bones of the half-body, one next contemplates the scalp.
Having seen the scalp, one next contemplates the thin skin.
Having contemplated the thin skin, one next contemplates the membranes.
Having contemplated the membranes, one next contemplates the brain.
Having contemplated the brain, one next contemplates the fat.
Having contemplated the fat, one next contemplates the throat.
Having observed the throat, one next observes the lung vertebrae (feetū).
Having observed the lung vertebrae, one perceives the heart, lungs, liver, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, kidneys, and the receptacles for raw and cooked food.

"There are forty families of worms within the stomach; each family leads eighty billion small worms. Each of these worms is born from the various channels, reproducing through incubation and birth until there are three hundred million in total, their mouths clutching the stomach."
Each worm has forty-nine heads, with heads and tails as thin as the point of a needle.
Among these various worms, twenty households consist of fire-worms, born from the essence of fire.
Twenty households consist of wind-insects, which arise from the wind-element.
These various insects enter and exit the various channels, sporting with sovereign ease.
The fire-insects move the wind, and the wind-insects move the fire; they breathe upon one another to ripen the organs of growth.
Moving up and down, they undergo this cycle seven times in total.
Each of these insects has seven eyes, and from each eye, fire issues forth.
They also have seven bodies; by inhaling the fire and moving their bodies, they cook the raw contents of the stomach.
Once the raw and cooked stores have been digested, they each return and enter back into the various channels.
Furthermore, there are forty families of worms, each family leading three hundred million small worms, their bodies red as fire.
There are worms with twelve heads, each head having four mouths that contain the matured intestines.
Blood flows between the vessels; one should contemplate all of this until it becomes clearly visible.
Having seen these things, one further sees various worms emerging from the throat.
Furthermore, one contemplates that the small intestine, liver, lungs, spleen, and kidneys all flow and enter into the large intestine, emerging from the throat and falling onto the ground before one.

Once this visualization is accomplished, one immediately sees the ground before them as a place foul with excrement and urine, where various worms entwine and bind one another; from the mouths of these worms flow pus and blood, filling the area with impurities.
"When this visualization is accomplished, one sees one's own body like a person made of white snow, with each joint connected to the next.
If one sees it as yellow or black, one should further repent."

Having already repented his transgressions, he saw that skin had grown upon his own bones; this skin completely peeled away and fell into a heap before him on the ground, gradually increasing in size until it was like a *pātra*.
It grows even larger, resembling a large jar or vat, until it is as vast as a gandharva palace; it expands or contracts according to the mind’s will.
It further increases in size like a great mountain, upon which various insects feed, causing pus and blood to flow out, while countless worms crawl and move within the pus.
Again, he saw the hideous mountain gradually rotting and decaying until only a small portion remained, which various insects vied with one another to devour.
Suddenly, four yakṣas emerged from the ground; fire issued from their eyes, their tongues were like venomous serpents, and they possessed six heads.
Their heads each have distinct characteristics:
the first is like a mountain, the second like a cat, the third like a tiger, the fourth like a wolf, the fifth like a dog, and the sixth like a rat.

Furthermore, his two hands were like those of a monkey, and on the tip of each of his ten fingers was a four-headed venomous snake; the first rained water, the second rained earth, the third rained stones, and the fourth rained fire.
Furthermore, his left foot resembles that of a kumbhāṇḍa ghost, and his right foot resembles that of a piśāca ghost; he manifests a hideous form that is most terrifying.
At that time, four yakṣas each carry nine kinds of corpses, standing in successive rows before the practitioner.
The Buddha told Kāṭhila Nanda:
"This is called the initial object of the perception of impurity.
The Buddha then told Ānanda:
"Uphold these words and be careful not to forget them.
For the sake of future sentient beings, expound and explain at length this nectar-like Dharma, the noble seed of the three vehicles."
At that time, when Kāṭhila-Nanda heard these words spoken by the Buddha, he contemplated each one with meticulous attention; for ninety days, he did not shift his mental focus.

When the *pravāraṇā* ceremony of the Saṃgha concluded on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the various bhikṣus paid homage to the World-Honored One and each returned to their respective lodgings. During the latter part of the day, Kāṭhila-Nanda successively cultivated and attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; he became fully endowed with the three knowledges (*trividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). With a heart of great joy, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!”

Today, through reflection, through right attainment, and by relying on samādhi, my births have come to an end; I shall not undergo further existence. Knowing this as it truly is, I am certain that I shall accomplish the pure holy life.
"World-Honored One!
This Dharma is a vessel of ambrosia; those who partake of it consume the flavor of ambrosia.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it further for us in detail."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāṭhila-Nanda:
"If you have truly and authentically attained this Dharma, you may now perform the eighteen transformations according to your own will."
At that time, Kāṭhila-Nanda stood in mid-air and performed the eighteen transformations with effortless mastery.

When the bhikṣus saw that even one so full of pride as Kāṭhila-Nanda could be tamed, they followed the Buddha’s teaching by fixing their minds on a single point and not following after the sense faculties; thus, they attained arhatship.

At that time, there were fifteen hundred bhikṣus in the assembly; those whose minds were most distracted, having seen this event, all gave rise to joy and immediately went to where the Buddha was to receive the Dharma in succession.
At that time, because of this arrogant bhikṣu Mahākaṭhina Nanda, the World-Honored One first established the method of binding mindfulness and addressed the fourfold assembly:

"Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, from this day forward, those who seek the path of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) should bind their mindfulness and concentrate their minds upon a single point."

If this mind runs wild among the six sense organs like a monkey, devoid of shame and remorse, you should know that such a person is a caṇḍāla, not of the lineage of the noble ones, and their mind is untamed and unpliant.
The wardens of the Avīci Hell constantly employ such a person.
An evil person such as this has no means of attaining liberation throughout many kalpas.
This thief of a distracted mind gives rise to the seeds of the three realms; depending upon and because of this mind, one falls into the three evil destinies.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Do you now see this bhikṣu Mahākausthila Nanda? Has he attained liberation through the contemplation of impurity?
You should receive and uphold this well, and explain it extensively for the sake of the assembly."
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
“Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well.
As for the second visualization, fix your mindfulness upon the forehead.
Observe the center of the forehead with precision, as small as a fingernail, and take care not to let your thoughts wander."
Contemplating the forehead in this manner, one causes the mind to abide therein, giving rise to no other perceptions, but focusing the thought solely upon the forehead.
Thereafter, one contemplates one's own skull, seeing the skull white as the color of crystal.
In this way, he gradually sees his entire body as white bones, bright and pure, with the physical form complete and the joints interlocking.
He further sees the various heaps of impurities on the ground before him, as described above.
When the perception of impurity is accomplished, one must be careful not to discard the body; rather, one should be taught the method of changing the visualization.
As for the method of changing the visualization: imagine white light streaming from between all the joints, its brilliance so intense as to resemble the Snowy Mountains.
Having seen this, the yakṣa who previously consumed the heap of impurities shall suck it away.
One should then further imagine a skeleton person before oneself, making it exceedingly white.
Once this visualization is accomplished, one next visualizes a second skeleton person.
Having seen two skeletons, one sees three skeletons.
Having seen three skeletons, one sees four skeletons.
Having seen four skeletons, one sees five skeletons, and so on, up to seeing ten skeletons.
Having seen ten skeletons, one sees twenty skeletons.
Having seen twenty skeletons, one sees thirty skeletons.
Having seen thirty skeletons, one sees forty skeletons.

Having seen forty skeletons, one then sees a single room filled with skeletons, arranged in rows facing one another from front, back, left, and right, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.

At that time, the practitioner gradually expands his vision until he sees an entire courtyard filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, as white as jade or snow, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.
The mind becomes further expanded, seeing a field of one *qǐng* filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.
The mind gradually expands further, seeing a distance of one *yóujùn* filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.

Having seen [this] for one *yojana*, he proceeds until he sees a hundred *yojanas* filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.

Having seen [this] for a hundred yojanas, one proceeds until seeing the entire Jambudvīpa filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.
Having seen one Jambudvīpa, he next sees the island of Pūrvavideha filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.
Having seen Pūrvavideha, one next sees Jambudvīpa filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.
Having seen Jambudvīpa, he then sees Uttarakuru filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.
Having seen the four continents filled with skeletons, his body and mind become peaceful and stable, free from any thought of alarm or fear.
The mind gradually expands, and one sees the entire hundred Jambudvīpas filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.
Having seen the hundred Jambudvīpas, one then sees the hundred Pūrvavidehas filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.
Having seen the hundred Pūrvavidehas, one next sees a hundred Aparagoyānīs filled with skeletons, arranged in rows facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.
Having seen a hundred Jambudvīpas, one next sees a hundred Uttarakurus filled with skeletons, arranged row upon row facing one another, each raising its right hand toward the practitioner.
Having seen this, his body and mind become peaceful and blissful, free from any thought of alarm or fear.
Because his mental perception is sharp, he sees the Sahā world filled with skeletons, all standing upright with both hands hanging down and their ten fingers extended, facing the practitioner.

At that time, once the practitioner has seen these things, whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, they constantly see skeletal figures; mountains, rivers, rocky walls, and all worldly affairs are entirely transformed so that they appear like skeletal figures.

"At that time, having seen these things, the practitioner sees four great bodies of water in the four directions; their currents are swift and rapid, and their color is white like milk. He sees the skeletons of people sinking away with the current."
"When this visualization is accomplished, one should again perform repentance.
One should simply continue to visualize water surging and abiding in mid-air; then, one should further give rise to the visualization of making the water tranquil.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This is called the Samādhi of the Ordinary Person’s Mind Contemplating White Bones with White Light Emerging; it is also called the Sign of the Realm of Birth and Death within the Ocean of the Ordinary Person’s Mind.

Now, because of Kāṭhila-Nanda, I shall explain for you and all sentient beings of the future this gate of the Samādhi of White Bones with White Light Emerging, in order to gather in the distracted mind and cross over the ocean of birth and death."
"You should receive and uphold this; be careful not to forget or lose it.
When the World-Honored One had finished speaking these words, he immediately manifested the various characteristics of the White Light Samādhi, causing Ānanda to perceive them all in their entirety.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
This is called the initial stage of the contemplation of white bones.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Once this visualization is accomplished, further instructions for another visualization are given. Regarding these further instructions:

one should contemplate one’s own body as a single skeleton, making it exceedingly white and pure. One should cause the head to fall backward and enter into the pelvic bone, concentrating the mind on a single point until it is extremely clear.”
Once this visualization is accomplished, one contemplates the four sides of the body, seeing skeletal figures surrounding it on all four directions.

When this visualization is accomplished, one then creates a white-boned figure upon the ground before oneself, resembling one's own body, and likewise causes it to fall head-first into the pelvic bone.
Once the visualization of one has been accomplished, one should next visualize two.
Once the visualization of two has been accomplished, one should next visualize three.
Once the visualization of three has been accomplished, one should next visualize four.
Having completed the visualization of four, one should next visualize five.
Having completed the visualization of five, one proceeds until visualizing ten.
In this manner, filling the interior of a single room, one sees all the skeletal figures with their heads inverted, entering into the pelvic bones.
Having seen this within one room, he proceeds until he sees it within a hundred rooms; in all these skeletons, the heads are inverted and enter into the pelvic bones.
Having seen this in a hundred rooms, he sees a yojana filled with skeletons, all of whom have their heads inverted and enter into the pelvic bones.
Having seen one *yojana*, he proceeds until he sees immeasurable white-boned figures, all with their heads inverted and entering into the pelvic bones.

Once this visualization is perfected, he sees these various bone-figures scattered hither and thither across the ground before him; some have their heads shattered, some have their necks broken, some are overturned, some are contorted, some have their waists broken, some have their legs extended, some have their legs drawn in, some have their leg bones split into two parts, some have their skull bones falling back into their chests, and some have their skull bones tilted, arched, or shriveled. Confused and disordered, they lie scattered across the ground before him, filling the entire interior of the room from top to bottom and on all sides.
Once this visualization is accomplished, one sees, even unto infinity and boundlessness, countless white-boned persons scattered and strewn about—some large, some small, some broken, and some whole.
"In all such matters, you should fix the mind and observe them with clarity until they are perfectly distinct.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, once the practitioner has seen these things, he should reflect within himself:"
"The bones of the former body were complete, but now they are shattered and scattered, lying in chaotic disarray beyond description.
Since even this white-boned body lacks stability, one should know that my own body likewise has no self."
Having observed this clearly, one should reflect within oneself:
"There are merely these various bones, scattered here and there in disorder; where in this is there a self or another body?"
At that time, the practitioner contemplates non-self; body and mind become serene, peaceful, and blissful.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Once this visualization is accomplished, one should further instruct the mind to expand it, so that the practitioner sees the scattered bones extending across the entire Jambudvīpa, both lengthwise and crosswise.”

He sees that around the perimeter of all the bones on the four sides, a great fire breaks out; the flames follow one another in succession, burning the disordered bones, and he sees fire erupting from every joint of the skeletal beings.
Regarding such signs of fire, there may be various fires resembling flowing water, their bright flames blazing intensely as they flow through the spaces between the bones;
or there may be various fires resembling great mountains, coming from the four directions.
Once this visualization is accomplished, one will experience extreme terror, and upon emerging from meditative absorption, the body will feel feverish.
One should then withdraw the mind and, as before, contemplate the bones; visualize a single person of white bone until it is perfectly clear.
At this time, when the practitioner enters meditative concentration, they are unable to emerge from it on their own; they must snap their fingers before they can arise.
When this visualization is perfected, the practitioner should spontaneously give rise to this thought and say:
"Throughout countless kalpas of past lives, I have created dharmas of burning affliction; drawn by the conditions of such karma, I now see this fire arise."
Furthermore, one should reflect:
"This fire arises from the four great elements; my body is empty and quiescent, and these four great elements have no master.
This fierce fire has arisen abruptly from emptiness; both my body and the bodies of others are likewise entirely empty."
"Such a fire as this arises from false conceptualization; what is there for it to burn?
Both my body and the fire are impermanent.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The practitioner should, with a sincere mind, carefully contemplate such phenomena as these: they observe that there is no fire and no multitude of bones within emptiness.
For one who performs this contemplation, there is no fear; body and mind become tranquil and peaceful, even more so than before.”
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the second contemplation on white bones, thus completed.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Having finished contemplating the second white bone, one should again be instructed in the method of binding the mindfulness (*smṛti*).

As for the method of binding the mindfulness: first, one should bind the mind to the big toe of the left foot and contemplate that big toe with single-minded attention, causing the flesh to become bluish-black and greasy, as if the sun’s rays were scorching fat."
Gradually it reaches the knees and even the hips.
Having observed the left foot, one observes the right foot in the same manner.

Having observed the right foot, one next observes the waist, proceeding to the back, the neck, the nape, the head, the face, and the chest; all the limbs and joints of the entire body become moist and black, like fat being scorched by the sun’s rays, with impurities overflowing like a heap of excrement and urine.
Contemplate your own body, making it as clear and distinct as possible.
Once you have visualized one, you should then visualize two.
Once you have visualized two, you should then visualize three.
Once the visualization of three is accomplished, one should next visualize four.
Once the visualization of four is accomplished, one should next visualize five.
Once the visualization of five is accomplished, one should next visualize ten.
Having completed the visualization of the ten [impurities], one sees a single room filled with dark, moist filth, like fat being scorched by the sun or a heap of excrement and urine.
Various impure beings stand in rows, both lengthwise and crosswise, filling the entire room.
Having seen one chamber, he then saw two chambers.
Having seen two chambers, he went on until he saw immeasurable multitudes of impure beings, filling the Sahā world in all four directions, above, and below.
Once this visualization is accomplished, the practitioner reflects:

"In my past lives, I was greedy, lustful, and deluded, failing to realize it myself. In the prime of my youth, I was dissolute and attached to sensual pleasures, devoid of shame or remorse, pursuing forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena."
"Now, observing my own body, it overflows with impurities; so too is it with the bodies of others.
What is there to find delightful in them?
Having seen this, he becomes utterly weary of his own body, feeling shame and reproaching himself.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, one sees all food and drink as if they were excrement and urine, becoming utterly loathsome and repulsive.
Next, one is instructed in the method of changing the visualization.
As for this method of changing the visualization, one should again give rise to mental conceptions.
When this mental visualization is accomplished, one sees that outside of one's body, amidst all the impurities, flames suddenly burst forth on all four sides.
Like a shimmering mirage in the heat, they are pure white in color and move like a wild horse, reflecting upon all the impurities.
At that time, when the practitioner has seen these things, they should feel great joy.
Because of this joy, their body and mind become light and supple; their mind becomes clear and bright, and their happiness is many times greater than usual.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This is called the third contemplation: the reproach of oneself through shame and remorse.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the completion of the third contemplation on the oozing of pus and the sense of shame and remorse.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Once this visualization is accomplished, you should further instruct [the practitioner] to bind the mindfulness and fix the mind upon the big toe of the left foot, causing them to contemplate the joint of the big toe with precision and give rise to the perception of swelling."
Having seen the bloated corpse, one gives rise to the perception of its putrefaction.
Having seen the putrefied corpse, one gives rise to the perception of various pus and blood—blue-black, red, and white.
This pus and blood is so extremely foul-smelling that it is difficult to endure.
In this manner, gradually reaching the knees and then the thighs, he causes them all to become bloated, putrid, and festering, becoming impure.
Having contemplated the left leg, he does the same for the right.

Proceeding in this way, he reaches the waist, the back, the neck, the nape, the head, the face, and the chest; every limb and joint of the entire body becomes swollen, entirely rotted and decayed, with pus of various shades—blue-black, red, and white—flowing forth, such that it is a place of foul stench and impurity beyond endurance.
Once the visualization of one has been accomplished, one further visualizes two.
Once the visualization of two has been accomplished, one further visualizes three.
Once the visualization of three has been accomplished, one further visualizes four.
Having completed the visualization of four, one further visualizes five.
Having completed the visualization of five, one proceeds until visualizing ten.

Having completed the visualization of ten, one sees within a single room, all around and above and below, many bloated corpses; they are all putrid and decaying, with greenish-black, reddish, and whitish pus flowing out from them, such that the mixture of filth and stench is unbearable.
Furthermore, one should further visualize a *yojana*.
Having visualized one *yojana*, one proceeds until visualizing a hundred *yojanas*.

Having visualized a hundred *yojanas*, one eventually sees the trichiliocosm, its surroundings above and below, the earth and the void, all completely filled with bloated and putrefying corpses; from which flow out pus of blue, black, red, and white hues, such that it is filled with various impurities and becomes an unbearable place.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, after the practitioner has seen these things, they observe their own body as being filled with impurities, and they observe the bodies of others in the same way."
One should form this thought:
"This body of mine is truly loathsome; it is filled everywhere with manifold impurities.
Having contemplated this thoroughly, one fears the afflictions of birth and death, and the mind becomes firm in its deep faith in cause and effect.
Whether emerging from or entering meditative absorption, one constantly perceives impurity and seeks to cultivate revulsion and renounce this body.
When forming this perception, one sees one's own entire body, with skin and flesh, falling away like autumn leaves.

Seeing the meat fallen upon the ground before him, his mind was immediately greatly agitated; terror arose within him, and his body and mind trembled so violently that he could find no peace. His vital energy became feverish and distressed, like a patient suffering from a heat ailment who is tormented by thirst.

Upon emerging from meditative absorption, it is as if a person traveling through a vast wilderness in the summer heat becomes parched with thirst for lack of water and their body is utterly exhausted.
Once this perception is established, even until the time of eating, they see the food they consume as a bloated corpse, and the drink they consume as pus and blood.
"Once this perception is accomplished, one develops an intense revulsion toward the body.
One contemplates both the interior and exterior of the body, yet finds no purity.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
Furthermore, one should again instruct them to change their perception, so that they do not abandon the body in vain without gaining anything.

As for the method of changing the visualization: one should imagine a pure object at a distance beyond the foul and impure; teach them to fix their mind on this pure object until the mental eye becomes clear, and they desire to go and take it.

In this manner, gradually, beyond the various impure things that he sees at a great distance, there appear pure grounds such as ground made of lapis lazuli; seeing these pure places, he immediately desires to go there.
"It becomes even more vast and distant, such that the mind cannot reach it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, you should instruct the practitioner in this way, saying:"
"What you perceive is the perception of impurity; this perception of impurity consists of foul substances.
You should know that this perception arises from inversion, and that this body was obtained entirely due to inverted conduct in previous lives."
Such a body as this has seeds and roots that are entirely impure.
Do you now truly see this impurity?

Although you see its impurity, you perceive it as pure from the outside; you should know that this purity and this impurity cannot endure for long, and are merely perceived through the mental constructions of the various sense faculties.
This impure body belongs to various causes and conditions: when conditions converge, it exists; when conditions disperse, it ceases to be.
That which you perceive likewise belongs to conceptualization: when conceptualization is established, it exists; when conceptualization is destroyed, it ceases to be.
Such a thought emerges from the five sensory faculties and returns to your mind; it exists due to the conditions of various desires.
This perception of impurity comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
"You should contemplate impurity with single-minded attention, seeking that 'self' and 'other,' yet finding them utterly unobtainable.
The World-Honored One has taught that both self and other are entirely empty and quiescent; how much more so, then, is impurity!"

Thus, in various ways, he rebukes his mind and instructs it to contemplate emptiness; seeing that hair, body hair, nails, and teeth are all entirely non-existent, he suddenly abandons all impure things and, as before, settles the mind to again contemplate the skeleton.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Hold these words; be careful not to forget this meditation on impurity and the method for transforming perceptions.
At that time, having heard these words of the Buddha, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the completion of the fourth contemplation on the bloated corpse, the festering with pus and blood, and the transformation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Once this visualization is accomplished, you should next further instruct [the practitioner] to bind the mind to a single point, sitting upright in meditative absorption (samādhi), and clearly observing the big toe of the right foot, causing the skin of the toe to appear as if it were about to split open, with the thin skin and thick skin transparently reflecting one another inside and out."
Within that thin skin there is a further thin membrane; one should likewise observe this clearly and gradually proceed from the knees to the hips.
The left leg is treated in the same way.
Proceeding to the waist, to the back, to the neck, to the nape of the neck, to the head, to the face, and to the chest—the entire body is treated in this manner.

The thin and thick layers of skin are translucent from both within and without; they are so thin they seem about to burst as if being blown by the wind, and the swelling of the skin is beyond description.
From each and every pore among all the body hairs, hundreds of thousands of immeasurable quantities of pus and various fluids emerge like raindrops, faster than a torrential downpour.
Flowing both internally and externally, it is filled with pus and blood; such an extreme impurity is difficult to endure.
It is like a pool of pus, or like a pool of blood, with various worms filling its midst.
When this visualization is accomplished, one should contemplate that within the chest and throughout the entire body there are worms, appearing like a swarm of insects.

One should further contemplate the big toe of the left foot as swollen and festering with pus—pus that is blue, yellow, red, black, crimson, green, and white; it is putrid and oozing in all directions, mixed with excrement and urine, while various worms sport within it, making the foul-smelling filth unbearable.
One feels revulsion for this body, no longer craving various desires, and takes no pleasure in rebirth.

When this perception is perfected, one sees the body of a great yakṣa as vast as a great mountain; its hair is disheveled like a forest of thorns, it has sixty eyes resembling flashes of lightning, and forty mouths, each with two fangs that all protrude upward like flaming banners. Its tongues resemble sword-trees and extend down to the knees; in its hands it grasps iron clubs that resemble mountains of blades, appearing as if about to strike people.
Thus, there are many such [visions], their number not being one.
When seeing these things, one is struck with extreme terror, and both body and mind tremble.

Such appearances are all the result of having violated the prohibitions and precepts in previous lives—the root of all evils—namely: conceiving of a self where there is no self, conceiving of permanence where there is impermanence, and conceiving of purity where there is impurity; being heedless and stained by attachment, greedily receiving various desires; falsely giving rise to the notion of pleasure within phenomena that are suffering, giving rise to perverted notions regarding phenomena that are empty, giving rise to the notion of purity regarding an impure body, and sustaining oneself through wrong livelihood while failing to contemplate impermanence.
When this visualization is accomplished, you should further be instructed:
"Do not be afraid.
Such yakṣas are the objects of your own malevolent mind and fierce poison; they arise from the six elements and are composed of the six elements."
You should now carefully contemplate the six elements.
These six elements are earth, water, fire, wind, consciousness, and space.
You should examine each of these one by one with close attention:
Is your body earth?
Is it water? Or is it fire?
Is it this wind? Is it this consciousness?
Or is it this space?
In this way, contemplate this body one by one: from which of the great elements does it arise, and into which of the great elements does it disperse?
The six elements have no master, and the body likewise has no self; why, then, do you now fear the yakṣa?
Just as you conceive in your mind, [the self] comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
the perception and vision of the yakṣa are likewise so.

Simply sit with a settled mind; even if the yakṣa should come to strike you, endure it with joy, contemplating thoroughly that there is no self. Within the dharma of non-self, there is no thought of alarm or fear.
"Simply straighten your mind and sit in the full lotus posture, clearly contemplating both the impurity and the yakṣa.

Having accomplished one such visualization, you should again accomplish two; in this manner, gradually increasing until they are immeasurable, clearly contemplate each one so that all are distinct and vivid.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should properly receive and uphold this method of contemplating the impurity of the thin skin; be careful not to forget it.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the fifth contemplation, "The Thin Skin," which is now complete.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Once this visualization is accomplished, you should further instruct [the practitioner] to fix their mindfulness upon the big toe of the right foot. They should carefully observe the toes so that the foot swells up; from the feet to the head, it becomes like a bellows being blown, swelling and turning a dark, bluish-black, becoming unbearable to behold. Within it, white worms fill the interior like grains of non-glutinous rice."
There are worms with four heads that crawl about in pursuit of one another, devouring each other in turn.
Worms grow within the flesh, muscles, marrow, and bones; all the worms within the five viscera have devoured them completely, leaving only thick skin remaining over the bones.

The thickness of their skin is like that of fine silk; as various insects enter and exit, it is as if piercing bamboo leaves, and the skin is so worn through from both inside and out that it seems about to tear.
Their eyes itch and sting; countless worms pierce the eyes seeking to emerge, taking up residence within the eye sockets.
The nine orifices of the body are likewise.
At that time, the various worms emerge from the thick skin and enter into the thin skin; the skin is thus completely perforated, and the worms all fall to the ground.
Their number is vast and beyond calculation; they form a great mass like a mountain of insects, standing before the practitioner, devouring one another or writhing about in mutual entanglement.

At that time, once the practitioner has seen the many worms, he should further fix his mindfulness and observe one worm with clarity, causing this single worm to devour all the other worms until, having finished eating them, only that one worm remains alone.

His mind gradually expanded until he saw the aforementioned insect become as large as a dog; its body was exhausted and its snout was curved like a horn as it sniffed before the practitioner, its eyes a vivid red like glowing iron balls.
Having seen this, one is struck with extreme terror and should reflect:
"How is it that my own body has suddenly come to such a state as this?
Previously I saw various insects devouring one another, but now I see these insects with such hideous forms; how truly terrifying they are!"
"When this visualization is accomplished, you should observe your own body:
'These various worms within me were originally non-existent but now exist; having existed, they will return to non-existence.
Such impurity arises from the mind's perceptions; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. It is neither I, nor is it another.'"
This body is formed through the causal conditions of the harmony of the six great elements; when these six elements disperse and perish, the body is likewise impermanent.
As for the various insects that were here before, they came from nowhere and go nowhere.
"My body is a collection of worms; what reality could there be in it?
The worms have no master, and I likewise have no self.
As he reflects thus, the worms he perceives will gradually diminish in size before his eyes.
Having seen this, his body and mind became harmonious and joyful; he was tranquil and at ease, feeling twice as much bliss as before.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You should well receive and uphold this method of contemplation on the cluster of thick-skinned worms; be careful not to forget it."
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Once this visualization was accomplished, it was called "The Sixth Meditation on the Mass of Thick-Skinned Worms.
The Buddha then said to Ānanda:
Furthermore, one should dwell with the mind focused and mindful on a single point, clearly observing the big toe of the right foot; from the feet up to the head, one should observe them thoroughly.

One should cause the skin and flesh to completely vanish, so that the intestines, stomach, abdomen, liver, lungs, heart, spleen, and kidneys—all the five viscera—fall entirely to the ground, leaving only the sinews and bones supporting one another.
The remaining membrane adheres to the bone; its color is extremely red, appearing like mud or like turbid water.
One should form the perception of it as turbid water and use it to wash the skin.
From the feet to the head, cause all parts to be thus, observing one's own body until it is extremely clear.
Having observed one's own body, further create another body in the space before you, standing in front, no different from oneself.
Once the visualization of one is accomplished, one should next visualize two.
Once the visualization of two is accomplished, one should next visualize three.
Once the visualization of three is accomplished, one should next visualize four.
Having completed the visualization of four, one should next visualize five.
Having completed the visualization of five, one proceeds until visualizing ten.

Once the visualization of ten is complete, one sees the interior of a single room, its perimeter and its upper and lower reaches, entirely filled with red-colored skeletal figures; some are the color of mud, and some are the color of turbid water, their skin washed by that turbid water.
In this manner, as it becomes increasingly numerous, it gradually expands until it fills one *yojana*.
Having visualized one *yojana*, one visualizes two *yojanas*.
Having visualized two *yojanas*, one gradually expands the visualization until it encompasses one hundred *yojanas*.

Having visualized a hundred yojanas, one proceeds until seeing the trichiliocosm filled with red-colored skeletal figures; some are the color of mud, others are the color of turbid water, their skin washed by that turbid water.
"It surrounds and fills every direction, above and below, lengthwise and crosswise.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Now, contemplate this mark of red color with close attention; be careful not to forget it."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the seventh completion of the complex visualization of the extremely red mud, turbid water, and washing of the skin.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Furthermore, you should again instruct [the practitioner] to bind the mind and settle the attention, observing the big toe of the left foot. From the feet up to the head, one should view it as being like the withered and yellowish complexion of a recently deceased person; one should observe that one's own body is likewise thus."
Having seen it turn yellowish, one should cause that yellow color to change into blue and red.
When this visualization is accomplished, one sees a recently deceased person on the ground before oneself, whose complexion is yellowish-red.
Having seen one, he sees two; having seen two, he sees three; having seen three, he sees four; having seen four, he sees five.
Having seen five, because his mental perception has become sharp, he constantly perceives his own body as being like that of a recently deceased person.
When this visualization is accomplished, one sees all people throughout Jambudvīpa as if they were newly deceased.

Once this visualization is perfected, it further expands until one sees the entire trichiliocosm filled with newly deceased persons; one then perceives one’s own body and the bodies of others as being exactly the same, without any distinction.
"When this perception is accomplished, the mind becomes weary and despondent, and lustful desire grows thin.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should carefully and attentively contemplate this perception of a newly deceased person; be careful not to forget it."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
When this visualization was accomplished, it was called the completion of the eighth visualization, the visualization of a recently deceased person.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

Furthermore, one should again be taught to bind the mindfulness and settle the mind, observing intently the big toe of the left foot; from the feet up to the head, one should cause the mind not to be distracted and see all the bones of the body, each distinct and clear, supporting one another and held together, with none of them broken.
The hair, nails, teeth, and all other parts are fully complete, brilliantly white.
Having visualized one's own body, one repeatedly contemplates it to make it pure white.
Having visualized one body, one then visualizes two bodies.
Having visualized two bodies, one further visualizes three bodies.
Having visualized three bodies, one further visualizes four bodies.
Having visualized four bodies, one further visualizes five bodies, and so on up to ten.

Having visualized the ten bodies, one sees within a single room that the entire circumference—above and below—is filled with skeletons, complete with hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, as white as conch shells or snow.
Having seen one chamber, he then sees a hundred chambers.
Having seen a hundred chambers, he sees one Jambudvīpa.
Having seen one Jambudvīpa, he proceeds to see a trichiliocosm filled with skeletons, complete with hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, their color extremely white, as white as jade or snow.
"When this visualization is accomplished, the mind and spirit become tranquil and peaceful, and joy will be twice that of usual.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should carefully and attentively contemplate the visualization of the complete body of bones; be cautious not to forget it."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
When this visualization was accomplished, it was called the completion of the ninth visualization, the "Complete Body Visualization.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

Furthermore, one should again be instructed to bind the mind and settle the attention, observing intently the space between the two joints of the big toe of the right foot, causing the mind to dwell single-pointedly without distraction. One should observe the two joints so that they separate from each other, with only their tips touching.
Having observed the two joints, one should cause it to be thus from the feet to the head, so that each joint is loosened, with only the ends touching one another.
From the head to the feet there are three hundred and sixty-three articulations; one should observe each of them attentively, causing each joint to be loosened individually.
If it is insufficient, settle the mind and observe with clarity, causing each joint to be disarticulated until only the bones at the extremities remain touching one another.
Having observed your own body in this way, you should then observe the bodies of others.
Having observed one, he observes two; having observed two, he observes three; having observed three, he observes four; having observed four, he observes five.
Having observed five, he proceeds until he observes immeasurable skeletal figures, with each joint separated, yet their tips touching one another.
Having seen this, one further sees numerous skeletal figures in the four directions, all likewise so.
When this contemplation is attained, one will naturally see that outside of these skeletal figures, it is like a great ocean, tranquil and pellucid.
His mind becomes clear and sharp, and he sees various multicolored lights surrounding him on all four sides.
Having seen this, his mind naturally becomes peaceful and joyful; his body and mind are pure, free from thoughts of sorrow or delight.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Observe carefully and thoroughly this visualization of the body being dismembered limb by limb; be cautious not to forget it.
Having heard what the Buddha said, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
One who attains this contemplation is said to have completed the tenth stage, the Contemplation of the Dissolution of the Joints.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Once this visualization is accomplished, you should further instruct them to fix their mindfulness and stabilize the mind by carefully observing the space between the two joints of the big toe of the right foot, causing the joints to appear separated by about the width of three fingers, and forming the visualization of white light to serve as a support."

When sitting at night, one should form the visualization of moonlight; when sitting during the day, one should form the visualization of sunlight. One should maintain the continuity of the bones so that they do not disperse.

From the feet to the head, there are three hundred and sixty-three joints; one should cause them all to be separated by a distance of three finger-widths, holding them with white light so that they do not fall apart.

When sitting during the day, one should sustain the practice with sunlight; when sitting at night, one should sustain it with moonlight, visualizing that white light emerges from all the joints of the body.
When this visualization is attained, one will naturally see within the sunlight a Buddha sixteen feet tall, with a halo one fathom wide, extending one fathom to the left, right, above, and below.
His body was golden in color, and his entire form was radiant with blazing red light, majestic and sublime; the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics were all brilliantly manifest.
Each mark and excellence could be seen with perfect clarity, no different from when the Buddha was in the world.
If you see this at such a time, be careful not to prostrate; rather, you should settle your mind and contemplate all dharmas with precision.
You should form this thought:
"The Buddha has taught that all dharmas neither come nor go, and that all their natures and characteristics are likewise empty and quiescent."
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the body of liberation; that which is the body of liberation is suchness (tathatā). Within the dharma of suchness, there is neither seeing nor attaining.
When one forms this thought, one will naturally see all the Buddhas.
"Because you have seen the Buddha, your mind and heart are serene, tranquil, and joyful.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Now observe this flowing light and white bones with careful attention; be sure not to forget them."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
One who attains this contemplation is said to have completed the eleventh contemplation: the Contemplation of the Flowing Light from White Bones.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Having attained this contemplation, you should further be taught to bind the mind and settle the attention, observing the vertebrae with precision.

Within the spaces between the vertebrae, use the power of concentration to form the mental image of a lofty terrace. Contemplate your own body as a person of white jade sitting in the full lotus posture, with the radiance of the white bones universally illuminating all things."
When performing this visualization, make it extremely clear and distinct.

Once seated upon this platform, like a person with supernormal powers dwelling on the summit of Mount Sumeru, one gazes upon the four directions without obstruction. One clearly perceives one’s own former body; one sees all the skeletal figures as white as jade or snow, arranged in rows facing one another, their bodies complete and without a single missing part, filling the trichiliocosm.
This is called the visualization of white light being perfected.
Next, one sees vertical bones, which also fill the trichiliocosm.
One further sees horizontal bones, which likewise fill the trichiliocosm.
One sees blue-colored skeletal beings, arranged in rows facing one another, filling the trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, one sees black-colored skeletal beings, arranged in rows facing one another, filling the trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, he saw bloated corpses, arranged row upon row facing one another, filling the trichiliocosm.
He also saw people with pus-soaked leprosy, and people with their bodies smeared with pus and blood, filling the trichiliocosm.
Again, he saw people with their entire bodies putrefied and decaying, from whom worms emerged, filling the trichiliocosm.
Again, he saw people whose bodies were covered only by thin skin, filling the trichiliocosm.
Again, he saw people whose skin and bones were separated from one another, filling the trichiliocosm.
Again, he saw people as red as the color of blood, filling the trichiliocosm.
Again, he saw people with the color of turbid water filling the trichiliocosm.
Again, he saw people with the color of mud filling the trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, one sees white-boned persons whose hair, body hair, nails, and teeth are all interconnected, filling the trichiliocosm.
Next, one sees three hundred and sixty-three joints disarticulated, with only the extremities touching one another; such bone-people fill the trichiliocosm.
Next, one sees a person whose joints are separated on both sides by an interval of three finger-widths, with white light filling the trichiliocosm.
Next, one sees a person of scattered white bones, held together solely by white light, filling the trichiliocosm.
In this way, one shall see many white-boned figures, their number beyond description.
When this contemplation is attained, one should give rise to this thought:
"This body of mine arises from the four great elements as branches, leaves, and seeds; it is thus exceedingly impure and utterly loathsome."
Such realms arise from my own mind; when the mind conceives them, they are formed, and when it does not conceive them, they are not seen.
One should know that this conception is a false perception, arising from deluded views, and belongs to the realm of causes and conditions.
I shall now contemplate the causes and conditions of all phenomena.
What are called the causes and conditions of all phenomena?
The causes and conditions of all phenomena arise from the four great elements.
"The four great elements are earth, water, fire, and wind.

One should further contemplate that these wind-elements arise from the four directions; each wind-element is like a great serpent with four heads—two facing upward and two facing downward—and this wind issues forth from all their many ears.
When this contemplation is accomplished, the wind transforms into fire.

Each and every venomous serpent spits forth mountains of fire; these mountains are steep and extremely terrifying. Within these volcanic mountains dwell various yakṣas, who move their bodies to inhale the flames and emit wind from their pores.
Such transformations pervaded the entire room.
Having filled one room, they further filled two rooms.
Having filled two rooms, they gradually expanded until they filled one yojana.
Having filled one *yojana*, it filled two *yojanas*.
Having filled two *yojanas*, it filled three *yojanas*.

Having filled three *yojanas*, it became even more vast, filling all of Jambudvīpa. There he saw various yakṣas within volcanic mountains, inhaling fire and carrying mountains upon their backs; wind issued from the pores of their skin as they frantically ran and rushed throughout all of Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, when yakṣas startle the practitioner by threatening him,
and he sees this occurrence, his mind becomes greatly terrified, and he seeks a method for transforming his visualization.
As for the method for transforming the visualization, one first visualizes the image of the Buddha.
At the tips of each flame, one should visualize a Buddha image one zhang and six chi in height.

When this visualization is perfected, the flames gradually subside and transform into lotus flowers; the many volcanic mountains become like masses of pure gold, transparent both inside and out, while the yakṣas and ghosts appear like figures carved from white jade.
Only the wind element remained, swirling and turning as it blew upon the lotus flowers.
Innumerable transformation Buddhas stood in mid-air, emitting great radiance like a mountain of adamant.
At that time, all the winds became still and ceased to move.
Then, four venomous snakes spat water from their mouths; the water was five-colored and filled an entire bed.
Having filled one bed, it further filled two beds.
Having filled two beds, he next fills three beds; in this manner, it gradually fills an entire room.
Having filled one room, he next fills two rooms.
Having filled two rooms, he next fills three rooms; in this manner, it gradually fills ten rooms.

Once the ten rooms were filled with water, he saw five-colored waters, within each of which was a white light like a crystal pillar, consisting of fourteen tiers, each of which was hollow; from these, white water surged forth and came to rest suspended in mid-air.

When this visualization is accomplished, the practitioner sees within his own body, inside the heart, a venomous dragon with six heads. It coils around the heart seven times; two heads spit water, two heads spit fire, two heads spit stones, and wind issues from its ears.
From each of the pores of his body, ninety-nine venomous snakes emerge.
These snakes move two upward and two downward.
The various nāgas spit forth water from beneath his feet, which flows into the white waters.
In this manner, gradually, within one *yojana* everyone saw these things.
Once it had filled one *yojana*, it further filled two *yojanas*.
Having filled two *yojanas*, it filled three *yojanas*, and so on, until it filled the entire Jambudvīpa.

After he had filled Jambudvīpa, at that time the venomous dragon emerged from his navel, gradually ascended upward, entered his eye, and emerging from the eye, came to rest upon the crown of his head.
At that time, there was a great tree in the midst of the waters, its branches and leaves spreading out in all directions to cover everything.
This venomous dragon, never leaving his own body, extended his tongue upward onto the tree.
Upon the tongues of these dragons are eight hundred spirits; some of these spirits have mountains upon their heads, hands like snakes, and feet resembling dogs.

There are also spirits with heads like dragon heads, whose pores all over their bodies contain hundreds of thousands of eyes from which fire issues forth; their teeth are like mountains of knives as they writhe upon the ground.
Furthermore, there were various ghosts, each with ninety-nine heads and ninety-nine hands.
The shapes of their heads were exceedingly hideous, resembling dogs, jackals, wildcats, domestic cats, foxes, and mice.
Each of these ghosts bore a macaque on its neck.
These evil ghosts played in the water, while some climbed trees to leap and hurl themselves about.
There were yakṣa-ghosts with fire blazing upon their heads; the macaques sought to extinguish the fires with water, but they could not stop them, and instead caused them to grow even more intense.

Thus, this fierce fire suddenly blazed forth from the sides of the crystal pillars within the water; it burned the crystal pillars as if melting pure gold, with successive flames encircling the body ten times, remaining above the practitioner like a canopy of pure gold, while various nets completely covered the tops of the trees.
This true-gold canopy was fully three layers deep.

At that time, suddenly from beneath the earth there appeared four great evil spirits with hundreds of thousands of ears; from their ears issued water and fire, from the pores of their bodies rained down various fine dusts, and from their mouths they spat forth winds that filled the world.
There were eighty-four thousand rākṣasa demons, each with a pair of tusks protruding upward one yojana in height, from the pores of whose bodies bolts of fire erupted.
Such a multitude ran and frolicked amidst the waters.
Furthermore, there are tigers, wolves, lions, jackals, leopards, birds, and beasts emerging from the volcanic mountains and sporting in the water.
When one sees this, skeletons appear one by one, filling the Sahā world, each raising its right hand.
At that time, the rākṣasas, holding iron forks in their hands, lifted up the skeletal figures and piled them together in one place.
Then, there appeared nine-colored skeletal figures, arranged in successive rows, which came to where the practitioner was.
"Such are the many hundreds of thousands of objects that cannot be described in their entirety.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When this visualization is perfected, it is called the Contemplation of the Four Great Elements."
"You should receive and uphold this well; be careful not to forget or lose it.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the twelfth [stage]: the contemplation of the earth element, the contemplation of the fire element, the contemplation of the wind element, and the contemplation of the water element; it is also called the sphere of the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Once this visualization is accomplished, you should further instruct [the practitioner] to bind the mindfulness and stabilize the mind, observing intently the vertebrae within the waist, visualizing all the vertebrae as white as jade or snow."
Having seen the backbone, he sees the bones of his entire body, with each joint interlocking with the next, becoming increasingly bright and pure, white as crystal.
He sees every single bone and limb, large and small, each clearly manifest like a crystal mirror.
The fire, wind, water, and earth elements—all these objective realms appear within a single joint.
When this visualization is accomplished, one sees the ground beneath one's bed gradually opening up from below.
Having seen the ground beneath one bed, he then saw the ground beneath two beds.
Having seen the ground beneath two beds, he then saw the ground beneath three beds.
Having seen the ground beneath three beds, he gradually saw the interior of the room.
Having seen one room, he next saw two rooms.
Having seen two rooms, he gradually saw three rooms.
Having seen three rooms, he further saw the ground within a courtyard, which gradually began to open up.
When seeing this matter, one should observe it with clear attention until there is no obstruction even below.
Within the wind-circle below, various winds arise; these move toward the yakṣas, who all inhale this wind.
Having inhaled this wind, kumbhāṇḍas emerge from all the pores of the body.
Each and every kumbhāṇḍa spits forth mountain fires that fill the great trichiliocosm.
Suddenly, from among these mountains, there appeared immeasurable, exquisite women who, with drums, music, lutes, and song, approached the practitioner.
Then the rākṣasas came again and vied with one another to seize and devour them.
Having seen this, the practitioner is overcome by extreme terror that he cannot withstand.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, he constantly suffers from heart pain and feels as though his cranial bone is about to shatter.
When he collects his mind and enters absorption again, he perceives all the objective realms of the four great elements exactly as before.

Having seen this realm, by the power of the concentration of the four great elements, one sees one’s own body white as a jade figure; from every joint fire rises above and water flows below, wind issues from the ears, and stones rain from the eyes.

Having seen this, he beheld ten venomous serpents upon the ground before him; their bodies were five hundred yojanas long, and they possessed twelve hundred feet, each foot resembling that of a poisonous dragon.
Water and fire emerge from the body as it rolls upon the ground.
When this visualization is accomplished, one should wholeheartedly repent for past transgressions.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, one must not speak much; except during mealtime, one should remain in a quiet place, binding the mind with single-minded mindfulness.
Furthermore, you should perform repentance and take various medicinal ghee; only then shall you be able to change this method of contemplation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This contemplation is called the second contemplation of the four great elements.”
"You should uphold this well; be careful not to forget or lose it.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the completion of the thirteenth contemplation on the roots of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Once this visualization has been accomplished, you should change your contemplation.
As for the method of changing the contemplation: when the fire element begins to move, you should give rise to the visualization of mountains."
One should contemplate that all mountains are like ice and frost, being melted by fire.
Such a fierce fire blazes with extreme intensity.
When the fire blazes thus, the body becomes steaming hot.
Furthermore, one should again visualize a dragon causing rain to fall from stones to extinguish the fierce fire.
One should then further visualize those stones being crushed into dust.
The dragon then breathes forth wind, gathering the fine dust until it accumulates into a mountain, upon which immeasurable trees, forests, thorns, and brambles all grow spontaneously.
At that time, the white water, complete with the five colors, flowed through the midst of the thorns.
Thus these waters rested upon the mountain peaks, motionless and firm like accumulated ice.
"When this visualization has been accomplished, it is called the fourteenth method of the 'Transformation Contemplation' (*yiguan*).
The Buddha told Ānanda:

'If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who have attained right concentration (*samādhi-samāpatti*), you should teach them this method of the Transformation Contemplation; be careful not to let it be forgotten.'"
Regarding this contemplation of the four great elements, if there are those who attain it, the Buddha permits the consumption of medicinal substances such as ghee and meat.
When eating meat, one should wash it until it is tasteless and maintain the thought that it is like eating the flesh of one's own child during a time of famine:
"If I do not eat this meat now, my body will go mad and die."
"For this reason, the Buddha, while in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, commanded the bhikṣus that for the sake of practicing dhyāna, they may eat meat of three kinds that are pure.
At that time, Ānanda heard what the Buddha had said.
They joyfully received and practiced it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Once you have taught the contemplation of ease, you should further instruct them as before to bind the mindfulness and dwell the mind, observing the vertebrae of the spine with such clarity that they appear white and pure many times more than before."
Because the spaces between the joints are clear and pure, one is able to see all manner of foul and evil things.
When this visualization is accomplished, one should contemplate one's own body as a skeleton, with each joint white, pure, and brilliantly clear, like a crystal mirror.
All the skeletal figures within Jambudvīpa, as well as all the objective realms of the four great contemplations, appear within a single bone joint.
Having seen this, one sees the skeletal figures coming from the east toward the practitioner, arranged in successive rows, their number like that of motes of dust.
In this way, all the white-boned people filling the Sahā world in the eastern direction come toward the practitioner, one after another in continuous rows;
it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Furthermore, there are blue-colored skeletal figures, arranged in successive rows, approaching the practitioner until they fill Jambudvīpa.
Gradually expanding, they eventually fill the Saha world in the eastern direction;
the same occurs in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Furthermore, there are skeleton-people the color of mud, arranged in successive rows, coming toward the practitioner until they fill Jambudvīpa.
Gradually expanding, they eventually fill the Saha world in the eastern direction;
the same occurs in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Furthermore, there are skeletal figures with the color of turbid water, arranged in successive rows, approaching the practitioner until they fill Jambudvīpa.
Gradually expanding, they eventually fill the Saha world in the eastern direction;
the same occurs in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Furthermore, there are red-colored skeletal beings, arranged in successive rows, coming toward the practitioner until they fill Jambudvīpa.
Gradually expanding, they eventually fill the Saha world in the eastern direction;
the same occurs in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Furthermore, there are red-colored skeletal figures, arranged in successive rows, approaching the practitioner until they fill Jambudvīpa.
Gradually expanding, they eventually fill the Saha world in the eastern direction;
the same occurs in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Furthermore, there are skeletal figures with their bodies smeared with pus and blood, proceeding one after another in succession toward the practitioner, filling Jambudvīpa.
Gradually expanding, they eventually fill the Sahā world in the eastern direction;
the same occurs in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Furthermore, there are yellow skeletal beings, arranged in successive rows, coming toward the practitioner until they fill Jambudvīpa.
