Gradually expanding, they eventually fill the Saha world in the eastern direction;
the same occurs in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Furthermore, there are green skeletal figures, arranged in successive rows, coming toward the practitioner until they fill Jambudvīpa.
Gradually expanding, they eventually fill the Saha world in the eastern direction;
the same occurs in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Furthermore, there are purple-colored skeletal beings, arranged in successive rows, approaching the practitioner until they fill Jambudvīpa.
Gradually expanding, they eventually fill the Saha world in the eastern direction;
the same occurs in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

Furthermore, there are "Narī-skull-colored bone-men" from whose joints, between every two bones, sixteen colors of foul, mixed pus flow out; proceeding in continuous rows, they come toward the practitioner and fill Jambudvīpa.
Gradually expanding, it eventually fills the Sahā world to the east;
the same occurs in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
When this visualization is accomplished, the practitioner becomes terrified, seeing various yakṣas coming to devour him.
At that time, one will further see various skeletal figures, with fire arising from every joint and flames succeeding one another, filling the entire Sahā world.
One will further see water gushing forth from the crowns of the skeletons' heads, like crystal banners.
Furthermore, one sees upon the head of the skeleton all manner of fires transforming into stone mountains.
At that time, winds issue from the ears of the various nāgas, blowing upon the fires and shaking the mountains.
At that time, all the mountains revolved and came to rest in mid-air,
like the wheel of a potter.
Yet there was no obstruction.
Having seen this, he was struck with extreme terror.
Because of his terror, one hundred million ghosts arrived at his location, carrying mountains and vomiting fire, their forms each different from the others.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there is a bhikṣu who dwells securely in right mindfulness and practices heedfulness, when he sees this matter, he should be taught the contemplation of the emptiness and selflessness of all phenomena."
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, you should likewise encourage them to go to a wise person and inquire about the profound meaning of emptiness.
Having heard the meaning of emptiness, you should observe yourself as follows:

"This body of mine arises from the impure union of father and mother; it is bound by sinews and smeared with blood, consisting of thirty-six foul and impure substances, subject to various karmic conditions, and originating from ignorance."
"Now, observing this body, not a single part is worthy of affection; it is like a decayed object.
While reflecting thus, all the skeletal figures come to press upon him. He should extend his right hand and snap his fingers at the skeletal figures, thinking:
"These skeletal figures appear through the forceful discrimination of false conceptualization."
"My own body is likewise; it is born from the four great elements and dwells together with the village of the six sense bases. How much more so these white bones, which have emerged from falsehood!
As he thought this, the white skeletal figures shattered and scattered like dust, piling up on the ground like a white snow mountain.
A great many skeletons of various colors were suddenly swallowed by a massive serpent.
Upon a mountain of white snow stood a man of white jade, his body majestic and upright, thirty-six *yojanas* in height, with a neck as red as fire.
There was a white light from the eyes.
At that time, all the white waters and crystal banners spontaneously entered the crown of the head of the white jade man.

Dragons, ghosts, snakes, vipers, monkeys, lions, raccoons, and cats were all terrified and fled; fearing the great fire, they scrambled up and down the tree, with ninety-nine snakes emerging from every pore of their bodies, all now upon the tree.
At that time, the venomous dragon coils and winds itself around the tree, and one further sees a black elephant standing beneath it.

Upon seeing these things, one should, with a profound mind, perform repentance during the six periods of the day, refrain from excessive speech, and dwell in a secluded place contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena.

Within the emptiness of all phenomena, there is no earth, no water, and no wind or fire; form is a perversion arising from illusory dharmas, while sensation is a causal condition arising from various karmas.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is a perversion; it is a non-abiding dharma.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is non-seeing; it belongs to the conditions of karma and gives rise to the seeds of craving.

Thus, one should contemplate this body in its various aspects: the earth element arises from the perception of emptiness, yet that perception of emptiness is also empty. How, then, can there be the notion of solidity regarding the earth?
When one analyzes in this way, asking "What is earth?
and having completed such contemplation, it is called the contemplation of external earth.
One contemplates each instance of the earth element with precision, seeing that it has no master.

When one forms this perception, one sees that the mountain of white bones further crumbles and disintegrates like fine dust, with only the skeletal person remaining amidst the dust, sustained by various white lights that connect and support one another.
From within the white light, various four-colored radiances further arise; from within these radiances, fierce fires further erupt, burning the yakṣas.

At that time, driven by the fire, all the yakṣas flee up into the trees; before they reach the tops of the trees, black elephants trample them, and the yakṣas emit fire to burn the feet of the black elephants.

At that time, the black elephant let out a roar like the cry of a lion, proclaiming suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and further declaring that this body is subject to decay and shall soon perish.

Having spoken thus, the black elephant engaged in battle with the yakṣa; the yakṣa pierced the black elephant’s heart with a great iron trident, and the black elephant roared again, causing the entire earth to tremble, at which time the roots, trunks, branches, and leaves of the great trees all shook simultaneously.
The dragon also spat forth fire, wishing to burn this tree; the various snakes, startled and bristling with agitation, each extended their ninety-nine heads to protect it.
At that moment, the yakṣa rose up in further alarm, grasping a great rock in his hand, intending to hurl it at the black elephant.
The black elephant immediately stepped forward and took up the stone with its trunk, tossing it onto the tree.
When the stone reached the top of the tree, it resembled a mountain of blades.
Thereupon, the yakṣa leaped upward with great force, and from all the pores of his body, various venomous dragons emerged.
The dragon has four heads, spewing forth smoke and flames that are most terrifying.

When this visualization is accomplished, one sees one's own body; within the heart-center of the body, there is a depth like a pit or well, and within this well is a snake emitting venom that appears rising and falling above the well.
There was a maṇi jewel suspended in the air, fastened by fourteen threads.

At that time, a venomous snake looked up with its mouth agape to suck the jewel, but it could not obtain it at all; losing its grip, it fell to the ground, fainting and unconscious, whereupon the fire from its mouth returned into the crown of its head.
If the practitioner sees these things, they should give rise to repentance.
They should beg for food that is pleasing to the mind to harmonize the four great elements, making them as peaceful and secure as possible.
They should sit in a secluded room where there is no sound of birds or sparrows.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās attain this contemplation, it is called attaining the contemplation of the earth element."
You should diligently maintain mindfulness and be careful not to be indolent.
If you practice non-indolence, you shall swiftly attain the "Summit Dharma" (mūrdha-dharma), faster than the flow of water.

Even if you are lazy, you will already have abandoned the realms of the three miserable paths; after casting off this body in another life, you will be born in Tuṣita Heaven, where you will meet Maitreya, who will preach for you the teachings on suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and so forth, until your mind is suddenly and clearly enlightened.
"He has attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You must now carefully receive this method of meditating on the element of earth; be cautious not to forget it, and expound and explain it extensively for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

One who attains this contemplation is said to have completed the Fourteenth Stage, the Great Contemplation; it is also called the Differentiation of the Characteristics of the Four Great Elements, and further named the Vision of the Coarse Characteristics of the Five Aggregates.
One who possesses wisdom can also know for themselves the extent of their fetters and afflictions.
Within the four foundations of mindfulness, this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body; at this stage, one perceives only the exterior of the body and has not yet seen its interior.
Among the four divisions of the objective sphere of the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), this is the first.
One who attains this contemplation experiences joy and happiness in body and mind, and has little contention or dispute.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Once this visualization is accomplished, you should next further contemplate the fire outside the body, which exists due to causes and conditions; it arises when there are conditions and ceases when the conditions depart.”
Regarding these various fires, they come from nowhere and go nowhere; appearing and vanishing in a flash, they never remain for even a moment.
While he was reflecting in this way, the external fires were immediately extinguished and did not appear again.
Furthermore, one should reflect:
"All external waters, such as rivers, streams, ponds, and flows, are produced through the transformative power of dragons; how is it that I now perceive these waters erroneously?"
"These waters come from nowhere when they arrive, and go nowhere when they depart.
While contemplating in this way, external water no longer appears.
One should then further give rise to this thought:
"This wind merges with empty space, and the various dragons roar; it exists only through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
One who conceives such an idea does not find it within, nor without, nor in between; it is due to a perverted mind that this phenomenon is seen erroneously."
While contemplating in this manner, the external winds do not arise.

One should further fix the mind and contemplate the spinal bones within the body, seeing the bones inside the body as white as jade or snow; within each and every joint, the thirty-six kinds of foul and impure substances all appear therein.

Or one may see the skin of the body like a leather bag filled with various impurities; within it are immeasurable carbuncles and hundreds of thousands of boils, from which pus flows out in an unceasing drip, resting upon the head of a skeletal figure—truly a sight most loathsome and distressing.
Alternatively, one may see within the body all five viscera running entirely into the large intestine, which becomes bloated, putrid, and festering beyond endurance.

At that time, by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whether emerging from or entering into samādhi, the practitioner sees all people and their own bodies as nothing but a mass of impurities. Seeing the bodies of women as filthy and impure, like those of worms or dogs, they will naturally attain freedom from thoughts of craving for form.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the fourteenth contemplation of the external four great elements, and it is also called 'gradually understanding the training in contemplating emptiness.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Hold fast to the Buddha’s words; be careful not to forget or lose them.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, joyfully received and practiced it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Once this visualization is accomplished, you should further be instructed to fix the mind and clearly contemplate the earth element within the body.

As for the earth element within the body, it consists of the bones, teeth, nails, hair, intestines, stomach, abdomen, liver, heart, lungs, and all other solid substances; these are all formed from the refined essence of the earth element, whereas external earth is impermanent.”

The reason we know this is as follows: for example, when two suns appear, the great earth becomes parched and withered; when three suns appear, the rivers, streams, ponds, and marshes all dry up completely; when four suns appear, two-thirds of the great ocean is diminished; when five suns appear, the great ocean is entirely exhausted; when six suns appear, flames rise from the great earth; and when seven suns appear, the great earth is consumed by fire.
If even external objects are thus, their power cannot endure for long; how much less, then, can the internal parts of the body be firm?
At that time, the practitioner should reflect to himself:
"Now, as for this body of mine, is the hair 'I'?"
Are the nails me?
Are the bones me?
Are the various five viscera of the body me?
"In this way, he observes that among all the limbs and joints of the body, there is absolutely no self.
Observing his own bones, he contemplates each one with precision:
'From where did these bones arise?'"

When the red and white essences of the parents unite—whether at the stage of milk, or the stage of a bubble, or likewise at the stage of the kalala, or the stage of the arbuda—at none of these stages is there any bone to be found anywhere.
One should know that these bones originally did not exist but now exist, and having existed, they will again cease to be.
These bones share the same characteristics as empty space.
Just as external earth is impermanent, so too is internal earth.
While reflecting thus, he carefully observed his own body; all the bones naturally shattered and dispersed like fine dust.
Entering meditative concentration to observe the bones, he saw only the locations where the bones had been, but no longer perceived the characteristics of the bones themselves.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, one sees that the body is no different than before.
One should then further contemplate the various fires within the body as originating from external fire.
External fire is impermanent; it does not remain still for even a moment.
"Why does the fire of my body remain hot for so long?
When one contemplates in this way, all the flames upon the bones are seen to be extinguished and no longer appear.
One should then further contemplate the various waters within the body, reflecting: "These waters of mine exist because of external water."
External water is impermanent; its force cannot be sustained for long. Internal water is likewise:
it exists only through the conjunction of conditions. Where, then, is there actual water or a collection of impurities?
External wind is impermanent; its force cannot be sustained for long; it arises from causes and conditions and likewise perishes due to conditions.
All the winds within my body now are but a false and artificial combination, forcibly constituting a mechanical apparatus; where, then, is there any wind?
They arise from deluded thoughts; this is a perverted view.
While reflecting in this way, he did not perceive the various nāgas within his body, and all the winds within his ears were extinguished and no longer appeared.
Thus, through various forms of careful self-reflection, he considered: "Wherein are there persons, or earth, water, fire, and wind?"
One contemplates this earth as a phenomenon subject to decay; one contemplates this fire as being like an illusion.
Furthermore, one contemplates this wind as arising from inversion, and contemplates this water as appearing from false conceptualization.

When practicing this contemplation, the practitioner sees the body as being like a plantain tree, devoid of any solid core within; or they see their own mind as being like a bubble upon the water, and hear external sounds as being like echoes from a valley.
When practicing this contemplation, one sees all flames upon the bones, sees white water, and sees all dragons and winds gathered together in one place.
One contemplates the body as tranquil and still, no longer perceiving its physical characteristics; body and mind become secure and at ease, filled with profound serenity and joy.
"This state is called the completion of the fifteenth contemplation on the four great elements.

The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"You must now receive and uphold this method of contemplation on the four elements with a sincere heart; be careful not to forget it, and you shall extensively expound it for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

"When performing this contemplation, because one is training in the contemplation of emptiness, the body becomes depleted and the mind exhausted; one should therefore consume ghee and various restorative medicines, and within deep meditative concentration, one should perform the contemplation on restoration."

Regarding the contemplation of the supplementary visualization: first, one contemplates one's own body, visualizing it as layers of skin enveloping one another like a plantain tree; then, settling the mind, one performs the visualization of opening the crown of the head.
Furthermore, one should exhort Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protecting devas to take golden vases filled with celestial medicine.
With Śakra-devānām-indra on the left and the world-protecting devas on the right, they shall pour the celestial medicine over his head until his entire body is completely saturated.
Day and night, during the six periods, one should constantly maintain this visualization.

When emerging from meditative absorption, one seeks various restorative tonics and consumes excellent food; thus, one remains perpetually seated in tranquility, with joy exceeding that of ordinary times.
After practicing this *pūṣan-sūtra* for three months, he then further contemplates other objects of focus.
By the power of his concentration in dhyāna, the various devas rejoice.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra expounds to him the profound Dharma of emptiness and non-self, praises the practitioner, and pays homage with his head at [the practitioner's] feet.
Because he has taken celestial medicine, when he emerges from meditative absorption, his countenance is harmonious and joyful, and his body is moist and lustrous as if anointed with oil.
One who perceives this phenomenon is said to have completed the sixteenth visualization on the four great elements.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Once this visualization is accomplished, you should further instruct him to bind his mindfulness and fix his mind, causing him to contemplate external forms:
'From what source do all forms arise?'"
When performing this visualization, one sees the five external colors like five-colored lights encircling one’s own body.
When this mental image appears, one observes one's own chest; the bones of the chest gradually become clear and pure like a crystal mirror, vivid and lovely.
Furthermore, one sees external forms, each and every form as bright as sunlight.
When this contemplation is attained, four black elephants naturally appear from the four directions; these black elephants roar loudly and trample the various forms until they are extinguished.
Thus, these various colors that were upon the ground vanished;
yet in the void above, the dark and yellow hues became lovely, surpassing the ordinary by many times.
At that time, the great elephant wound its trunk around the tree, and the four elephants from the four sides attempted to uproot it, but they could not move it even slightly.
Furthermore, there were four elephants that coiled their trunks around the tree, yet they could not move it either.

When the practitioner has seen these things and emerges from meditative absorption, he should go to a quiet place—whether among burial mounds, beneath a tree, or in a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka)—and cover his body so as to remain secluded.
One should remain in tranquility and further seek excellent medicine to restore one's own body.

Having practiced the aforementioned method for restoring the body for another three months, one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence, as if putting out a fire on one's head, without any negligence of mind.
One should not give rise to thoughts of transgression regarding the precepts one has received, and should repent of all sins during the six periods of day and night.
Furthermore, one should contemplate that the body is selfless and empty, observing each of the aforementioned objects with clear mindfulness until they are thoroughly understood.
When this visualization is accomplished, the sternum gradually becomes luminous, like a divine pearl transparent both inside and out.

Within the heart, the poisonous snake again leaps upward, rising and remaining suspended in mid-air; fire issues from its mouth as it seeks to suck up the maṇi-jewel, yet it is utterly unable to do so.
As before, having lost his way and abandoned his course, he threw himself to the ground; his body and mind were dazed and distressed as he gazed toward the four quarters.
At that time, the elephants again rushed forward in competition to reach the place where the tree stood.
At that time, the yakṣas, rākṣasas, predatory beasts, nāgas, and serpents all simultaneously spat forth venom to battle the black elephant.
Then, the black elephant wound its trunk around the tree and pulled it with a roar.
When the elephant pulled at the tree, various nāgas and yakṣas spat forth poison and fought in front of it, refusing to rest.
At that time, there was a lion beneath the earth whose two eyes were as brilliant as vajras; suddenly leaping up, he fought with the nāgas, whereupon the nāgas surged upward and stayed in mid-air.
Because the elephant continues to pull at the tree without ceasing, the earth gradually begins to shake.
At that time, when the practitioner observes the shaking of the earth, they should contemplate that this earth exists only from emptiness and is not a solid or substantial reality.
This stage is like a city of the gandharvas or like a mirage; arising from falsehood, by what cause could it move?

While contemplating in this way, one sees one’s own body—from the breastbone down to the facial bones—gradually becoming clear and pure, and perceives all that exists in the world with complete clarity.
When this contemplation is attained, it is like holding a bright mirror and observing the reflection of one's own face.
At that time, the practitioner sees all external forms and various impurities, as well as all the internal impurities within the body.
"When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the seventeenth contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You should well receive and uphold these consecrated verses on the foundation of mindfulness of the body; be careful not to forget them. Open the Dharma-gate of the Ambrosia and extensively expound them for all sentient beings of future ages."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Once this visualization has been perfected, you should further instruct [the practitioner] to bind the mind in contemplation and carefully observe the facial bones."
He sees the bones of his own face as being like a mirror of white jade, pure both inside and out, as clear as a bright mirror.
Gradually expanding, he sees the bones of his entire body as white as crystal mirrors, pure both inside and out, with all manner of forms appearing within them.
In an instant, one sees the body like a person made of white jade; then one sees it as clear and transparent as lapis lazuli, empty both inside and out, with all manner of colors appearing within it.

Again, he sees his own body as a person of white silver, with only a thin layer of skin remaining; this skin is exceedingly delicate and fine, thinner than heavenly *karpāsa* cloth, transparent both inside and out.
Again, he sees his own body like a person made of Jāmbūnada gold, empty both within and without.
Again, he sees his own body like a person made of vajra.
When he sees this ground, black elephants become twice as numerous; they coil their trunks around the tree, yet even exerting all their strength, they cannot cause it to move.
At that time, the roar of the multitude of elephants was fierce and thunderous, shaking the great earth.
When the great earth shook, a diamond mountain emerged from the ground below and stood before the practitioner.

At that time, the practitioner sees that the four sides are surrounded by vajra mountains; he further sees that the ground before him is like vajra; he further sees various nāgas moving up and down the trees, spitting vajra-beads, whereby the tree becomes so firm and solid that the elephant cannot move it.

Only water of five colors issued forth from the trees, flowing upward along the branches, descending from the treetops through the interstices of the leaves down to the trunks, and also flowing among the Vajra Mountains; it spread and overflowed, filling the great earth, the subterranean realm beneath the Vajra Mountains, and extending even to the Vajra Mountains themselves.
These five-colored waters emit five-colored rays of light, which move up and down in an unstable and impermanent manner.
At that time, a black elephant emerges from the Vajra Mountains, desiring to suck up this water.
The dragons spat poison as they fought with the great elephants.
At that time, the snakes entered the ears of the dragons and, exerting their strength together, joined them in the battle against the black elephant.
Then the black elephant used all its might to kick and lash, yet it could do nothing at all.
When seeing this scene, the radiance of all the waters performs music; some manifest transformations resembling celestial maidens, singing and performing music that is most delightful.
This woman is so upright and beautiful that there is no one to compare her to among gods or humans; the music she performs and her exquisite voice have no equal even in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Thus, these transformed women perform various arts and skills in numbers of hundreds of millions and billions that cannot be fully described.
When you see these things, you must be careful not to follow after them; rather, you should fix your mind on the previously mentioned impurities.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, one should approach a wise person and inquire about the meaning of profound emptiness.
At that time, the wise person should explain the emptiness of non-self (*anātman-śūnyatā*) to the practitioner.

Thereupon, the practitioner should again fix their mindfulness as before and observe the bones of their own body, seeing the breastbone as luminous, pure, and beautiful, wherein all impurities appear.
Having seen these things, one should reflect within oneself: "As for me now, is the hair me?
Is the bone me?"
Are the nails the self?
Are the teeth the self?
Is form the self?
Is feeling the self?
Is perception the self?
Is consciousness the self?
Contemplate each one with discernment: Is ignorance the self?
Are volitional formations the self?
Is consciousness the self?
Is name-and-form the self?
Are the six sense bases the self?
Is contact the self?
Is feeling the self?
Is craving the self?
Is grasping the self?
Is existence my self?
Is birth my self?
Are aging and death my self?
If death were the self, then when one is devoured by worms or when the body is scattered, destroyed, and disintegrated, where would that self be?
If birth were the self, it would not abide from moment to moment; since there is no perception of permanence within this life, one should know that this life, too, is not the self.
If the head were the self, the skull consists of eight segments, each distinct from the others, and worms are born within the brain.
Observing this head, one finds that in reality there is no self.

If the eye were the self, the eye has no substantiality; it is a combination of earth and water, relying on fire for its illumination and wind for its movement. When it disperses, perishes, and decays, crows, magpies, and other birds all come to devour it, and it is gnawed and consumed by maggots and various insects.
Contemplate this eye: if the mind were the self, it would be driven by the power of the winds without a moment’s rest.
Furthermore, there are six dragons that lift up this mind; within it, there are immeasurable poisons, with the mind itself as their root.
If one investigates these various poisons as well as the nature of the mind, they all arise from emptiness; it is through deluded thought that they are named "self.

Thus, regarding all such phenomena—the earth, water, fire, and wind; form, sound, smell, taste, and touch; and the twelve links of dependent origination—if one examines each one with earnest scrutiny, where is there a self?
Contemplating that the body is without self, how could there be "what belongs to the self"?
As for what belongs to the self: is blue the self?
Is yellow the self?
"Is red the self?
Is white the self?
Is black the self?"

These five colors arise from what is lovable; they are born of attachment that follows and binds, stained by the waters of desire, produced from the river of old age and death, arisen from the thieves of affection, and originating from delusion and false views.
These various forms are truly not the self.
Deluded and attached sentient beings falsely claim them to be the self, and those with false views further refer to them as "mine.
All things are like illusions; where is there a self?
"In these illusory phenomena, how could there be anything that belongs to a self?
While reflecting thus, he saw his own body's bones as bright, pure, and lovely, and all things rare for the entire world to behold appeared within them.
Furthermore, one sees one's own body as a person made of lapis lazuli, empty both internally and externally.
It is like a person wearing a lapis lazuli banner and looking up into the sky, seeing everything clearly.
At that time, because the practitioner contemplates emptiness within his own body and outside of it, he studies the dharma of non-self.
He sees his own two feet as if they were tubes of lapis lazuli, and he also sees all those rare and wondrous things found throughout the worlds below.
When this visualization is accomplished, the ground before the practitioner becomes bright, pure, and lovely, as transparent as beryl.
Those who possess the full precepts see the ground as pure as the palace of Brahmā.
If one’s deportment is incomplete, even though one sees the pure ground, it still appears like crystal.

When this visualization is perfected, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of innumerable yakṣas and rākṣasas emerge from the earth, holding white sheep horns, tortoise shells, and white stones in their hands to strike the Vajra Mountain.
Furthermore, there were various ghosts who held iron hammers in their hands and struck the Vajra Mountains.
At that time, upon the mountains were five spirits with a thousand heads and a thousand arms, who held a thousand swords in their hands and fought against the rākṣasas.
Vicious snakes and venomous dragons all spat forth their poison to surround this mountain.
Furthermore, there were various women who sang and chanted, performing various transformations to protect and assist this mountain.
If you see these things, you should contemplate them with a single mind.
When these women appear, you should view them as being like a painted jar—a vessel filled with foul-smelling impurities—produced from falsehood; they come without cause and go nowhere.
Such an appearance as this is seen because of the karmic conditions of my evil deeds in past lives.
This woman is merely my own delusion, perceived through false vision due to the causes and conditions of craving throughout countless lifetimes.

One should, with a sincere mind, contemplate the dharma of non-self: my own body is without self, and so it is with the bodies of others; what is now perceived here belongs to various causes and conditions, and I do not seek or desire it.
I contemplate this body as impermanent and subject to decay, devoid of anything belonging to a self; where, then, is there a person or a sentient being?
Having reflected thus, I single-mindedly and attentively contemplate the dharma of emptiness and non-self.

When contemplating selflessness, four great spirits naturally arrived from the depths of the lapis lazuli ground below, carrying the Vajra Mountains; at that time, various yakṣas and rākṣasas also assisted these spirits in shattering the Vajra Mountains.
At that time, Vajra Mountain gradually crumbled away; after a long period, it was completely exhausted until only the adamantine ground remained.
Then, the elephants and the various malevolent spirits pulled at the tree with all their might, but the tree was so firm it could not be moved.
Having seen this, he rejoices even further and repents of all his transgressions.
Having repented of his transgressions, he again fixes his mindfulness as before and contemplates the person made of lapis lazuli.
Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, four lotus flowers arise in the four directions.
The flowers were golden in color, each with a thousand petals, and their pedestals were made of vajra.
Upon each was a golden image seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), complete in all physical marks and lacking nothing in its radiance;
these were situated in the east, and likewise in the south, west, and north.

Furthermore, he saw his own body made of lapis lazuli become even more brilliant and pure; it was transparent from within and without, free of all obstructions, with transformation Buddhas filling both the interior and exterior of the body.
Each of these transformation Buddhas emitted light, which was subtle and exquisite, as magnificent and majestic as ten billion suns.

Throughout the entire trichiliocosm, transformation Buddhas filled every space; each transformation Buddha possessed the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary signs, and from each mark and sign, a thousand rays of light were emitted, their brilliance as intense as the combined light of a hundred thousand suns and moons.
Between each ray of light there were countless Buddhas, which gradually increased and expanded until their number could not be known.
Between each flame, moreover, there were twice as many countless transformation-Buddhas; these transformation-Buddhas circled and turned, entering into the body of the person made of lapis lazuli.
At that time, he saw his own body like a mountain of the seven treasures, lofty and magnificent to behold; it was further adorned and radiant like Mount Sumeru composed of various jewels.
This mountain shone brilliantly upon a ground of vajra, and at that moment, the vajra ground became even more manifest, like the deep purple-blue mani-jewels of the Yāma heaven.
The body became even more radiant and pure, like the light of countless Buddhas; it transformed into a jeweled pavilion and entered the crown of the person’s head made of lapis lazuli.
Again, he saw the ground before him, within the Cakravāḍa mountains, filled with Buddhas sitting cross-legged upon lotus pedestals, both on the earth and in the sky, with no gaps between them.
Each of these emanated Buddhas fills the world with their bodies, yet these emanated Buddhas do not obstruct one another.
Furthermore, he sees that the various mountains of the Iron Ring Range are as pure as lapis lazuli, free from any perception of obstruction.
He beheld the Jambudvīpa, with its mountains, rivers, rocky cliffs, trees, and thorns—all were entirely these wondrous transformation Buddhas.
As his mind gradually expanded, he saw the trichiliocosm, including both the void and the earth, all of which were entirely subtle and wondrous Buddha-images.
At this time, the practitioner should contemplate only non-self; one must carefully refrain from giving rise to a mind that pursues the Buddha’s image.
Furthermore, one should reflect:
"I have heard the Buddha say that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess two kinds of bodies: [the Dharma-body and the form-body]."
The first is the birth-body, and the second is the dharma-body.
What I now perceive is neither the dharma-body nor the birth-body;
it is a conceptualized vision arising from delusion.
"The Buddhas do not come, nor do I go.
How is it that a Buddha-image has suddenly appeared here?
When these words are spoken, one should simply contemplate one's own body as being without self, and must carefully refrain from following after the various manifested Buddha-images.

Furthermore, one should contemplate with clarity: this body of mine was impure even in the past; from its nine orifices flows pus; it is bound by sinews and smeared with blood; it contains the raw and cooked intestines, as well as feces and urine; and within it dwell eighty thousand families of worms, each worm having eight billion smaller worms as its retinue.
"What purity could there be in such a body?
While reflecting thus, he saw his own body as being like a leather bag.

Even when emerging from meditative concentration, he saw that within his body there were no bones and that his skin was like a bag; he likewise observed the bodies of others as being like leather bags.
When seeing this matter, one should approach a wise person and inquire about the various phenomena of suffering.
Having heard the teachings on suffering, one should contemplate this body with discernment as belonging to various causes and conditions, and that it is subject to the arising of suffering.
Once born, there are sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress; separation from what is loved, and union with what is hated—such various things are the laws of suffering in this world.
Now this body of mine will soon perish; caught within the net of suffering, it belongs to the realm of birth and death.

The thieves of the "wind-swords" follow my body, and the fierce fires of the Avīci Hell shall soon incinerate me. I shall pass through and endure all manner of evil forms, such as those of camels, donkeys, pigs, dogs, and all other beasts and fowl.
Such sufferings as these are called external sufferings.

Now, within my own body, there are four great poisonous dragons and countless venomous snakes; each snake has ninety-nine heads, and rākṣasas, evil ghosts, kumbhāṇḍas, and various other malevolent spirits have gathered in my heart.

Such a body and mind are utterly impure; they are a collection of evils, the sprouts of the seeds of the three realms that do not cease. How can I now give rise to the perception of purity within this impurity?
To conceive the notion of a vajra regarding illusory objects?
To conceive the notion of a Buddha image where no Buddha exists?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the world, by their very nature and characteristics, are entirely impermanent and will soon perish.
Just as this body of mine shall perish in the space of a finger-snap, I employ these false imaginings to perceive purity within what is impure.

When I contemplate in this way, I see my own body as pure as lapis lazuli; the various characteristics of this skin-bag naturally vanish and dissolve, and I am unable to find either the body or the self.
He saw only black elephants from the four directions trampling the ground before him, so that the entire vajra-ground was completely shattered.
He saw the roots of the trees on the ground, extending even down to the subterranean realm, where the multitude of roots was so vast as to be beyond counting.
At that time, the black elephant encircled the tree with its trunk as before, while immeasurable dragons and yakṣas fought against the black elephant.
The mad elephant trampled those spirits and ghosts, who fell to the ground in a swoon.
In the sky there were many spirits and ghosts, their number being vast; holding wheel-shaped blades in their hands, they assisted the black elephant in its desire to uproot this tree.
After such a long time, a single root of the tree moved.
When this tree shakes, the practitioner will see the ground beneath his own meditation seat naturally tremble.
This shall occur daily for ninety days; at that time, he should request excellent food and various medicinal tonics.
Having replenished the body,
sit upright in tranquility once more according to the previous method.

Just as previously observed, contemplate each successive stage of the initial realm from beginning to end, repeating this process back and forth sixteen times, until it is rendered utterly clear and pure.
Once it has become clear and pure, one again fixes the mind and contemplates that the body is suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self, and that all things are likewise entirely empty.
While performing this contemplation, one observes the body but does not see a body; one observes the self but does not see a self; one observes the mind but does not see a mind.
At that moment, this great earth, its mountains, rivers, and rocky cliffs, will suddenly all vanish.

Upon emerging from meditative concentration, one will be like a person who is dazed or intoxicated; at such a time, one should with a sincere heart practice the method of repentance, prostrate, smear the ground [with incense paste], and relinquish this visualization.
At the moment of prostration, before his head had even been raised, he naturally beheld the true image of the Tathāgata, who stroked his head with his hand and praised him, saying:
"O Son of the Dharma!"
“Excellent, excellent!
You have now skillfully contemplated the empty dharmas of all Buddhas.
Because he beheld the shadow of the Buddha, his heart was filled with great joy, and he regained his composure.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with five hundred arhats, flew before him and extensively expounded the profound Dharma of emptiness.
Because he saw the five hundred śrāvaka bhikṣus, his heart was filled with great joy, and he prostrated himself with his head to the ground in repentance.
Furthermore, seeing the reflections of the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and twelve hundred and fifty śrāvakas, he then beheld the reflection of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Having seen the shadow of Śākyamuni Buddha, they further behold the shadows of the six past Buddhas.
At that time, the shadows of these Buddhas appear as clearly visible as in a crystal mirror; each extends its right hand and strokes the crown of the practitioner’s head.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, each spoke their own names. The first Buddha said: "I am Vipaśyin.
The second Buddha said:
"I am Śikhin," said the third Buddha.
"I am Viśvabhū," he continued.
The fourth Buddha said:
"I am Krakucchanda.
The fifth Buddha said:
"I am Kanakamuni," said the sixth Buddha.
"I am Kāśyapa," he said.
The seventh Buddha said:
"I am Śākyamuni Buddha; I am your preceptor.
You contemplate the dharma of emptiness, and I have come to bear witness for you."
"The six Buddha-Bhagavāns bear witness to this in their presence.
When he saw the Buddha speak these words, he saw the Buddha’s physical body with perfect clarity, and he also saw the six Buddhas with perfect clarity.

At that time, each of the seven Buddhas emitted from the white tuft between their eyebrows the light of the mark of a great man; this radiance was exceedingly magnificent, illuminating the Sahā world and the lapis lazuli body, causing both to appear clearly manifest.

At that time, when the Buddhas manifested these signs, they emitted great radiance from all the pores of their bodies; countless transformation Buddhas filled the trichiliocosm, so that both the earth and the void became entirely the color of yellow gold.

Among these World-Honored Ones, some fly through the air; some perform the eighteen transformations; some walk the path of practice; some enter profound meditative concentration; some remain in silent stillness; and some radiate great light. Only the Great Preceptor Śākyamuni Buddha expounds the Four Noble Truths for the practitioner, analyzing the meaning of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and the emptiness of all phenomena.
The six Buddhas of the past likewise analyzed the twelve links of dependent origination, or expounded upon the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, praising the noble practices.
At that time, the practitioner, seeing the Buddhas and hearing the Dharma, felt joy arise in his heart.
At that time, he reflected to himself:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess two kinds of bodies.
What I have seen now is the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya); I have not yet seen the Tathāgata’s body of liberation, knowledge, and vision—the fivefold dharma-body."
While reflecting in this way, one should further repent with earnestness and without slackening, constantly cultivating samādhi during the six periods of day and night, and should form this thought:
"This physical body is like an illusion, like a dream, like a flame, like a whirling firebrand, like a city of the gandharvas, and like an echo."
Therefore, the Buddha has said that all conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning.
Regarding all such phenomena, I shall now contemplate each one individually with focused attention until they are perfectly clear.
When he contemplates in this way, the transformation Buddhas do not appear;
if there are still some remaining, he again contemplates emptiness. Because of this contemplation of emptiness, the transformation Buddhas immediately vanish, and only the seven Buddhas remain.
At that time, the seven Buddhas, together with their assemblies of śrāvaka followers, extensively expounded for the practitioner the thirty-seven factors conducive to the noble path.
Having heard this Dharma, his body and mind were filled with joy; he then further contemplated in detail the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
While he was performing this contemplation, the mad elephant roared loudly and pulled at the tree, causing it to shake.
When the tree first began to move, he saw the entire floor of the room tremble in six ways.

Furthermore, a yakṣa pierced and killed the black elephant; many black elephants lay dead upon the ground, soon to rot and disintegrate. White pus, black pus, blue pus, yellow pus, green pus, purple pus, red pus, and crimson blood flowed out, defiling the ground.
Furthermore, dung beetles and various other insects gathered upon it; moreover, there were insects that emitted fire from their eyes, burning and killing the dung beetles.

At that time, at the edge of the adamantine ground in the lower direction, there were five adamantine wheels, and between these wheels stood five adamantine men. With their right hands they held adamantine swords and with their left hands they held adamantine maces; with the maces they struck the ground and with the swords they hacked at the tree.
When seeing this, the great earth gradually shakes; one sees the ground within the city tremble in six ways.
Having seen one city, one then sees two cities.
Gradually expanding, one sees [the vision] extend for one *yojana*.
Having seen one *yojana*, it became even more vast; he saw the entire three-thousandfold world-system trembling everywhere.

As it shook, the east surged up and the west sank down; the west surged up and the east sank down; the south surged up and the north sank down; the north surged up and the south sank down; the center surged up and the periphery sank down; and the periphery surged up and the center sank down.
When this earth shook, he saw the roots of the great tree reaching down to the adamantine foundation.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi man used a sword to cut through them, severing the tree roots.
When the roots of the tree were severed, the various nāgas and sarpas all spat forth flames that climbed up the tree.
At that time, there were also many rākṣasas who piled up firewood upon the tree.
Then the Vajra-man, using his vajra-pestle, struck the tree branch until it broke.
While striking this tree, from one blow up to eighty-four thousand blows, the branch finally broke.
At that time, fire spontaneously issued from the tip of the vajra, burning this tree until nothing remained but its heartwood.
Like a diamond drill, it extended from the summit of the triple world down to the adamantine base, remaining utterly immovable.
At that time, when the practitioner attains this contemplation, they experience peace and bliss upon emerging from meditative absorption.
Whether entering or emerging from absorption, their mind remains constantly tranquil and still, free from thoughts of sorrow or joy.
Furthermore, they apply themselves with diligent effort, never ceasing day or night.

By virtue of his diligence, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, together with the six Buddhas of the past, will appear before him and expound for him the profound samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of wishlessness, and the samādhi of non-action.
Having heard this, he rejoiced and followed the Buddha’s teaching; he contemplated the dharma of emptiness as deeply as a great flowing river, and before long he was to attain the path of Arhatship.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“This contemplation on the perception of impurity is a great ambrosia; it extinguishes lustful desire and can eliminate the mental afflictions and fetters of sentient beings.”
You should receive and uphold this well; be careful not to forget or lose it.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās hear this sublime Dharma of the ambrosial consecration, they will be able to restrain their sense faculties, focus their minds with sincerity, and contemplate the parts of the body with clear observation, so that the mind does not scatter. They shall gather their minds and cause them to abide for even a brief moment.
When such a person’s life ends, they will attain rebirth in the heavens.

Furthermore, if there is another person who follows the Buddha’s teaching and fixes their mindfulness to contemplate a single fingernail or a single toe, causing the mind to dwell in stillness, you should know that this person shall never fall into the three evil realms.
If there is another person who, binding their mindfulness, contemplates with clear vision and sees the white bones of their entire body,
this person, upon the end of life, will be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven and encounter the Bodhisattva Maitreya, who is in his final birth before Buddhahood.
Having seen those devas, he followed them and experienced their pleasures.

When Maitreya attains Buddhahood, he will be the very first to hear the Dharma, whereupon he will attain the fruit of Arhatship, possessing the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.

Furthermore, if there is anyone who contemplates this impurity until it is perfected, they will see the true image of the Buddha upon this very body, hear the Buddha preach the Dharma, and attain the exhaustion of all suffering.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, and with palms joined and kneeling on his right knee, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What is the essential core of this Dharma? How should it be upheld?
What should this Dharma be named?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This is called 'The Contemplation of the Impurity and Filth of the Body,' and it is also called 'The Contemplation that Destroys the Dharma of Self and Realizes Non-self and Emptiness.
You should receive and uphold it well; for the sake of sentient beings in the turbid and suffering world of future ages who abound in lustful desire, you should explain it in detail."

When the Buddha had spoken these words, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and countless sons of gods took celestial *mandārava* flowers, *mahā-mandārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahā-mañjūṣaka* flowers, and scattered them over the Buddha and the great assembly. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and praised him, saying:

“The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is truly rare; he is able to subdue the arrogant and heterodox Kāṭhila-Nanda, and also preaches the nectar-like medicine for sentient beings of future ages who are greedy and lustful, thereby increasing the seeds of the devas and ensuring that the Three Jewels are never severed.”
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
How wonderful it is that you have so eloquently expounded this Dharma.
The nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others likewise praised the Buddha, just as the devas had done.

Venerable Ānanda, Kāṭyāyanīputra, and the thousand bhikṣus, along with immeasurable devas and the eight classes of beings, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly; they prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.
One who attains this contemplation is said to have mastered the ten types of impurity of form, which is also called the sphere of discerning various worms.
This is the first gateway of impurity.
It comprises eighteen skillful means, and the nature of its various spheres cannot be fully described.
When entering samādhi, one shall spontaneously attain this eighteenth single-gate contemplation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that moment, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly named Śreṇika—who had long since attained mastery in profound meditative concentration, become an arhat, possessed the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and was endowed with the eight liberations—rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, knelt on his right knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata now dwells in the world, bringing benefit, peace, and security to all."

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Buddha is no longer present, if there are members of the fourfold assembly who possess karmic obstructions, and when they focus their minds, the meditative objects do not appear before them; and regarding such afflictions and all transgressions—from minor *duṣkṛta* offenses up to grave crimes—those who wish to repent, how should they eliminate these various manifestations of sin?
"If there are people who kill living beings and hold wrong views, yet wish to cultivate right mindfulness, how should they eliminate the evil afflictive hindrances of wrong views and killing?
Having spoken these words, like a great mountain collapsing, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground to worship the Buddha’s feet, and again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me, so that all sentient beings in future ages may constantly attain right mindfulness and never be separated from the worthy and holy ones."
At that time, the World-Honored One, like a compassionate father consoling his son, addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"

"You have practiced a mind of loving-kindness that arises together with compassion; you now possess great compassion and are accomplished in the untainted faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment.
Today, for the sake of all sentient beings of future ages, you ask about the method for eliminating transgressions. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately emitted light from the crown of his head.
This light was golden in color, and five hundred transformation Buddhas emerged from it; they circled the Buddha seven times, and the Jeta Grove was likewise illuminated, turning entirely golden.
Having manifested this sign, it returned and entered through the Buddha’s occipital bone.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cienanti and commanded Ānanda:
“You all should instruct those among future sentient beings who have committed many sinful deeds, so that they may eliminate their transgressions; teach them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.”
By means of mindfulness of the Buddha, one eliminates all karmic obstructions, retributive obstructions, and afflictive obstructions.

One who practices mindfulness of the Buddha should first sit upright, join the palms, close the eyes, and press the tongue against the palate; with single-minded focus, they should bind their thoughts to the Buddha, ensuring that each moment of mind flows into the next without distraction.
Once the mind is settled, one should first contemplate the image.

As for contemplating the image, one should give rise to mental visualization and observe the ground before oneself until it is utterly pure and white. One should take as the object a square area of two *zhang* in length and breadth, making it increasingly bright and clear, like a polished mirror.

Having seen the ground in front, he causes the ground on his left side to be clear and pure, the ground on his right side to be clear and pure, and the ground behind him to be clear and pure as well, making the ground in all four directions as level as the palm of a hand.
First, one should visualize each of the four directions as being two zhang square, making them extremely bright and pure.
Once the ground is thus visualized as clear, one should again collect the mind and contemplate the ground before one, forming the visualization of a lotus flower.
Its petals are a thousand in number, adorned with the seven treasures.
Furthermore, one should visualize a golden image one zhang and six chi in height, seated in the full lotus posture upon this lotus flower.
Having seen this image, one should carefully observe the *uṣṇīṣa* on its crown.
One sees that the hair of the *uṣṇīṣa* is a deep blue-black color; each strand, when extended, is thirteen feet long, and when released, it curls to the right in a graceful spiral.
There is a lapis lazuli light abiding atop his head.
In this manner, a single hair grows spiraling from each and every pore; he contemplates all eighty-four thousand hairs until they are clearly perceived.

Having seen this, one next contemplates the face of the image; the face is perfectly round like the moon on the fifteenth day, its majestic radiance becoming increasingly manifest and its features clearly defined.
Again, he contemplates the broad, level, and upright forehead, with the tuft of hair between the eyebrows (ūrṇā-kośa) as white as snow or crystal, curling gracefully to the right.
He further contemplates the image’s nose, which is like a cast gold ingot or the beak of a king of eagles, positioned at the center of the face.
Again, one contemplates the mouth of the image: the color of the lips is a beautiful red, like the *bimbara* fruit.
Next, one contemplates the teeth of the image: there are forty teeth in the mouth, square, white, even, and level.
Upon the teeth are seals, from which light issues forth like white pearls.
Between the teeth is a crimson hue, from which red light flows out.
Next, one contemplates the neck of the image, which is like a tube of lapis lazuli, manifesting a golden countenance.
Next, one contemplates the syllables "De" and "Van" on the chest of the image, making them extremely distinct among the various marks and seals; each seal emits light, complete with all five colors.
Next, one contemplates the Buddha’s image, whose arms are like the trunks of elephant kings—supple and lovely.
Next, observe the hands of the image: the ten fingers are distinct and do not overlap, each remaining in its proper place.
The hands are held with the palms slightly cupped, and fine hairs grow upon them, shining like the radiance of lapis lazuli.
The hairs all point upward, like nails of red copper, with golden color upon the nails;
the inner surface of the nails is red, like a mountain of red copper joined with purple gold.
Next, one contemplates the joined palms, which are like those of a king of geese; when extended, they appear like a net of pearls.
When he withdrew his hand, he could no longer see it.

Having contemplated the image’s hands, he next contemplated the image’s body: it sat upright and serene like a mountain of true gold, neither leaning forward nor leaning back, seated in the center with perfect composure.
Again, he contemplates the image’s calves, which are like those of a deer king—smooth, straight, and perfectly rounded.

Next, he contemplates the insteps, which are level, full, and well-proportioned; beneath the feet, the lotuses are complete with a thousand spokes, and upon the feet grow hairs like dark blue lapis lazuli, all of which point upward.
The toes are even and well-proportioned;

the color of the nails is like red copper, and at the tips of the toes there are also the marks of thousand-spoked wheels. The webbing between the toes is like woven silk, resembling the feet of a king of geese.

Such were these various matters, as well as the light from his body, the circular halo, and the light from his neck; within these lights there were emanated Buddhas, great bhikṣus, and a multitude of emanated bodhisattvas.
Thus, these manifested beings are like a whirling firebrand, chasing after the light as it spins.
Those who observe in reverse order do so from the feet up to the crown protuberance;
those who observe in the natural order do so from the crown down to the feet.
Contemplating the image in this manner, one should cause the mind to become clear and focused exclusively on a single Buddha image.
Having seen one image, one should further contemplate until two images are perceived.

When he beheld the two Buddha images, their bodies became made of lapis lazuli and emitted rays of light in myriad colors; the flames succeeded one another like a mountain of burning gold, manifesting countless transformational images.
Having seen two images, he saw three images;
having seen three images, he saw four images;
having seen four images, he saw five images.
Having seen five images, he saw up to ten images.
Having seen ten images, his mind became increasingly clear and sharp, and he saw Jambudvīpa extending as far as the four seas.

The mind of an ordinary person is narrow and cannot be made broad; if it should become expansive, one must withdraw the mind and bring it back, limiting it to within the four seas with Mount Cakravāḍa as its boundary.
He beheld within this sea countless Buddha images, their thirty-two major marks and eighty minor secondary characteristics all clearly manifest;
from each mark and characteristic issued forth infinite rays of light.
If, within the various lights, one perceives individual realms as defiled and impure, this is obtained from the retribution of past offenses.
One should further arise to sweep the stūpa and smear the ground, prepare pure tally-sticks, and with the utmost humility and submissiveness, practice various forms of repentance.

Furthermore, one should settle the mind in right mindfulness on a single point, visualizing the image as before without focusing on other matters; one should clearly contemplate the space between the eyebrows of the image.
Having contemplated the space between the eyebrows, one should then successively contemplate the remaining marks and signs, ensuring that each and every mark and excellence is made distinct.
If it is not yet clear, one should again repent and perform various arduous services; thereafter, one should collect the mind as before and contemplate the image.
One will see the bodies of the Buddhas, their colors majestic and dignified, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks, filling the four seas, all seated upon lotus flowers.
Having seen the seated image, he further reflected:

"When the World-Honored One was in the world, he carried his alms bowl and held his mendicant's staff, entering villages to beg for food and traveling everywhere to teach and transform, delivering sentient beings through merit."
"Today I see only images that sit, but do not see images that walk.
What transgression have I committed in past lives?
Having had this thought, he again repented.
Having completed the repentance, one should again concentrate the mind and fix the mindfulness upon the image as before.

While contemplating the image, one sees all the seated images rise; their massive bodies are sixteen feet tall, square and upright without leaning, and they are fully endowed with the radiance of their physical marks.

Having seen the image standing, he further saw it walking; holding its alms bowl and carrying its mendicant’s staff, its majestic deportment was composed and orderly, and the multitudes of devas and humans all surrounded it.

Furthermore, there were many images soaring through the void, emitting golden light that filled the sky, appearing like golden clouds or like mountains of gold, with peerless marks and signs of excellence.

Furthermore, he saw various forms performing the eighteen transformations in mid-air: water issued from their upper bodies while fire issued from their lower bodies; they manifested massive bodies that filled the void, and then these large bodies again appeared as small as a mustard seed; they walked on land as if on water and walked on water as if on land; in the midst of the sky, they leaped east and vanished west, leaped west and vanished east, leaped south and vanished north, leaped north and vanished south, leaped from the center and vanished at the edges, leaped from the edges and vanished at the center, leaped above and vanished below, and leaped below and vanished above; walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, they moved with sovereign ease according to their will.
Having seen this, one should further form this thought:
"While the World-Honored One was in the world, he instructed the bhikṣus to lie on their right sides.
I, too, should now observe the images lying down."
He then saw the various images folding their saṃghāṭī robes, resting their heads on their right elbows, and lying on their right sides.

Beneath their sides, golden beds spontaneously appeared, with canopies of golden-colored sandalwood and various multicolored, wondrous lotus flowers serving as bedding. Above them were jeweled curtains from which various necklaces hung down.

The Buddha emitted a great light that filled the interior of the precious canopy; it was like golden flowers and resembled the stars and moon. Immeasurable jewel-lights were like masses of clouds appearing clearly in the sky, within which manifested Buddhas filled the void.
Having seen the reclining image, one should further form this thought:

"In the past there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni; he alone taught and transformed sentient beings, dwelling in this world for forty-nine years, then entered great nirvāṇa and attained parinirvāṇa, just as when fuel is exhausted the fire is extinguished, forever extinguished without remainder."
I now contemplate with my mind; because of this conceptualizing mind, I see these many images.
These many images come from nowhere and go nowhere; they are merely seen through the deluded perceptions of my own mental conceptualization.
While he was reflecting thus, [the images] gradually vanished until all the various forms had disappeared; he saw only a single image sitting alone upon a flower pedestal in the full lotus posture.
He gazed intently at this image until the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics were all clearly manifest.
"Having seen this image, it is called the 'Method of Contemplating the Image.
The Buddha addressed Śāṇakavāsin and commanded Ānanda:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās wish to repent or wish to extinguish their transgressions, although the Buddha is no longer present, those who bind their mindfulness and contemplate the physical image with clarity will find that all evil karmic offenses are swiftly purified."
Having contemplated this image, one should further contemplate that from the navel of the image a single ray of light is emitted.
This golden light divides into five branches:
one ray illuminates the left, one illuminates the right, one illuminates the front, one illuminates the rear, and one illuminates the zenith.
These five lights, upon each and every ray, have transformation Buddhas; these Buddha-forms appear in succession, filling the entirety of space.
When seeing this sign, one must make it extremely clear and distinct.
Furthermore, he saw emanated Buddhas extending upward as far as the Brahma world, filling the trichiliocosm.
Within that trichiliocosm, he saw golden light like a mountain of purple gold, with no obstruction between its interior and exterior.
When seeing this phenomenon, the mind and heart feel joyful, and the image sitting before one appears like the true likeness of the Buddha.
Having seen the Buddha’s likeness, one should further reflect:
"This is merely a reflection."
"The World-Honored One possesses sovereign power and wisdom; it is he who has manifested this deed.
I should now contemplate the true Buddha with focused attention.
At that moment, he beheld the Buddha’s body as subtle and exquisite as pure lapis lazuli, with a diamond core within.
Within the vajra, there is purple-gold light that mutually reflects and illuminates one another, forming the various marks and signs of excellence.
The thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs are like the impressions of a seal, vividly manifest, subtle, wondrous, pure, and beyond full description.

Holding a *kamaṇḍalu* in his hand, he stands poised in mid-air; within the vessel is water resembling nectar, its five colors and five radiances pure and clear, like a beryl bead, soft, fine, and smooth, which pours over the practitioner’s crown and fills his entire body.
He perceives within his own body that wherever it is touched by water, eighty families of worms gradually wither and fall away.
Once the worms have withered, his body becomes supple and his mind is filled with joy.
One should reflect to oneself:
"The Tathāgata, my compassionate father, has sprinkled the supreme flavor of the nectar of this Dharma-water upon the crown of my head.
This rite of consecration is certainly not in vain."
At that time, one should further give rise to this thought:
"May the World-Honored One please preach the Dharma for me.
Those whose karmic offenses have been eliminated will hear the Buddha preach the Dharma.

When the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he teaches the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, and the five powers; he teaches the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path. These thirty-seven factors of enlightenment he explains to the practitioner by distinguishing each one individually.
Having taught this Dharma, he further instructed him to contemplate suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.

Having been taught this Dharma, because he had seen the Buddha and heard the sublime Dharma, his mind was opened and liberated like water following its current; before long, he also attained the path of Arhatship.
Those whose karmic obstructions are heavy see the Buddha move his mouth but do not hear him preach the Dharma, just as a deaf person has nothing to hear or know.
At that time, they should further practice repentance.

Having finished the confession, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and wept before the Buddha; after spending a long time cultivating various meritorious deeds, they were finally able to hear the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
Although he heard the Dharma being preached, he did not understand its meaning.

Furthermore, he saw the World-Honored One pour water from his ritual pitcher onto the practitioner’s head; the color of the water transformed, becoming the color of pure vajra as it entered through the crown of the head. Its colors were each distinct—blue, yellow, red, and white—and various impure and mixed appearances also manifested within it.
The water entered through the crown of the head, passed straight down through the body, and emerged from the heels, flowing into the earth.
At that moment, the earth transformed into light about one zhang in size, which entered deep into the ground, gradually descending until it reached the limits of the waters.
Having reached the edge of the water, one should again direct the mind to follow this light as it departs.
One should further observe this water; beneath the water is pure emptiness.

One should further observe that beneath the emptiness is a ground of deep blue lapis lazuli; beneath the lapis lazuli ground is a golden ground; beneath the golden ground is a diamond ground; and beneath the diamond ground, one again perceives empty space.
Behold this space; it is a vast, open void, entirely devoid of anything whatsoever.
Having seen this, once again withdraw the mind and, as before, contemplate a single Buddha image.

At that time, the light of that Buddha becomes even more manifest beyond full description; furthermore, he takes water from his ritual pitcher and pours it over the practitioner’s head, and the appearance of the water and its light are also as described above.
"Recite this seven times.
The Buddha told Xuan Nanti:

"This is called the Samādhi of Contemplating the Image; it is also called the Concentration of Mindfulness of the Buddha, and further named the Eradication of Karmic Offenses, and next, the Salvation of Those Who Have Broken the Precepts."
"May those who have violated the prohibitions and precepts not lose their meditative concentration.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should carefully receive and uphold this method of the empowerment of the Buddha-contemplation samādhi, and you shall extensively explain it for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the Venerable Cāndanā, along with the assembly of devas and the one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all said:
"Today the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has taught the Dharma for the removal of transgressions for the sake of those among sentient beings whose minds are greatly distracted."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will further open the gate of the Deathless (amṛta), so that all sentient beings may attain the path to Nirvana after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Upon hearing the Buddha speak of this Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, the bhikṣu Dhyānabhadra rejoiced in body and mind; at that very moment, he attained immeasurable gates of samādhi, his mind was suddenly enlightened, and he became an Arhat, fully endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge (vidyā) and the six higher powers (abhijñā).
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the Nineteenth Meditation on the Buddha Samādhi, and it is also called the Empowerment Method (Abhiṣeka-dharma).
You should receive and uphold it well; be careful not to forget or lose it, and explain it in detail for all sentient beings of future ages."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the assembly of bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

“Those whose lust is excessive, even if they attain this samādhi of contemplating the Buddha, it will be of no benefit to them; they will be unable to obtain the fruits of the path of the noble ones.”
Next, one should further be instructed to observe one’s own body, causing it to become a skeleton according to the previous method, making it brilliantly white like the Snowy Mountains.

One should then fix the mindfulness and dwell the mind within the navel or the waist, following the inhalation and exhalation of the breath. Count one and follow one; or count two and follow three; or count three and follow four; or count four and follow five; or count five and follow six; or count six and follow seven; or count seven and follow eight; or count eight and follow nine; or count nine and follow ten. When the cycle ends, begin again. Following the breath as it goes out and comes in up to ten, one then abandons the counting and ceases.
At that time, the mind and mental factors become tranquil and unconditioned; one perceives one's own skin as being like a polished leather bag.
Having seen this, one no longer sees the bones of the body and is unaware of the location of the mind.
At that time, one should further be instructed to give rise to a visualization, causing the mind, body, and limbs within the body to appear like a person made of white jade.
Having seen this, one should again fix the mindfulness upon the great joint of the spinal vertebrae at the waist, ensuring that the mind does not become distracted.
At that time, one will naturally see a luminous mark appear upon one's body, about the size of a coin; it gradually expands until it is as large as a makara fish, gathering like clouds all around.
It further resembles white clouds; within these white clouds there is white radiance like a crystal mirror, which gradually intensifies until the entire body is clearly manifest.
Furthermore, there is white light, perfectly round and even like a chariot wheel, luminous both inside and out, its brilliance surpassing that of the sun.

When seeing this phenomenon, once again as before, one counts one and follows one; or counts two and follows three; or counts three and follows four; or counts four and follows five; or counts five and follows six; or counts six and follows seven; or counts seven and follows eight; or counts eight and follows nine; or counts nine and follows ten. Whether single or double, long or short, it is according to one's preference.
Thus, one should fix the mindfulness upon this secret place so that the mind does not scatter.
One should further fix the mindfulness and, as before, again observe the great joint at the waist.

When observing the great joint, with the concentrated mind unmoving, one again sees one's own body become even more radiant and magnificent, several times superior to before, appearing about the size of a large coin.
Doubly increasing his diligence, he then perceives again that the radiance of his body increases twofold, like the opening of a water jar; no worldly luminous object can serve as a simile for it.
Having seen this light, he redoubles his diligent application with a mind that does not slacken or retreat, and he further perceives this light appearing before his chest like a bright mirror.
