Upon seeing this light, one should apply oneself with diligent effort as if extinguishing a fire on one's head, persevering without ceasing; thereupon, one will see this light become even more intense and flourishing, such that the precious jewels of the devas cannot serve as a comparison.

It was pure and clear, free from all blemishes and impurities, and possessed seven kinds of colored light; these lights, the colors of the seven precious gems, issued from his chest and entered into the radiance.
When this sign appeared, he experienced great joy and spontaneous delight, his mind becoming exceedingly peaceful and serene, beyond all comparison.

Furthermore, with even more diligent effort and an undaunted mind, they see light like clouds encircling their bodies seven times; each individual ray of light transforms into a circle of light, and within these circles of light, they naturally behold the fundamental characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination.

If one is not diligent but is instead indolent and lazy, and violates even minor precepts down to the level of a *duṣkṛta* offense, then upon seeing this light it appears black like a wall, or one sees this light as resembling ash and charcoal, or again, one sees this light as similar to a worn-out, tattered rag. Because the mind is unrestrained and treats minor offenses lightly, it obstructs the noble, untainted radiance of the sages.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“This Dharma-gate of the Empowerment of the Contemplation of Impurity has been commanded by all the noble sages to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās: if there are those who wish to cultivate the dharmas of the noble sages, they should contemplate all dharmas as suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self, according to their causes and conditions. Just as one learns to count the breaths so that the mind does not become distracted, they should diligently uphold the precepts and maintain single-minded concentration. Regarding even minor transgressions, they should give rise to earnest shame and remorse, and perform repentance; they must be careful never to conceal even a minor offense.”
If one conceals a transgression, one will see all luminous phenomena as like rotten wood.

Upon seeing this, one immediately realizes that one has violated the precepts; thereafter, filled with shame and remorse, one should repent and reproach oneself. One should sweep the stūpas, smear the ground [with cow dung], and perform various menial labors. Furthermore, one should provide offerings and show reverence to one’s teachers and parents, regarding them as if they were the Buddha and generating the utmost respect. Moreover, one should seek from one’s teachers and parents a great vow, speaking thus: "I now make offerings to my teachers and parents."
"By this merit, may I always attain liberation in every lifetime.

Having thus cultivated merit with a sense of shame and remorse, he again practices counting the breaths as before, and once more beholds this light appearing lovely and beautiful, no different from what was seen previously.
Furthermore, one should again fix the mind and attentively observe the great joint at the waist, maintaining a state of mental stability and composure without any distraction.
Should the mind become disturbed, one must reproach oneself, feel shame, and perform repentance.

Having already performed the confession, one again sees light from the navel, complete with seven colors like the seven treasures; one should cause this light to merge into a single ray, pure white and lovely.
Having seen this, one should again be instructed as before to bind the mindfulness and contemplate, observing the white-boned person as white as jade or snow.

Once the white-boned person has been seen, one should further be instructed to bind the mindfulness and fix the mind upon the crown of the bone-person’s head. One sees the crown of the bone-person’s head naturally emitting light; the light is intensely brilliant, resembling the color of fire, and its length, shortness, thickness, and fineness are exactly equal to a spear. From the top of the head it hangs downward in reverse, entering into the skull and exiting through the skull; it enters the neck bone and exits the neck bone; it enters the chest bone and exits the chest bone; it returns to enter the navel and exits from the navel; it then enters the great joint of the spinal column, and once it has entered the great joint, the radiance immediately ceases.

When that radiance had vanished, there immediately appeared at that moment a great cloud of natural light, adorned with various jewels, pure with precious flowers, and of the most excellent color. Within it was a Buddha named Śākyamuni, fully endowed with radiant marks, possessing the thirty-two primary characteristics and the eighty secondary signs of excellence.
From each of his primary and secondary marks, a thousand rays of light are emitted; these lights are so intensely brilliant that they are like the blazing, scorching radiance of ten billion suns.
That Buddha also preaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; the radiant signs of light remain vividly before the practitioner, who then touches the practitioner’s head with his hand.
The transformation Buddha further instructed him, saying:

"In your previous lives, due to the causes and conditions of greed, anger, and delusion, you pursued all manner of evils; because you were shrouded by ignorance, this caused you to undergo the body of birth and death life after life."
"You should now observe the various withered and decayed things within your own body, and how all external fires undergo transformation and extinction.
Having spoken these words, he again instructed him as before in the method of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), observing that all the worms within the body wither and fall away.
Having seen this, one should again give rise to fire to burn and kill the insects.
When the insects do not die, one further sees one's own body as being like white crystal, naturally pure white.

Having seen the white bones, light issues forth from the head; the light is as large and thick as a spear, extending fifteen feet in length. One should then form the thought to cause the head to turn backward, and further apply the mind to cause the head to turn backward, so that the entire body is overturned, with the head resting against the spine at the great joint opposite the navel.
Having seen this, one should further observe with clear attention so that the white-boned person becomes the same color as the light.
Once they have become the same color, one sees various colored fruits at the tips of the light.
Having seen these fruits, he further saw various rays of light emanating from the crowns of the fruits.
There was white light, its brilliance so intense it resembled white jewel-clouds.
These skeletons were of a brilliant white, indistinguishable from the light itself.

Furthermore, one sees various bones broken and fallen; some have their heads fallen to the ground, some have their skeletal joints scattered in every direction, and some appear as entire skeletons of white bone, like heavy snow driven by a fierce wind, gathering and dispersing without fixed order, or like a flash of lightning that appears and vanishes the moment it is seen.
These skeletons fall to the ground and form a heap like a mound, resembling a pile of decayed wood shavings gathered in one place.

The practitioner observes for himself that from atop this mound, a natural vapor emerges and reaches into space; it is like smoke or clouds, its color a brilliant white, filling the entirety of space.
They swirl and revolve to the right, then gather back together and merge into a single place.
When seeing this phenomenon, one should further be instructed to visualize a skeleton.

One sees that this skeletal body has nine colors, with nine distinct lines clearly defined; within each line, there is a skeletal figure of nine colors, their brilliance so vivid it cannot be fully described.
Each individual skeleton should further be made to have its body fully complete, appearing clearly within the previously visualized skeletons without causing any obstruction.
Having performed this contemplation, one should then further contemplate each and every form as being like lapis lazuli, free from all obstructions.
Within that form, there are ninety-nine forms; within each of these forms, there are again nine forms of numerous skeletal beings.
These skeletal beings possess various characteristics and differing natures, yet they do not obstruct one another.
Having seen this, one should apply diligent effort to extinguish all evils.
Having seen this, the previously gathered clouds of light, resembling unbaked earthen vessels, enter his body, entering through the navel.
Having entered the navel, it enters the spinal column.
Having entered the spinal column, one perceives one’s own body as no different from its original state, restored exactly as before.
Whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, because of the practice of counting the breaths, one constantly perceives these aforementioned phenomena.

When seeing this phenomenon, one should further be taught to bring the mind back and fix the attention within the light at the original navel, not allowing the mind to scatter; at that time, the mind and spirit will become exceedingly peaceful and secure.

Once they have attained peace and security, they should further train themselves to discern with precision the various noble liberations; at that time, they will again see the seven Buddhas of the past preaching the Dharma for them.
The teacher of the Dharma expounds the Four Noble Truths and explains that the five aggregates of clinging are empty, devoid of self, and devoid of what belongs to a self.

At that time, the Buddhas and the various worthy sages constantly appear before the practitioner, teaching them various dharmas, and also instructing them in the contemplation of the samādhis of emptiness, non-self, wishlessness, and signlessness, saying:
"O Son of the Dharma!..."

You should now carefully contemplate that forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles are all impermanent and cannot endure for long; they are as fleeting as lightning, vanishing in an instant, and are likewise like illusions, like a mirage, like a heat haze, like a city of the Gandharvas, like what is seen in a dream which one knows not where it has gone upon waking, like light seen when striking a stone that vanishes in a moment, like the track of a bird flying through the sky which cannot be traced, and like an echo that has no corresponding source.
"You should now also contemplate in this way: the three realms are like illusions and like magical transformations.
Thereupon, you will see that everything within and without the body is empty and non-existent; like a bird flying through the sky with no place of reliance, the mind transcends the three realms.
He contemplates that all worlds, including Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans, do not endure for long and are like illusions or transformations.
He then observes his own body and does not perceive its physical form, whereupon he reflects:
"The world is impermanent; the three realms are unstable; everything is empty."
Where is there a self?

As for these forms and desires encountered by the eye, and these women, they arise from inversion; one mistakenly perceives them as lovely, yet in reality, they are phenomena subject to swift decay and destruction.
Now, female beauty is like shackles and fetters that exhaust the consciousness and spirit of men.
Foolish people are attached to it, never knowing contentment and unable to extricate themselves; thus they cannot escape their manacles and chains, nor can they sever their bonds.

Once the practitioner has recognized the characteristics of phenomena and understood that phenomena are empty and quiescent, these various forms and desires are like hostile bandits—how could one cherish them?
Furthermore, they are like a prison, solid and dense, difficult to abandon.

I now contemplate emptiness and feel weary detachment from the three realms. I observe that the world is like a bubble upon the water, perishing in an instant, and my mind is free from all discursive thoughts.

I have realized that worldly phenomena are heavy afflictions and burdens; ordinary people are deluded, failing to awaken until death, unaware that amidst manifold sufferings they are attached to things from which it is difficult to escape, indulging their passions in wild confusion without limit.
I now observe this delusive female form; it is like an echo in response to a call, or like a reflection in a mirror, impossible to find when sought.
Where, then, does this female form reside?
False views bring about ruin and harm, deceiving all ordinary people; the damage they inflict is immense.
Now, observe this form: it is like wildflowers that scatter with the wind, emerging from nowhere and going nowhere; it is an illusion without substance, yet the foolish delight in and cling to it.
Now, observing this form, it is entirely impermanent, like a leper who has been cured by a skilled physician.
I now contemplate suffering, emptiness, and impermanence; I see that these marks of form are all devoid of solidity or substance.

I contemplate all ordinary beings with profound pity; they are attached to this form, honoring and cherishing it without weariness, indulging in delusion and obsession with endless craving for its pleasures. They have become slaves to their own attachments, pierced by the spears of desire that penetrate to the very marrow of their bones, and bound by the shackles and fetters of affection.
Having reflected thus, he further contemplates that all things are entirely empty and quiescent.
These various lusts and all manifestations of passion arise from the five aggregates and the four great elements.
The five aggregates have no master and the four elements have no self; since both their nature and characteristics are empty, by what means could they exist?

When one contemplates in this way, wisdom becomes manifest. One perceives the body as brilliantly luminous like a mani jewel, free from all obstruction, resembling the pure, clear blue-white luster of diamond essence. It is like a deer breaking through an enclosure and escaping the suffering of being harmed by a hunter.

Contemplating the nature and characteristics of the five aggregates as all pure, and contemplating the six elements as like a bird soaring high with no place for its body to rest; having swallowed the hook of form and attained liberation through rising and falling, one leaves behind all female forms without further giving rise to passion, naturally transcending the ocean of lustful desires.
All fetters and latent tendencies are like a multitude of fish running and chasing one another, falling into a pit of darkness.
Ignorance and old age and death are consumed by the fire of wisdom.

"Contemplate form as defiled, loathsome, foul, and impure; it is like a deceptive illusion that does not remain for even a moment. Thus one should forever be free from the taint of form and not be bound by form.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who have much greed and lust, first instruct them to contemplate the Buddha so that they may leave behind all transgressions; only then should you further instruct them to fix their mindfulness so that the mind does not scatter."
To keep the mind from scattering is what is called counting the breaths.

This method of counting the breaths is the medicine for lustful desire; it is the sphere of practice of the Unsurpassed Dharma King. You should receive and uphold it well; be careful not to forget or lose it.
"When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the completion of the twentieth stage of the mindfulness of breathing.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, along with Cīrṇavāsas and all the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was traveling through Śrāvastī to teach and transform beings, and arrived at the village of Tāla.
Having reached the village, he entered with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus to beg for food.
Having returned from his almsround, he sat down beneath a tree; having washed his feet and put away his robes and bowl, he spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana) and sat cross-legged.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly named Kātyāyana, who had a disciple named Panthaka. Although he had been a renunciant for a long time, after eight hundred days he was still unable to master a single verse through recitation. Six times throughout the day and night, he constantly recited these words: "Cease evil and practice good; cultivate heedfulness," yet despite reciting only these words, he could never achieve mastery.

At that time, the Venerable Kātyāyana exhausted his spiritual power in instructing his disciples but was unable to enable them to attain realization. He then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated before him, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata has appeared in the world for great benefit; he brings peace and security to devas and humans, universally delivering all beings."
"Only I, among your disciples, have alone not yet received your transformative grace.
I pray only that the World-Honored One will enlighten me, so that I may attain liberation.
The Buddha said to Kātyāyana:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well.
The Tathāgata shall now explain for you the causal conditions of the past.
Kātyāyana replied:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha told Kātyāyana:

"In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
When that Buddha appeared in the world, he taught and transformed sentient beings until his work of delivering them was complete; he then entered parinirvāṇa and attained extinction.

After the Buddha’s extinction, there was a bhikṣu who was clever and possessed great wisdom, having mastered the recitation of the Tripiṭaka. Relying on himself, he became arrogant, distracted, and negligent; when others came to him as disciples, he refused to instruct them, remaining solely foolish and conceited, and failing to cultivate right mindfulness.
After his life ended, he fell into the Black Darkness Hell, remaining there for ninety kalpas in constant darkness, ignorant and devoid of wisdom.
Due to the power of his former merit from leaving the household life, he emerged from hell and was reborn in the heavens.
Although he was born in the heavens, the radiance of his celestial palace and all its offerings were completely dark and inferior to those of the other devas.
Because he had recited the Tripiṭaka, when his life in heaven ended, he was reborn in Jambudvīpa and encountered the era of a Buddha.
"Because of his former arrogance, although he encountered the Buddha, he did not understand the characteristics of the Dharma.
I shall now explain various skillful means for him and instruct him in the method of fixing the mind.
At that time, Kātyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that the Tathāgata will, for the sake of this foolish bhikṣu Pañcakasikha and all sentient beings of future ages who possess deluded thoughts, expound the Dharma of Right Contemplation.”
The Buddha told Bandhaka:

"From this day forward, you should always dwell in a quiet place, sitting upright with a single mind, with hands joined and eyes closed, restraining body, speech, and mind; be careful not to be negligent."
"Because of your negligence, you have long endured arduous suffering throughout many kalpas.
Now, follow my words and contemplate all phenomena with clear attention.
At that time, Bandhaka followed the Buddha’s instructions, sitting upright and binding his mind in concentration.
The Buddha told Pāñcika:
"You should now carefully observe the joint of your big toe, causing the mind not to wander.
Make a blister gradually arise upon the joint, then cause it to swell; furthermore, you should use your intention to make this swelling gradually grow as large as a bean."

Furthermore, one should use the mind to visualize [the body] becoming bloated and putrefied, with the skin and flesh peeled apart on both sides, yellow pus flowing out, and blood gushing profusely amidst the pus.
Upon a single joint, the skin and flesh have completely rotted away, leaving only the joint of the right toe as white as jade or snow.
Having seen one joint, it gradually expands from the right foot until it covers half the body; it becomes bloated and putrid, with yellow pus and flowing blood.
It causes the skin and flesh of the half-body to split apart on both sides, leaving only the bones of the half-body starkly white.
Having seen the half-body, he further sees the entire body completely bloated, entirely putrefied, with foul-smelling pus and blood, and various worms sporting within it.
"Various kinds such as these, as described above," means that having observed one, one then observes two;
having observed two, one then observes three.
Having seen three, he further saw four.
Having seen four, he further saw five.
Having seen five, he went on to see ten.
Having seen ten, the mind gradually expands until one sees within a single room.
Having seen within a single room, one proceeds until seeing the entire world-system.
Having seen the entire world-system, if it becomes too vast, one withdraws it again until it is as before in the visualization.
Having performed this first contemplation, one should again shift the visualization and fix the mind, observing the tip of the nose with precision.
Having observed the tip of the nose, the mind shall not be distracted.
If it is not distracted, one should contemplate the bones as previously described.

Furthermore, one should contemplate that the flesh, muscles, skin, and so forth of one's own body are all formed through the union of the father and mother from impure seminal and vital essences; such a body has impurity as its seed.

Next, one should be instructed to bind the mindfulness and contemplate the teeth. Among the parts of the human body, only these teeth are white; [one should think: "The bones of this body of mine are as white as these teeth.
Because the mental visualization is sharp, one sees the teeth grow large until they are equal in size to the body.
At that time, one should again shift the focus of contemplation to observe the forehead, causing the white bone on the forehead to become as white as jade or snow.
If it does not appear white, one should change the visualization and practice the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*), as explained in detail in the *Navasaṃjñābhāvanā-dharma*.
When performing this contemplation, those of dull faculties must observe this matter diligently for one month or up to ninety days before they finally see it;
those of sharp faculties see it in a single thought-moment.
Having seen this, one is further instructed to contemplate the large joint of the white bone at the waist.
Once it is seen, one should again contemplate the skeleton of various colors as previously described.
If this method does not succeed, one should then be instructed in the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Regarding the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*), it is explained in detail as in the *Maitrī-samādhi*.
Having been instructed in loving-kindness, one is further taught to contemplate white bones.
If other things appear, one must be careful not to follow after them; rather, one should ensure that this mind is clear and distinct, seeing the person of white bones like a white snow mountain.
If one perceives other objects and gives rise to thoughts [of them], one should resolve to eliminate them, thinking:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has instructed me to contemplate bones.
How is it that there are still objects of perception belonging to other mental images?"
"I should now single-mindedly contemplate bones.
Having seen the white bones, he causes the mind to become clear and still, free from all external thoughts, and perceives throughout the entire trichiliocosm skeletons filling it completely.
"Having seen these skeletal remains, each and every one must be extinguished, just as previously observed regarding suffering.

At that time, the bhikṣu Panthaka, having heard these words spoken by the Buddha, contemplated them one by one with undistracted mind; seeing them clearly and distinctly, he immediately attained the path of Arhatship, possessing the three knowledges, the six superknowledges, and the eight liberations.
He reflected that the Tripitaka he had studied throughout his past lives was now perfectly clear and free from any error.
At that time, because of this foolish and arrogant bhikṣu Panthaka, the World-Honored One established this method of pure contemplation on white bones.
The Buddha told Kātyāyana:
"Even this foolish bhikṣu Panthaka attained arhatship by means of focused mindfulness;
how much more so should a wise person practice dhyāna?"
At that time, having witnessed this event, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Dhyāna is the nectar-like Dharma; A concentrated mind extinguishes all evils.
Wisdom slays all ignorance and delusion, So that one never again undergoes future existence.”
"If even the foolish Panthaka attained this through a concentrated mind,
how much more so for those who are wise— if they do not diligently practice mindfulness!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kātyāyana and commanded Ānanda:
"You should now receive and uphold the Buddha’s words, using this sublime Dharma to universally save all living beings.

If there are foolish and ignorant sentient beings, or arrogant, conceited, and evil sentient beings, in future generations who wish to practice seated meditation, they should begin with the method of contemplating dharmas taught by Kāṭyāyanīputra, as well as the method of contemplating images taught by Śreṇika, and further study this method of contemplation practiced by the bhikṣu Bandhula."
Thereafter, one observes one's own body and sees all the white bones as white as jade or snow.
At that time, the skeletal figures return and enter the body, and one perceives the flowing light from all the white bones dispersing and vanishing.
Having seen this, the practitioner’s mind naturally becomes harmonious, joyful, tranquil, and effortless.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, the crown of their head is warm, and various fragrances constantly issue forth from the pores of their body.
Whether emerging from or entering meditative absorption, they constantly hear the sublime Dharma;
furthermore, they personally perceive their own bodies as warm, joyful, and blissful, with a serene countenance, little sleep, and freedom from physical ailments.
Having attained this stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), one constantly and personally realizes that the mind is inwardly warm and the mind is always peaceful and happy.
If people of later generations wish to study meditation, they should proceed from the initial practice of impurity up to this dharma.
"One who attains this contemplation is said to have attained the Dharma of Warmth.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who, amidst this turbid world, wish to study right reception and reflection, they should begin by binding their mindfulness to contemplate impurity and proceed until they reach this dharma; this is called the Dharma of Warmth."
"If one attains this Dharma, it is called the completion of the twenty-first stage of the 'Heat' (ūṣmagata) contemplation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You must now uphold these teachings on the 'Heat' as asked by Kātyāyanīputra; be careful not to forget or lose them."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings in future generations who are able to receive and uphold this samādhi, and who with single-minded tranquility attain the stage of ‘warmth,’ how shall such a person know it for themselves?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If one contemplates the characteristics of the various fetters (saṃyojana) with discernment, from the initial stage of impurity up to this dharma, and personally realizes that both body and mind are entirely warm, with the mind succeeding the mind in continuity, free from all afflictions and anger, and with a serene and joyful countenance—this is called the Dharma of Warmth (uṣmagata)."
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If there is a practitioner who has attained the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), he should next be further instructed to bind his mindfulness so that it rests upon the white light that exists within all the spaces between the white bones.
When you see the white light, the white bones will disperse and vanish.

If other objects appear before you, you should again collect your mind and return to contemplating the white light, until you see all the white lights blazing one after another, filling the entire world.
One observes one's own body again, making it even more luminous and pure, such that even crystal or the Snowy Mountains cannot be compared to it.
One then sees the skeletons of each person dispersing individually.
When performing this contemplation, one must cause the concentrated mind to remain for a long duration.
Once the mind has been settled for a long time, one will naturally see a great radiance like the light of a fire upon the crown of one's head, emerging from the region of the brain.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If you see this phenomenon, you should further instruct [the practitioner] to repeat the process from the head to the feet and back again, totaling fourteen cycles.”

Having performed this contemplation, whether emerging from or entering meditative absorption, one constantly sees fire emerge from the crown of the head like the light of genuine gold; from the pores of the body, golden light also issues forth like scattered fine gold, bringing peace and bliss to both body and mind, like the radiance of purple-gold.
It returns and enters through the crown of the head;
this is called the "Crown Dharma" (mūrdha-dharma).
If a practitioner attains this contemplation, they will be able to achieve the "Crown Contemplation" (mūrdha-vipaśyanā).
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“You should well receive and uphold this method of the Contemplation of the Crown, and explain it extensively for the sake of all sentient beings in the future.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
One who attains this contemplation is said to have completed the twenty-second method, the Contemplation of the Summit.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Once this visualization is accomplished, you should further instruct them to fix their mindfulness and contemplate all the white bones, causing the scattered bones to gather in one place like snow blown by the wind, naturally forming a heap as white as a snowy mountain."
If one perceives these matters, attaining the Way will not be difficult.

If there are those who violated the precepts in a previous life or violate them in this present life, and they see their scattered bones and remains like ash and dust, or see various black objects upon them, they should further repent and confess their own transgressions before a wise person.
Having finished the confession, one sees a great white light upon the heap of bones extending even to the Formless Realm.
Whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, one constantly attains peace and bliss; that which was formerly cherished and enjoyed gradually becomes faint and thin.
Furthermore, one should again contemplate as previously reviewed, clearly visualizing the impure substances—pus flowing from the nine orifices—until the mind is free of doubt or regret.

One should then proceed as before, imagining fire arising within the bones to burn away all impurities; once the impurities are exhausted, golden light flows forth and returns to enter the crown of the head.
When this light enters the crown of the head, the body experiences a bliss beyond compare.
One who attains this contemplation is said to have completed the twenty-third contemplation: the preparatory method for the "Aiding the Crown" (*zhùdǐng*) dharma.
Furthermore, one should again be instructed to bind the mindfulness and fix the mind, observing one's own body as being like a bundle of grass.

When emerging from meditative absorption, one likewise sees one's own body as being like a plantain tree with its layers of bark wrapped around one another; furthermore, one should observe the various leaves of the plantain tree as being like a leather bag.
Within the body, it is like air, and even the bones are not seen.

Whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, one constantly perceives this state where the body is emaciated and weak; one should then further be instructed to observe the body again, gathering it back into a single unit like a bundle of dry grass, until the body is seen to be firm and strong.
Having seen it as solid and firm, one should further consume clarified butter and maintain a balanced diet.
Thereafter, one contemplates the body as being like an empty sack, with fire arising from within to burn this body entirely away.
Once the body has been completely consumed by fire, during the time of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one constantly perceives flames.
Having observed the fire, one sees all fires arising from the four directions.

Whether emerging from or entering concentration, the body is as hot as fire; one sees this element of fire (*tejodhātu*) arising from the joints and members, with flames issuing forth from every pore.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, one also perceives one’s own body as being like a great mass of fire; the body is steaming hot and cannot be sustained.
At that time, great volcanic mountains appear from the four directions, all coming together and converging before the practitioner.
One sees one's own body merging with the various fires;
this is called the perception of fire (*tejasa-saṃjñā*).
One should further cause the fire to burn the body until it is completely consumed.
Once the fire has finished burning, at the time of entering meditative concentration, one contemplates that the body is no-body and sees that the body has been entirely consumed by the fire.
When the fire has burned it away, one naturally comes to know that there is no self within the body; all fetters and afflictions are likewise thus, beyond full description.
"This is called the twenty-fourth contemplation on the fire element, the true fire element of the perception of fire.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should well receive and uphold this contemplation on the non-self of the fire element."
This contemplation of the fire element is called "the fire of wisdom that burns away all afflictions.
You should receive and uphold it well, and for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages, you should propagate and expound it widely.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there is a practitioner who has attained the contemplation of the fire element, he should further be instructed to fix his mindfulness and reflect, binding his attention to the tip of the nose, and further contemplate from where this fire arises."
When observing this fire, one observes that one's own body is entirely devoid of a self; since there is no self, the fire naturally extinguishes.
One should further reflect:
"My body is without self; the four great elements have no master."
These various fetters and the roots of those fetters arise from inversion; yet inversion itself is empty.
How can one, within this emptiness of dharmas, perversely perceive the fire of the body?
"When one performs this contemplation, both the fire and the self are sought for but found nowhere.
This is called the contemplation of the non-self of the fire element.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“You should well receive and uphold this contemplation of the fire element, and for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages, you should extensively analyze, expound, and explain it.
Having heard what the Buddha said, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
This concludes the twenty-fifth contemplation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"I see that when the fire is extinguished, it first ceases from the nose, and thereafter the fires within the body and mind are simultaneously extinguished; likewise, the eighty-eight fetters are also all extinguished."
The body becomes cool and harmonious within, attaining its proper state; one awakens deeply to this, clearly and distinctly realizing with certainty that there is no self.
Whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, one constantly knows that within the body there is no "I" or "mine."
"This concludes the contemplation on the extinction of non-self.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Furthermore, you should next instruct them in the method of contemplating the consecration."
Regarding the visualization of the consecration: one sees oneself as having a body like the radiance of lapis lazuli, transcending the three realms.
One perceives the true Buddha, who pours water from a ritual flask over the crown of the head, filling the entire body.
Once his body was completely filled, his limbs and joints were also filled, and [the water] flowed out from the center of his navel.

It remained on the ground before him as the Buddha constantly poured water; at that moment, once the World-Honored One had completed the consecration of his head, the water immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
Water emerges from the navel like lapis lazuli; its color is like that of deep blue lapis lazuli light, and its radiant energy fills the trichiliocosm.
Once the water has completely emerged, one should further be instructed to fix the mind with this thought:
"May the Buddha, the World-Honored One, once again confer the empowerment upon me."
At that time, he naturally perceives his own body as being like breath—vast, immense, and transcending the three realms.
He sees water entering through the crown of his head; he perceives his body becoming as vast as the water itself, filling the entirety of the water.
Furthermore, he sees his own navel as being like a lotus flower from which a spring gushes forth, filling his entire body and encircling it like a pool.

There are various lotus flowers, each emitting light of seven colors; this light expounds the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, with a voice like the Brahma-voice that delights the faculty of hearing.

When this sign appears, you should further be instructed: with palms joined and eyes closed, sit upright with single-minded concentration and observe within your own body from the crown of the head, not perceiving the thought of bones.
Whether emerging from or entering meditative absorption, one should see one’s own body as being like a crystal jar.
One should further give rise to the thought of regarding the four great poisonous dragon-kings of one's own mind.
One sees within one's heart, as if hair-pores were opening, six kinds of dragons; each dragon has six heads, and from these heads they spit poison, which is like wind and fire pervading the pond.

From each of the lotus flowers, rays of light stream forth and enter the crowns of the nāgas; as the light enters their crowns, the nāgas' venom naturally subsides, leaving only great volumes of water filling the interior of their bodies.
When this visualization is accomplished, it is called "contemplating the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment.

Although one sees this visualization, one has not yet fully mastered profound meditative concentration; therefore, one should further be instructed to practice the aforementioned counting of breaths, so that the mind becomes settled, tranquil, and free from discursive thought.
"When this visualization is accomplished, it is called the 'Contemplation of the Correspondence with the Four Great Elements.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

'You should well receive and uphold this Contemplation of the Correspondence with the Four Great Elements of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment; be careful not to forget or lose it. For the sake of all sentient beings of the future, you should extensively analyze it and expound and explain it to the fourfold assembly.'"
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Furthermore, he was instructed to continue binding his mindfulness and stabilizing his mind, clearly contemplating the water element as it issues from the pores and pervades his entire body.
Whether emerging from or entering meditative absorption, he sees his body as a pool of water, green in color.
This green water resembles a spring on a mountain peak, flowing out from the crown of his head and re-entering through the crown.
He saw seven lotuses, pure vajra in color, emitting golden light.
Within that golden light were vajra-men, who, holding sharp swords in their hands, struck down the six dragons before them.
Again, he saw many fires issue from the mouths of the dragons, and his entire body was ablaze with fire.
All the waters dried up, and the fire was immediately extinguished.
Once the water and fire had both been extinguished, he saw his own body gradually become pure white, like a vajra.

Whether emerging from or entering meditative absorption, the mind and spirit are as joyful as if butter were being poured upon them; like consuming the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*), body and mind are at peace and happy.
Furthermore, one should again be instructed to fix the mindfulness and contemplate others and external objects.
Due to external perceptions, one naturally sees a tree growing extraordinary sweet fruits; these fruits are of four colors and are endowed with four kinds of light.
Such fruit trees, like beryl trees, pervade everywhere.
Having seen this tree, he saw everywhere all sentient beings of the four modes of birth, oppressed by the fire of hunger, all coming to beg.
Having seen them, he rejoiced, gave rise to a heart of compassion, and immediately produced a mind of loving-kindness.
Seeing this beggar, he felt as though his own parents were undergoing great suffering and distress, thinking:
"How shall I now rescue and deliver them?
Having formed this thought, he immediately contemplated his own body, which returned to being pus and blood as before, and then became a mass of flesh, which he took and gave to the hungry one.
These hungry ghosts scramble to seize and eat it.
Once they have eaten their fill, they scatter and run in all directions.
— *Dhyāna-guhyārtha-sūtra*, Middle Fascicle.
The Sūtra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna, Scroll II,
translated at the Xiaoyao Garden in Chang’an by Kumārajīva and others during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
"At that time, one should further observe both one's own body and the bodies of others.
My body and the bodies of others arise from inversion; in reality, there is no 'mine.
If there were a self, why would these hungry ghosts suddenly appear and come to my side?"

At that time, he further saw immeasurable hungry ghosts, their bodies vast and boundless, with heads like Mount Tai and throats as thin as a single hair; oppressed by the fires of hunger, they cried out in distress, seeking food.
Having seen this, one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and offer one's body to the hungry ghosts.
Once the hungry ghosts have received it, they devour the body until they are fully satiated.
Having witnessed this event, one should further be instructed to observe many more hungry ghosts.
He sees hungry ghosts encircling his body four times, just as before he used his own body to feed those hungry ghosts.
Having seen this, he is further instructed to withdraw his body and prevent the mind from scattering, observing for himself that his own body is a mass of impurities.

When performing this contemplation, one immediately sees one's own body—its pus, blood, and various flesh—all breaking apart piece by piece and heaped upon the ground before one, seeing all sentient beings scrambling to seize and eat it.

Having seen this, one should further observe one's own body: it arises from various sufferings and exists through various sufferings; it is subject to decay and will soon be extinguished, to be devoured by hungry ghosts.

While performing this visualization, he suddenly saw a fierce fire within his own heart that burned all the lotuses upon the pond before him, as well as the hideous and evil forms of the various hungry ghosts and the waters of the pond itself, until they were completely consumed.
Having seen this, one should further be instructed to contemplate one's own body with clear attention until it is restored to its former state, complete and intact.
One should then further observe all the pores of one's own body; because of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the blood transforms into milk and flows out from the pores.
Upon the ground there was a pond filled with abundant milk.
He further saw many hungry ghosts arrive at the side of this pond; yet, due to their past transgressions, they were unable to drink the milk.

At that time, he looked upon the ghosts with a compassionate heart as if they were his own children, wishing for them to drink the milk; however, because of the ghosts' karmic offenses, the milk transformed into pus.
In a brief moment, his compassionate mind arose once more; because of this compassion, milk flowed from every pore of his body, many times more than before.
He thought of the hungry ghosts who were oppressed by the suffering of hunger: "Why do they not come to drink?"

At that time, a hungry ghost, its form vast and tall for several tens of yojanas, approached the practitioner with a sound like five hundred chariots rolling as it lifted and set down its feet, crying out:
"I am hungry! I am hungry!"
At that time, the practitioner immediately bestows milk with a mind of loving-kindness, causing the hungry ghosts to drink it.
When the milk reaches their mouths, it transforms into pus; yet, although it becomes pus, because of the practitioner’s mind of loving-kindness, they immediately become fully satiated.

Having seen the ghosts satiated, he again observed his own body; he immediately saw fire emerge from beneath the soles of his feet, burning the aforementioned sentient beings as well as all the trees until they were completely consumed and vanished.

At that time, if you see many beings of diverse kinds, you should again fix your mindfulness and contemplate your own body with clarity, causing the mind to remain unmoving, tranquil, and free from thought.
Being without such thoughts, you should make this vow:
"May I, in future births, not undergo further existence and take no pleasure in the world."

Having made this vow, he immediately saw the ground before him as if it were lapis lazuli; beneath the lapis lazuli, he saw golden water, and he saw his own body as being level with the ground and identical in color to the water.
The water is warm, and within it grow trees like those made of the seven treasures, their branches and leaves lush and verdant.
Upon them are four fruits; the sound of these fruits is like that of bells, proclaiming suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Having heard this sound, he saw his own body submerge into the water and proceed toward the location of the tree.
He carefully observed his own body; water emerged from the crown of his head and overflowed throughout the pool of lapis lazuli.
In an instant, fire broke out once more; from within the fire, wind arose like lapis lazuli.
Again, he saw above his head, from the crown of his head down to his feet, that it was as firm and solid as a diamond (*vajra*).
Again, a fire broke out, burning the vajra until it was completely consumed, and the warm water dried up.

He immediately observed his body again and saw that within the pool inside his body, there suddenly appeared a tree with full branches and leaves; at the top of the tree were fruits whose sound was like that of bells, proclaiming the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and purity.
"Such a wondrous fruit possesses a beautiful sound and is replete with fragrance and flavor.
I should now eat it.
Having formed this thought, he immediately reached up to climb the tree, took the fruit, and ate it.
As soon as he obtained one fruit, its flavor was so sweet and exquisite that nothing could serve as a simile for it.
Having eaten the fruit, he saw that the tree had withered and dried up, yet the remaining three fruits still possessed a radiant luster.
After eating the fruit, his body and mind became tranquil and serene, free from thoughts of sorrow or joy.
He observed for himself that the mental consciousness is a phenomenon subject to decay, arising from various forms of suffering.
The root of all suffering has consciousness as its causal condition.
Now, observe this consciousness: it is like a bubble upon the water, never pausing for a moment.
The four great elements have no master; the body has no self; and consciousness has no abiding place.
Thus, regarding all these phenomena, one should further contemplate the mind and consciousness for seven times seven, forty-nine times, as being phenomena subject to decay and disintegration.
At that time, one sees one's own body as white as jade or snow, with each joint supporting the next.
One should further be instructed to rub and touch this body with one's right hand, seeing the body as like dust, the bones as fine powder, like powdered dust upon the ground.
Next, he was further instructed to contemplate the body as being like breath, existing only through the counting of the breaths, such that the body is like a bag of air with no momentary stability.
He was then instructed again to immediately contemplate his own body as before, returning it once more to the form of a single white-boned person.
Having seen the skeleton person, one observes one's own body as before, dissolving back into something like fine dust, just as a person uses powder to smear upon the ground.
Immediately, one sees a blue-colored skeleton person on the ground; again observing as before, one grinds this blue-colored skeleton person to powder and uses it to smear the ground.

Furthermore, one again contemplates the body as being like fine blue dust; this dust transforms into a skeletal figure, its bones entirely black. One should then, as before, smear powdered [bones] upon the ground.
One further contemplates one's own body as being like a black ground, and sees within that black ground four black snakes with eyes red as fire.
A snake came and pressed against his body, spitting venom intending to harm him; yet it could not cause him injury, and instead transformed into fire and burned its own body.
At that time, a spontaneous voice arose in the air, constantly preaching the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
When seeing this, each of the eighty-eight heads of the poisonous snakes is consumed by fire.
At that moment, water spontaneously appears from the sky and sprinkles the bodies of the poisonous snakes; all the fires are extinguished, and all eighty-eight heads completely vanish.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, one perceives the body as peaceful, blissful, tranquil, and unconditioned.

One should then further be instructed to observe one's own body without thoughts of it being large or small; soon thereafter, one will see the body naturally become vast and tall, clearly visible like a mountain of the seven treasures, while seeing one's own mind as a *maṇi* jewel.
At that time, one should again contemplate emptiness as described above.

While contemplating emptiness, one will personally experience one’s own body as harmonious, joyful, supple, and incomparably blissful. The seven-jeweled colored light from the lotus flower before one flows into one's heart, filling it ten times within a mani jewel, with all seven branches and seven colors fully complete.

Observing his own body as empty and free from all conceptualizations, at that moment there was a natural light upon the crown of his head, resembling a golden cloud and also like a precious canopy; its color further resembled silver, entering from the crown of the head and covering the radiance of the *maṇi* jewel above.

Whether emerging from or entering meditative absorption, they constantly perceive this matter; those who perceive this matter naturally refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if any of the fourfold assembly of disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—practices this contemplation, it is called the twenty-sixth right contemplation, and it is also called attaining the path of srotāpanna.”

If one attains this contemplation, one must examine it with thorough sincerity so that the body spontaneously abandons the five kinds of evil, thereby accords with the Sūtras, does not contradict the Vinaya, and conforms to the Abhidharma.
"This is called the mark of the fruit of Srotāpanna.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"If there be a practitioner who attains this contemplation, they should keep it secret and not proclaim it recklessly; rather, they should practice with single-minded diligence and vigor.
Having practiced with diligence and vigor, they should further be taught to contemplate the earth element with careful attention."
The method for contemplating the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is also as described above.
Having contemplated the earth element, one is next instructed to contemplate the water element (*ab-dhātu*).
As for contemplating the water element, one contemplates the various waters within one's own body; the body is like lapis lazuli, firm and difficult to destroy.
If one perceives one's own body as entirely water, one should be taught to change the visualization.

If, moreover, one perceives the body as being completely made of lapis lazuli, one should also be taught to change the visualization by observing the earth element, so that the lapis lazuli body becomes like a subtle vapor, and one sees water manifesting from the eyes.
If one perceives this phenomenon, it is called the contemplation of the subtle four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
One should further be instructed to fill the area from the head upward with water, perceiving the water emerging from the eyes without falling to the ground.
One sees one's own eyes as being like foam upon the water, filling the water.
If one perceives this phenomenon, the water on the head is neither hot nor cold, but is perfectly balanced and harmonious.
If the water were hot, that would be a false and artificial contemplation.
The color of the water is clear and limpid, neither warm nor cool.
Next, one should further be taught to observe that the water from the waist upward is neither warm nor cold.

One then observes the throat as being like a tube of lapis lazuli; the water enters the chest, then descends to the abdomen, and even to the thighs and knees, but must not enter the arms, causing the water to remain clear and limpid with the brilliant color of crystal.
If one perceives the water as warm, this is true contemplation.

Once this visualization is perfected, one is further instructed to cause it to penetrate through all four limbs and joints, so that the water fills them entirely, like a vessel of lapis lazuli being used to hold water.
Gradually it expands until it fills an entire bed, and others outside can also see it.
If one sees this water as clear and cool, it is true water; if one perceives other appearances, it is not called real.

Entering the Water-Light Samādhi, it gradually expands and fills a single room; the water becomes as clear and pure as the luster of lapis lazuli, and it continues to expand until it pervades the entire trichiliocosm.
When you see this phenomenon, you should sit with single-minded concentration in a quiet place, instructing all your fellow students to remain pure and not to cause any commotion.
At that time, you will further see purple flames arise upon the water; you should then reflect to yourself:
"From where does this water arise?"
How should it be brought to an end?
If one says, "I am water," then my body is without self; as was previously observed, there is no self.
Now, from within the state of non-existence, how could water arise?
When he formed this thought, the watery element became like vapor and gradually vanished from the crown of his head; the water slowly disappeared until only the skin of his body remained.
He saw that his own body had become extremely subtle and thin, beyond all comparison, like a mote of dust or a bundle of straw.
Again, one sees fire suddenly arise within the body, burning it entirely away.
One contemplates that the body has no location and that there is forever no self; both the self and sentient beings are entirely non-existent.
At that time, the practitioner’s mind and mental states become tranquil and exceedingly subtle, beyond all analogy.

When this visualization is perfected, it is called the twenty-seventh contemplation of true non-self (*bhūta-anātman*), also known as the visualization of the extinction of the water element, and also termed "heading toward the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin."
The remaining subtle and wondrous dharmadhātu of the noble ones is profound and difficult to surpass; it cannot be fully described.
When a practitioner sits and cultivates various samādhis, upon attaining the *anātman-samādhi*, they shall naturally behold the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should now properly receive and uphold this subtle and wondrous realm of the true water element, and extensively expound and proclaim it for the sake of all sentient beings of the future."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Having attained this contemplation, you should further be taught the method for the contemplation of the water element."

This contemplation of the water element is extremely subtle; it causes this water element to merge with the fire element, so that one sees the body as being like vapor or like a reflection in lapis lazuli. One contemplates flames arising simultaneously from all four sides of the navel, seeing those flames as if reflected by the sun.
If one sees a flame arise from above the navel, or emerge from the nostrils, or emerge from the mouth, or enter and exit the ears and eyes at will.
If one sees this phenomenon, one sees all fires emerging from the pores of the body.
After the fire emerges, green-colored water follows immediately behind it.
One then sees within one's own body that the water is above and the fire below, or the fire is above and the water below; thus, one contemplates the body as being without a body.
When this visualization is accomplished, one sees that the body’s water and fire elements are neither warm nor cold; body and mind dwell in tranquil stillness, unimpeded.
This is called the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin, and it is also termed the true reality of the objective realm.
When seeing these things, one never perceives the body, whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration.
At the time of entering concentration, outsiders also see water and fire issuing from and entering through the pores.
For one who has much lust, they see fire entering from the crown of the head and emerging from the sense organs of the body, thereafter filling the entire body;
water likewise does so.

Furthermore, one should observe the fire upon one's own head as being like a golden cloud-canopy of Jāmbūnada gold, or see the lower part of the body as being like a flower of the seven jewels. The mind becomes tranquil, peaceful, and blissful, such that no worldly pleasure can serve as a metaphor for it.

Upon emerging from meditative absorption, his body is likewise peaceful and blissful; he causes external sentient beings who behold him to perceive the tranquil golden light and golden complexion of his dhyāna-samādhi.
Śakra and the various devas pay him respectful homage and all say:
"O Virtuous One!"
"Now your suffering is exhausted; you shall certainly attain the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin.

Having heard this, he rejoiced and cultivated the meditative concentration of the body. His mind was free from fetters and obstructions, abiding in peace and happiness as he sported within the *anātman-samādhi*. He also gradually entered the gate of the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, and all samādhis such as *apraṇihita* and *anabhisaṃskāra* appeared before him.
Such a subtle, excellent, and superior realm is naturally discerned by the practitioner while seated in meditative concentration.
For those of dull faculties, the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, appears before them to explain it.
Because he has seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma with joy, he immediately attains the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin at that very moment.
He should then again, with a sincere mind, review the previous contemplation twenty-five times, making it extremely clear and sharp.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“You should well uphold this twenty-ninth contemplation on the great element of water; be careful not to forget or lose it.

One who attains this contemplation is also called a Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner) and is also called ‘One Who Goes Well. Because of the causes and conditions of wholesome roots and karma from past lives, such a person encounters virtuous friends and the pure practice of the Dharma, and you shall thereby attain this path of the Sakṛdāgāmin.”
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who have attained this subtle and wondrous contemplation of the great element of water, they should further be instructed in the method for the peaceful, subtle, most excellent, and extraordinary contemplation of the great element of fire."

When performing this visualization, one sees within one's own navel a subtle fire-light, shaped like a lotus flower, its color and radiance like that of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Jāmbūnada gold combined together.
Having seen this, one should further be instructed to contemplate the fire within the body.

When contemplating the internal fire, one will see that the fire of the heart constantly possesses radiance, surpassing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bright moon-gems; the purity of the light of the heart is likewise so.

Emerging from and entering meditative absorption is like a person walking while holding a bright fire-jewel; fearing that others might see it, he understands it clearly only within his own mind, while others do not see it.
Gradually, as it grew bright, he saw his own body as if it were a crystal mirror; he saw his mind as well, like a bright moon or a divine pearl.
He feared that others might see this, yet in reality, others did not see these things.

At the time of entering meditative absorption, because his mind was luminous, he saw the coarse features of the trichiliocosm; he saw Jambudvīpa, Mount Sumeru, and the great oceans, all with perfect clarity. Furthermore, he saw within the great oceans the king of maṇi jewels, from which flames of fire issued forth.
Having seen this, the Buddha then extensively expounded for him the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
As for the nine successive attainments, they consist of the nine unhindered stages (*navānantarya*) and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
For those who contemplate in this manner, there is no need for prior preparation, because the Buddha appears before them and speaks for them himself.

Those of sharp faculties, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching during the nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*), immediately attain the path of Arhatship at that very moment, transcending the stage of Anāgāmin, just as fine white cotton cloth is easily dyed with color.
If one is of dull faculties, they should further be instructed in the method of contemplation on the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).

As for this method of contemplation on the wind element: one perceives all winds as being extremely subtle; among the subtle, they are the most subtle, such that they can be seen with the mind’s eye but cannot be fully described.

Wind further mingles with fire, and fire further mingles with wind; water enters into fire, wind enters into water, and fire enters into wind; wind, fire, and water each follow their respective pores with sovereign mastery as they wish.

Furthermore, there is a wind endowed with the ten colors, like the radiance of ten kinds of jewels; it issues from the pores of the body and enters through the crown of the head, issues from the navel and enters through the soles of the feet, issues from all parts of the body and enters through the space between the eyebrows, issues from the space between the eyebrows and enters through all parts of the body.

All such immeasurable realms—the radiance of the noble ones, the seeds of the noble ones, and all the dharmas of the noble ones—arise from this great element of wind and enter into this great element of wind.

This contemplation of the wind element possesses a complete array of subtle and wondrous characteristics; only an Arhat can analyze it in detail, for it cannot be fully described. When the practitioner sits in meditation, they shall naturally perceive it.
If one perceives this matter, one refines all afflictions and becomes an Anāgāmin.
This contemplation of the wind element is called the thirtieth sign of the realm corresponding to the stage of Anāgāmin.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should well receive and uphold this supreme meditative method on the element of wind corresponding to the stage of an Anāgāmin; be careful not to forget or lose it."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had a disciple who was the son of the Nigaṇṭha Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana from the great city of Rājagṛha; his name was Ajita. He sought ordination and the study of the Path under the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, practicing austerities and observing the twelve dhūta-pāramitās. After five years had passed, he attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin, yet he was unable to progress further to become an Arhat.
He immediately rose from his seat, went to where Kāśyapa was, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself before Mahākāśyapa, and said:
"Upādhyāya!"
Following my preceptor, I have practiced with diligent vigor as if my head were on fire for five years.
Now that I have attained the fruit of Anāgāmin, my body and mind have become weary and lax, and I am unable to advance further toward supreme liberation.
"I only pray that the Upādhyāya will explain this to me quickly.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa immediately entered samādhi and observed the bhikṣu’s mind; he knew that this bhikṣu had not yet exhausted all outflows (āsravas) and would, upon passing away from this life, be reborn in the realm of the Anāgāmins.
Rising from samādhi, he addressed him, saying:
"Son of the Dharma!

My body and mind are now entirely sovereign; having entered the Samādhi of Sovereignty, I have observed all the karmic retributions of your past lives and see that within this present body, there is no condition for you to attain the path of an Arhat."
Having heard these words, Ajita wept with tears falling like rain and said,
"Upādhyāya! As for me now,
I do not delight in being born in the heavens."
"Just as a person suffering from illness seeks the power of impermanence, so too am I fearful of birth and death.
At that time, Kāśyapa said:
"O Son of the Dharma!..."
Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!
Birth and death are as evil as a fierce fire that burns and destroys all things; they are truly to be loathed and abhorred.
"I observe that your faculties are not yet clearly discernible; furthermore, the World-Honored One is currently with the bhikṣus in the Jeta Grove. Let us now go together to the Buddha's presence."
Then that bhikṣu, having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, followed behind Kāśyapa to the Jeta Grove and arrived at the place where the Buddha was.

There he saw the World-Honored Buddha, whose body was like a mountain of gold, dwelling amidst the great assembly with sovereign majesty and virtue, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

He prostrated himself before the Buddha, circumambulated him seven times, and then withdrew to stand to one side. Kneeling with his right knee on the ground and joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

This disciple of mine, Ajita, has followed behind me in practicing the twelve dhūtas and abiding in profound meditative concentration; yet, having reached the stage of Anāgāmin, he is unable to progress further and exhaust the ocean of afflictions."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for me the profound practice of the pure liberation of the nectar of consecration.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ajita, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"Ajita! It is well that you ask about this matter; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Listen attentively and reflect well."

In the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a Buddha in that world named Mahāprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
When that Buddha appeared in the world, he taught and transformed sentient beings through three kinds of manifestations, completing his work of delivering all people.
During the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī, where the king was named Brahmadatta.

The king had a crown prince named Kṣāntivarmā (Armor of Forbearance), who firmly resolved upon the profound mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and sought all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). He vowed not to kill and cultivated the ten wholesome paths of action, never feeling weary or indolent regarding the six pāramitās.

At that time, there was a householder in that land named Candrasūryaghoṣa, who possessed immeasurable sovereignty. He had an only son who suddenly contracted a fever; the wind-element entered his heart, causing him to become deranged and devoid of reason. Grasping a sharp sword, he ran into the streets and alleys, slaughtering sentient beings.
At that time, out of love for his son, the elder took a censer in his hand and went outside the four city gates to burn incense and scatter flowers. He made a great vow, saying:
"If there be any seers, sages, physicians, or mantra-masters in the world who can cure my son’s madness, I shall offer them everything I possess."

At that time, the Prince went out of the city for recreation and saw a great elder practicing the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and making a vow for his son. His heart was filled with joy, and he spoke these words:
"This great elder diligently cultivates the mind of loving-kindness for the sake of all beings, yet the elder’s son has fallen gravely ill.
I pray that the various celestial deities (*deva-rṣi*) will surely arouse compassion, come to this place, and save the elder’s son."
As he was speaking, a great seer named Prabhārasa descended from the Snowy Mountains through the air and arrived at the householder’s location. He addressed the householder, saying:

"The ailment of your son arose from a fever; because of that fever, he gave rise to great anger. His heart-vessels were all opened and the wind-element entered his heart, which is why he has gone mad."

Regarding such a patient, as stated in the *Rishi-sūtra*, one whose wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*) is agitated must apply the heart-blood of a non-angry virtuous man to the body and consume the marrow of a virtuous person, the size of a soybean, to achieve a complete cure.
At that time, having heard the words of the seer, the elder immediately prostrated himself before the Prince on the road and said:
"The great seer Bhūmideva has stated that my son’s ailment can only be cured by using the blood and marrow of a person who possesses a mind of loving-kindness and is free from anger."
I now wish to pierce my own body to draw out blood for my son to eat, and break my bones to extract the marrow to give him to drink.
I only pray that the Prince will grant permission for this matter.
At that time, the Prince said:
"Householder!
I have heard the Buddha teach that if any sentient being causes suffering to their parents, they will fall into the great hells with no prospect of escape."
"How can the elder wish to break his own body to cure his son?
Wait but a moment; we shall employ a great expedient for the elder.
At that time, having heard the Prince's command, the elder was filled with great joy; he prostrated at the Prince's feet and returned home.
The elephant carried its calf to deliver it to the Crown Prince; upon seeing it, the Crown Prince poured the *sarpis* (clarified butter) over it.
At that time, the seer said to the Crown Prince:
"Even if one were to pour this medicine over this man for ninety days, he would ultimately not recover."
"To obtain a person of compassionate heart who has no anger toward human blood.
At that time, the Prince reflected within himself:
"Aside from my own body, all other sentient beings will surely give rise to anger."

I now vow to seek the path of Buddhahood in order to save all from the suffering of illness and to rescue their lives from birth and death; if I attain Buddhahood in a future age, I shall likewise bestow this Dharma-body and eternal life.
Having made this vow, he immediately pierced his own body and smeared the blood upon the son of the great elder; he then broke his own bones, extracted the marrow, and gave it to him to consume.
Once the son of the elder had consumed it, his illness was cured.
At that time, because his bones had been broken, the Prince fainted and fell to the ground.
Then the heavens and earth shook in six ways, and Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and countless sons of gods all descended together to where the Prince was, and addressed him, saying:
"Now you use your own body to save suffering sentient beings; what do you seek to obtain?"
"Are you seeking to become Śakra, Māra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin King?
What is it that you seek within the three realms?
At that time, the Prince addressed Śakra, saying:
"What I now seek is not the honor, glory, or noble status within the three realms.
That which I seek is my vow to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, having heard these words, Śakra addressed the prince, saying:
"Now that you have pierced your body and broken your bones to extract the marrow, your frame is trembling; do you feel any resentment or regret?"
At that time, the Prince immediately made this vow:
"From the moment I first pierced my body until now, if I have not harbored even a hair’s breadth of resentment or regret, may my body be restored to its former state."
Having made this vow, his body was restored to its former state without any difference.
At that time, Śakra, having witnessed this event, said to the Prince:
"The Prince’s majestic virtue is extraordinary and peerless; possessing such a powerful resolve, you will certainly attain Buddhahood."
"When the Crown Prince attains Buddhahood, I pray that you will deliver me first.
When he made this vow, the Crown Prince remained silent for a moment and then spoke these verses:
"I pray that when I attain Buddhahood, I shall universally deliver all devas and humans."
With body and mind free from hindrance, universally loving and compassionate toward all,
you shall likewise deliver yourselves and cause all classes of sentient beings to abide in great nirvana and forever enjoy happiness.

When the Prince had finished speaking these verses, the devas rained down flowers as an offering; they further rained down immeasurable hundreds of thousands of precious jewels, which filled the palace walls.
Having obtained these, the Prince used them for giving; he gave without ceasing, fully perfected all the *pāramitās*, and attained Buddhahood.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“The king of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī at that time was my father, King Śuddhodana.”
The elder Candraghoṣa at that time was none other than you, Mahākāśyapa.
The son of the elder at that time was none other than the bhikṣu Ajita.
The Crown Prince Kṣāntivarmaka at that time was none other than I, Śākyamuni Buddha.
"At that time, Śakra was none other than the present Śāriputra.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"This bhikṣu Aghida, in a remote past, became deranged and lost his senses due to the agitation of the wind element (vāyu-mahābhūta). For this reason, although he has now entered the meditative absorption on the four great elements, his mind harbors doubt regarding the wind absorption and does not proceed therein."

If this person were to enter the meditative concentration on the wind element and contemplate the four great elements, their head would split into seven pieces and their heart would tear asunder, leading to death.
One should instead instruct this person to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ajita:
"You should now observe that all sentient beings are tormented by the five kinds of suffering.
You should now give rise to a mind of great compassion, desiring to deliver them from these manifold sufferings."
"Contemplate form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they are all impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self.

Upon hearing these words from the Buddha, Aṅgada was suddenly enlightened in mind; at that very moment, he attained the path of Arhatship, possessing the three insights, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
Immediately before the Buddha, he leaped into the air and performed the eighteen transformations.
Having performed the eighteen transformations, he descended from mid-air, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has now expounded for me the causes and conditions of the past, as well as taught the mind of loving-kindness and extensively elaborated upon the Four Noble Truths.
By the power of the Buddha, I have immediately shattered the fetters of karma within the three realms and attained the state of an Arhat.
