I only pray that the World-Honored One, for the sake of sentient beings in the turbid and evil world of future ages who, due to the sins of their evil karma, are born into such a world of five corruptions—beings like myself whose minds harbor doubts and who remain stationary without practicing—may explain what Dharma they should cultivate to attain liberation from the bounds of suffering?
The Buddha told Ajita:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well.

Now, on account of you, Ajita, the Tathāgata shall extensively explain for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages everything from the stage of Anāgāmin to Arhatship, including all the subtle states that exist therein; you should discern them for yourself."
If one who has a predominance of wind disorders enters the meditative concentration of the wind element, they may, due to that wind element, become prone to developing madness;

in such a case, they should be taught to contemplate the Buddha. To teach them to contemplate the Buddha means to teach them to contemplate the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, great kindness and great compassion, and the dharma of the three foundations of mindfulness.
When contemplating this Dharma, one naturally comes to see immeasurable form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) with subtle and wondrous marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Some Buddhas soar through the air and perform the eighteen transformations; others manifest hundreds of thousands of immeasurable transformations from each of their individual marks and signs.
When seeing these things, one should give rise to a mind of reverence and make offerings, imagining fragrant flowers and scattering them universally before all Buddhas.
Thereafter, one should further reflect to oneself:

"The five aggregates (*skandha*) and four great elements (*mahābhūta*) within my present body are entirely impermanent; they arise and perish without ceasing. The branches of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the roots of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are all entirely impermanent."

What I contemplate is the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, great kindness, and great compassion; his physical body adorned with such merits is like a precious vase containing a wish-fulfilling jewel. By the power of the jewel, this vase is illuminated and embellished; yet the jewel has no sense of "mine," and the vase likewise has no abiding.
It is only for the sake of sentient beings that the Buddha likewise appears; yet he possesses no intrinsic nature of form nor any physical image, being liberated and pure.

Why is it that as I now contemplate the Tathāgata’s ten powers—from the power of knowing what is possible and impossible to the power of the exhaustion of outflows—along with the eighteen unique qualities, great kindness, and great compassion, I further perceive these immeasurable forms and images?

Having formed this thought, he saw images of pure gold filling the Sahā world, which—in all four modes of conduct: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—were all preaching suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Even though one sees these things, one should further give rise to this thought:

"These Buddhas are all composed of the common synthesis of such merits as the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, great kindness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness; how could they have physical form?"
When forming this thought, contemplate each point with thorough attention, causing all Buddhas to be without obstruction in body or mind and devoid of any perception of form.

Behold your own body as being like a cloud in the sky; observe that the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) possess neither intrinsic nature nor characteristics, and you will suddenly experience great joy.
Again, he saw his own body become like a cluster of lotuses, filling the trichiliocosm on all sides.
He saw the seated Buddhas sitting upon his flowers, expounding for him the fourteen gateways of the noble and sagely realms—profound emptiness, selflessness, wishlessness, and non-action.
The Buddha told Ajita:
"If there is a practitioner who has seen these things, they should be taught the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*).
To teach the mind of loving-kindness means to teach the contemplation of the hells."

At that time, the practitioner immediately beholds the eighteen hells—those of the flaming chariots, the cauldrons of burning coals, the mountains of knives, and the trees of swords—and sees the sentient beings undergoing suffering therein as all being their own former parents, kinsmen, and relatives, or perhaps their teachers, disciples, and various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
He saw one person after another with their bodies being burned by the fierce fires of the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, some had fire blazing from every joint; some were ascending the Sword-Tree (Asipatravana); some were treading upon the Mountain of Blades (Kṣuradhāra-parvata); some were being cast into boiling cauldrons; some were entering the River of Ashes (Kṣāranadī); some were drinking boiling excrement; some were devouring hot iron balls; some were drinking molten copper; some were lying upon iron beds; some were embracing copper pillars; some were entering the Forest of Swords (Śūlavana), their bodies shattered in countless ways; and some had their eyes gouged out in great numbers, with hot copper balls placed into their eye sockets.

Or they see hungry ghosts with bodies many tens of yojanas in height, devouring fire and charcoal, or drinking pus and blood that turns into molten copper; flames erupt from their entire bodies, and molten copper flows from their heels.
Or he may see sentient beings filling the dark spaces between the Cakravāḍa mountains, resembling rākṣasas who devour one another.

He sees various yakṣas who are naked, black and emaciated, with double fangs protruding upward, fire blazing from their heads, heads like those of oxen, and blood raining down from the tips of their horns.
Furthermore, he saw tigers, wolves, lions, and various other predatory beasts of the world devouring one another; he also saw all the sufferings of the various animals.
Or he saw asuras having their ears and noses cut off, undergoing all manner of painful experiences.
Furthermore, he saw all sentient beings within the three realms driven by desire and undergoing every form of suffering and affliction.
He observed that even the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva) is like a flash of lightning or a magical illusion, for before long they shall fall into the great hells.
To state the essentials: all sentient beings within the twenty-five realms of the three worlds possess the karma for the sufferings of the three miserable paths.

At that time, the practitioner perceives the sentient beings suffering within the three worlds with such clarity as if looking at the palm of their hand, giving rise to profound compassion and a heart of pity.

Seeing that sentient beings undergo evil retributions because of their past performance of unwholesome karma, and having witnessed this, he weeps with tears falling like rain, desiring to provide rescue and protection; yet, despite exhausting his mind and strength, he is unable to save them.

At that time, an extreme sense of compassion arose within his heart; he grew weary of birth and death, having no desire to remain there for long, and felt a surge of terror as if someone were grasping a blade and coming to harm him.
Having seen this, he gives rise once more to compassion, thinking: "Alas, those who wish to uproot suffering are helpless! At that time, the practitioner reflects within himself:

"These sentient beings, due to ignorance (*avidyā*), condition volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); volitional formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*); consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); name-and-form conditions the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the six sense bases condition contact (*sparśa*); contact conditions feeling (*vedanā*); feeling conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*); craving conditions clinging (*upādāna*); clinging conditions existence (*bhava*); existence conditions birth (*jāti*); and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress."
At that time, the practitioner reflects within himself:
"From where does this ignorance come? How does it incubate, nourish, and give birth until it pervades the three realms?"

"Contemplating this ignorance, it attains growth by depending on the earth element; it attains movement by relying on the wind element; it remains indestructible due to the solidity of the body from the earth element; it is illuminated and nurtured by the fire element; and the water element forms its manifold natures."
In such movements, the nature of wind is instability, the nature of water flows downward, the nature of fire blazes upward, and the nature of earth is solidity.
These four elemental natures move two upward and two downward.

The various directions are likewise twofold: the eastern direction constitutes the nature of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha); the southern direction constitutes the nature of the aggregate of sensation (vedanāskandha); the western direction constitutes the nature of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha); the northern direction constitutes the nature of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha); and the upper direction constitutes the nature of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).
These five aggregates of clinging exist dependent upon ignorance and arise from contact.

With pleasant contact as a causal condition, various feelings are produced; with feeling as a causal condition, craving, grasping, and becoming arise. Because of the causal conditions of becoming, the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) and various fetters and karmas of the three realms are produced, binding sentient beings so that there is no time of escape.
Such karmas arise from ignorance and exist through it; they are produced by delusion and craving.
From what source does this ignorance emerge, which spreads throughout the three realms and acts as a great fetter for all sentient beings?
"I should now contemplate from where the characteristics of ignorance and consciousness arise.
Is this ignorance the earth element,
or is it separate from the earth element?"
Does it merge with the earth?
Does it arise from the earth?
Or does it perish into the earth?

The nature of earth is fundamentally empty; when one analyzes earth, no master is found. How then can ignorance give rise to delusion, craving, and perception, which in turn condition volitional formations?
Furthermore, do these volitional formations, as well as craving, grasping, and becoming, arise from wind?
Does it arise from water?
Is it illuminated by fire?
Thus, one should contemplate each of these four great elements with careful attention.
These great elements are in reality devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics; they are identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
How then can they entangle all sentient beings within the triple world and cause them to be scorched by the great afflictions?

Having reflected thus, he feared birth and death and took offense at the pleasures of rebirth in the heavens; he contemplated the celestial palaces as being like dreams, like illusions, like dew, like lightning, and like the sound of an echo.
He universally beholds all sentient beings within the three realms, circling like a wheel and undergoing endless suffering.
Having seen this, he becomes sorrowful and finds no joy; perceiving that the world is like a swift-flowing stream, he seeks the path to nirvāṇa, desiring liberation at every single moment.

At that time, one should further instruct them in the practice of counting the breaths: count one and follow one; count two and follow two; count three and follow three; count four and follow four; count five and follow five; count six and follow six; count seven and follow seven; count eight and follow eight; count nine and follow nine; count ten and follow ten; count a hundred and follow a hundred; count a thousand and follow a thousand. Following the number of breaths, one should collect the vital energy (*prāṇa*) and cause it to abide.

"At that time, one sees one's own body as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lotus flowers, all withered and fragile. Winds come from the four directions and blow away the withered flowers, which transform into lapis lazuli. Like a vessel of lapis lazuli, one sees one's own mind as a great flowering tree extending from the adamantine base below up to the summit of the triple world, bearing four fruits upon it."
That fruit is subtle and wondrous like a wish-fulfilling jewel, emitting six kinds of light that pervasively illumines the trichiliocosm.
When the practitioner sees this, they see all the Buddhas from the adamantine ground below up to the summit of the triple world above, surrounded by their great disciples and retinues.

Some Buddhas flew through the void, emitting water from their upper bodies and fire from their lower bodies, or emitting water from their lower bodies and fire from their upper bodies; they leaped up in the east and sank down in the west, leaped up in the west and sank down in the east, leaped up in the south and sank down in the north, leaped up in the north and sank down in the south, leaped up in the center and sank down at the edges, or leaped up at the edges and sank down in the center.

Sometimes they manifest a massive body that fills the void of space, and then that great body again manifests as small as a mustard seed; their transformations are sovereign, proceeding at will without obstruction.

Or one may see various śrāvakas entering the four great meditative absorptions, their bodies like masses of fire, with the tips of the flames appearing like golden tubes filled with water of many colors.
Furthermore, one sees one's own body as entering that meditative concentration.
At that time, the practitioner should be instructed, saying:
"What you see, although it consists of many Buddhas and śrāvakas, you should now contemplate these World-Honored Ones as the formless body, as great liberation, and as the fruit of no-more-learning."
"You should skillfully restrain your mind, as in the previous method of counting the breaths.
This method of counting the breaths consists of sixteen stages, which cannot be explained in full detail.
"At that time, once the practitioner has finished counting the breaths, the mind becomes tranquil and serene, and there is no further perception."
Furthermore, one should again be instructed to contemplate the mind as a lotus flower, like a flowering tree; upon the tree is fruit resembling a maṇi jewel, manifesting six kinds of light.
These radiance and brilliance shine forth from the summit of the triple world, illuminating the region below down to the limit of the vajra-ground.
One sees that the roots of the mind-flower tree are on the verge of withering, yet they remain profoundly immeasurable.
At that time, one should contemplate the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas exists because of the form-body.
The form-body (rūpakāya) is like a golden vase; the dharma-body (dharmakāya) is like a mani jewel.

One should carefully contemplate that within the form-body there exist the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and unimpeded liberation—immeasurable and most sublime states of spiritual wisdom that are not seen by the eye nor conceived by the mind.
"All dharmas neither come nor go; they neither abide nor perish, being identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Yet foolish ordinary beings are pursued by the great thieves of old age and death, perceiving through deluded inversions."
Because of these inversions, I have fallen into the river of craving and desire within the three realms of suffering, being swept away by its swift current and submerged in the triple world.
How could I now act like an ordinary person, seeking to see the Buddha through deluded thoughts?

My Great Preceptor, Śākyamuni Buddha, in times past, gave away his head, eyes, marrow, and brain, as well as his kingdoms, cities, wives, and children as acts of almsgiving; he underwent hundreds of thousands of ascetic practices to seek the Dharma of liberation.
Now, having already transcended birth and death and abiding in Great Nirvāṇa, he has reached ultimate quiescence and shall never again be born.

Just as the Buddha-dharma of the past abides in the state of permanence and bliss, and likewise lacks the coming and going of present cognitions, so too is this body accomplished through such wisdom—unmoving in body and mind, tranquil and unconditioned.
What perceptions could there be regarding such a body?
"What is meant by 'change and movement'?
What I now perceive arises from false conceptualization and belongs to various causes and conditions; therefore, it is a phenomenon of inverted form and appearance.
While he was reflecting thus, all the Buddhas and the worthy sages remained silent, withdrew their bodies, and did not appear again.
Only the Buddha remained, with four great disciples serving as his attendants.
At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni further expounded the four methods of pure contemplation for the practitioner, saying:
"O Son of the Dharma!
When the sages and saints of the three periods of time past contemplated this practice, they naturally all contemplated the wind element and the contemplation of phenomena.
Regarding the contemplation of the wind element: first, one contemplates within the body that from the heart-flower tree, a single subtle wind arises.
In this way, that subtle wind gradually increases and pervades the entire body.
Having filled the body, it issues from the pores and fills a single room.
Having filled the room, one sees this subtle wind fill the courtyard.
When it had filled the entire courtyard, he again saw it gradually filling one *qǐng* of land.
When it had filled one *qǐng*, it further expanded to fill one *yóujùn*.
Having filled one *yóujùn*, it filled two *yóujùn*.
Having filled two yojanas, it filled three yojanas.
Having filled three yojanas, it filled four yojanas.
Having filled four yojanas, it filled five yojanas.
Having filled five *yojanas*, it gradually expands until it fills ten *yojanas*.

With the slightest movement of a gentle breeze, it gradually expands to pervade the entire trichiliocosm, reaching upward to its zenith and downward to the adamantine base (*vajratala*). Once it has filled all these places, it returns from the zenith and causes all the flowers and leaves of the tree of the mind to wither and fall away, so that one sees one's own body as clearly transparent inside and out, like a crystal mirror.
"At that time, one should further be taught to contemplate the water element (*āpas*).

As for contemplating the water element: first, one contemplates within the body that from the tips of the heart-lotus trees, a minute particle of water emerges like the vapor of lapis lazuli; this gradually expands, appearing like white clouds that fill the interior of the body."
Having filled the interior of his body, [the water] emerges from the six sense organs.
It surges forth from the crown of his head, circling his body seven times like drifting white clouds.
Droplet by droplet, the rain falls; this water is so soft that it fills an entire bed.
Having filled one bed, it gradually expands to fill one room.
Having filled one room, it fills one courtyard.
Having filled one courtyard, it fills one city.
Having filled the entire city, it fills ten *krośas* of land.
Having filled ten *krośas*, it fills one hundred *krośas* of land.
Having filled one hundred *krośas*, it fills one *yojana*.
The color of the water was pure white, like the luster of white lapis lazuli.
Its vapor was so subtle as to exceed the range of the ordinary person's visual faculty.
Gradually expanding, it filled an area of two yojanas.
Having filled two yojanas, it filled three yojanas.
Having filled three yojanas, it filled four yojanas.
Having filled four yojanas, it filled five yojanas.
Having filled five yojanas, it gradually expanded until it filled ten yojanas.
Having filled ten yojanas, it gradually expanded until it filled one hundred yojanas.
Having filled a hundred yojanas, it gradually expanded until it filled the entire Jambudvīpa.
Having filled Jambudvīpa, it gradually expanded until it pervaded the trichiliocosm, reaching upward to the summit of the triple world and downward to the adamantine base.
The appearance of this water, its vapor like clouds, returns and enters through the crown of the head.
"Having seen this, one is further instructed to contemplate the fire element (*tejas*).

To contemplate the fire element: one observes within the heart of one's own body that among the various flowers and leaves at the tips of the flowering trees, there is a subtle fire, like golden light."
Emerging from the tip of the heart, it fills the interior of the body.
Emerging from the pores, it gradually expands until it fills a single bed.
Having filled the bed, it fills the room.
Having filled one room, it gradually expanded to fill an entire courtyard.
Having filled the courtyard, it filled an entire city.
Having filled the city, it filled ten *qīng* of land.
Having filled ten *krośas* of land, it fills a hundred *krośas*.
Having filled a hundred *krośas* of land, it fills one *yojana*.
The color of the fire changes to white; it is as bright and white as the luster of a pearl, such that even crystal or the Snowy Mountains cannot be compared to it.
The red light intermingled and formed patterns;
it gradually expanded until it filled two yojanas.
Having filled two yojanas, it then filled three yojanas.
Having filled three yojanas, it fills four yojanas.
Having filled four yojanas, it fills five yojanas.
Having filled five yojanas, it gradually expands until it fills one hundred yojanas.
Having filled a hundred yojanas, it gradually expanded to fill Jambudvīpa.

Having filled Jambudvīpa, it gradually expanded until it pervaded the trichiliocosm, reaching upward to the summit of the triple world and downward to the adamantine base, before returning and entering through the summit.
"Having seen this, one should further be taught to contemplate the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).

In contemplating the earth element, one sees within one's own body the various flowers on the inner tree gradually expanding until they are like clouds of vajra that completely fill the interior of the body."
Having filled his entire body, it further fills one bed;
having filled one bed, it fills one room;
having filled one room, it fills one courtyard.
Having filled one courtyard, it fills an entire city.
Having filled the city, it gradually expands until it fills ten *qīng*.
Having filled ten *qīng*, it fills a hundred *qīng*.
Having filled one hundred *krośas*, it fills one *yojana*.
Having filled one *yojana*, its color turns blue, gradually expanding until it pervades two *yojanas*.
Having filled two yojanas, it filled three yojanas.
Having filled three yojanas, it filled four yojanas.
Having filled four yojanas, it filled five yojanas.
Having filled five yojanas, it gradually expanded until it filled one hundred yojanas.
Having filled one hundred yojanas, it gradually expanded until it filled Jambudvīpa.

Having filled Jambudvīpa, it gradually expanded until it pervaded the entire trichiliocosm, reaching upward to the summit of the triple world and downward to the adamantine base, before returning and entering back through the summit.
“Having seen this, one should further be instructed to again contemplate the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
One should contemplate this earth element as being like a diamond cloud, difficult to shatter; how then could it be extinguished?”

When performing this visualization, one sees the Buddha, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, seated upon the vajra-seat together with his venerable disciples and an assembly of five hundred, sitting before the practitioner and praising the Truth of Cessation with one voice in harmony.
Having heard these words, one should contemplate that the earth element arises from causes and conditions and is sustained by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Ignorance has no intrinsic nature; delusion and craving have no master. These are false causes and conditions, conventionally designated as "ignorance," and craving, grasping, becoming, and so forth all belong to this same category.

While performing this contemplation, one sees fire gradually arise from the tips of the various flowering trees within one's own heart, burning the vajra-clouds; each cloud merges with the fire amidst the leaves and fills the interior of the body.
Having filled his entire body, the earth and fire both quaked, filling one bed.
Having filled one bed, they filled one room.
Having filled one room, they filled one courtyard.
Having filled one courtyard, it fills an entire city.
Having filled one city, it gradually expands until it fills ten *qing*.
Having filled ten *qing*, it fills one hundred *qing*.
Having filled one hundred *krośas*, it fills one *yojana*.
Having filled one *yojana*, it fills two *yojanas*.
Having filled two *yojanas*, it fills three *yojanas*.
Having filled three yojanas, it fills four yojanas.
Having filled four yojanas, it fills five yojanas.
Having filled five yojanas, it gradually expands until it fills one hundred yojanas.
Having filled a hundred *yojanas*, it gradually expands until it pervades Jambudvīpa.

The two great elements of earth and fire, being of different natures, mutually stimulate one another, filling the trichiliocosm from the summit of the three realms above down to the adamantine foundation below, before returning and entering back through the summit.
“Having seen this, one should further be instructed to contemplate the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).

To contemplate the wind element: one observes that from within the heart-lotus tree of the body, purple-colored wind emerges. The water element follows it in, extinguishing this wind until their colors become identical as the color of water. The wind moves and the water surges, filling the interior of the body; gradually expanding, it fills the entire bed.”
Having filled one bed, it fills one room.
Having filled one room, it fills one courtyard.
Having filled one courtyard, it fills one city.
Having filled the entire city, it gradually expanded until it pervaded one *yojana*.

Having filled the one *yojana*, the two natures of wind and water, being distinct in their characteristics, caused the wind to blow upon this water like beryl foam, its color blazing intensely; as they further struck against one another, they filled two *yojanas*.
Having filled two yojanas, it filled three yojanas.
Having filled three yojanas, it filled four yojanas.
Having filled four yojanas, it filled five yojanas.
Having filled five yojanas, it gradually expanded until it filled one hundred yojanas.
Having filled one hundred yojanas, it gradually expanded until it completely filled Jambudvīpa.
Having filled Jambudvīpa, it gradually expanded until it pervaded the entire trichiliocosm, reaching upward to the summit of the triple world and downward to the adamantine base.

“Having seen this, one sees within one’s own body all the pores of the skin from which fire arises; these flames of fire fill the triple world and extend beyond it, like flowers of pure gold, upon which there are fruits, with leaves following one after another.”
Within the radiance of those fruits, he expounds the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination—the Dharma for crossing over birth and death.
Furthermore, he sees all water arise within his body; this water is warm and moist, emerging from his pores and flowing throughout the three realms, filling them everywhere without exception.
The color of water emerges as light that illuminates the summit of the triple world and enters the fire-light fruit.

Again, one sees all the winds arising within the body, filling the interior of the body; they emerge from the pores, gradually expanding, blowing with great speed and force until they fill the triple world, transforming into golden clouds that enter the fire-light fruit.
Furthermore, there is an earth-element energy that is extremely subtle and pervasive throughout the four great elements.
Having seen this phenomenon, one should further be instructed to contemplate the five aggregates with clear discernment,
beginning with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

This aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) exists in dependence upon the great element of earth; yet the great element of earth is not fixed, arising from ignorance (avidyā). Through the causal conditions of ignorance, one falsely perceives what is called "form.
When one contemplates these characteristics of form, they are seen to be deceptive and unreal, having no place of origin, appearing only through the conjunction of provisional causes and conditions.
The nature of causes and conditions is empty, and the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is likewise so.
The nature and characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are all empty; within them there is no solid core.
Contemplating these five aggregates, one finds that they truly have neither causes and conditions nor any recipient of existence.
"How do these four great elements increase and pervade the triple world?
While reflecting thus, he saw all fires emerge from every pore, filling the triple world, and then re-enter through every pore.
Furthermore, he saw the great element of earth appearing like vajra-clouds, emerging from all his pores, pervading the triple world, and then re-entering through all his pores.
Again, he saw the water element appearing like fine dust, emerging from all his pores, filling the triple world, and then re-entering through all his pores.
Again, he saw the wind element, its force weak and inferior, emerging from all his pores, filling the triple world, and then re-entering through all his pores.
In this manner, the four great elements emerge from the pores and enter through the pores, circulating back and forth eight hundred times.
"Having witnessed this phenomenon, and having completed the counting of breaths as before, one remains with the breath held for seven days."
At that time, he naturally saw this great earth gradually becoming empty;
he saw the space beneath a single bed gradually becoming empty; he saw a single room gradually becoming empty.
Having seen the room become empty, he saw the courtyard ground gradually becoming empty.
Having seen one courtyard, he sees the ground of one city gradually become empty.
Having seen one city, he sees ten *qing* of ground gradually become empty.
Having seen ten *qing*, he sees a hundred *qing* of ground gradually become empty.
Having seen one hundred *krośas*, he sees the ground of one *yojana* gradually becoming empty.
Having seen one *yojana*, he sees the ground of two *yojanas* gradually becoming empty.
Having seen two *yojanas*, he sees the ground of three *yojanas* gradually becoming empty.
Having seen three yojanas, he sees the ground for four yojanas gradually becoming empty.
Having seen four yojanas, he sees the ground for five yojanas gradually becoming empty.
Having seen five yojanas, he gradually sees the ground up to ten yojanas becoming empty.
Having seen ten yojanas, he gradually sees the ground up to one hundred yojanas becoming empty.
Having seen [the land] for a hundred yojanas, he gradually sees the eight thousand yojanas of Jambudvīpa becoming empty.
Having seen Jambudvīpa, he sees the ten thousand yojanas of Pūrvavideha gradually becoming empty.
Having seen Pūrvavideha, he saw that Jambudvīpa, thirty thousand yojanas in extent, was gradually becoming empty.
Having seen Jambudvīpa, he saw that Aparagoyānī, forty thousand yojanas in extent, was gradually becoming empty.

Having seen Uttarakuru, one sees Mount Sumeru, the four great oceans, mountains, rivers, rocky cliffs, and all that exists within the four continents; all solid and hard objects gradually become entirely empty.

Having seen the four continents, his mind then expanded until it pervaded the trichiliocosm; all solid and hard objects—the great earth, mountains, rivers, rocks, and walls—were entirely empty, and his mind had no place to rest upon.
At that time, one spontaneously beholds the vajra-limit, where there are fourteen vajra-wheels.
From beneath these vajra-wheels, they naturally surge upward, striking against one another, until they arrive before the practitioner.

At that time, a natural fire arises from the tips of the exquisite flowers upon the tree of the mind, burning the petals and leaves and the four fruits atop the tree; these fall onto the practitioner’s crown, enter through the crown, and settle within the heart.
At that time, this mind suddenly became clear and lucid, and he saw external objects beyond the obstruction.
Furthermore, there were six elephants, their color jet black, trampling the great earth into ruin and drinking up all the waters.
The wind blew and killed the elephant; fire issued from its ears and burned the elephant entirely away.
The four great venomous snakes fled to the top of a tree.
There they saw a man who resembled a great athlete, who uprooted this massive tree, shaking it so that it reached from the adamantine base below to the summit of the triple world above.
Within the practitioner’s mind, four bright jewel-fruits further emit great flames that burn the tree roots until they are severed; at that moment, the great tree disperses like fine dust.
Having seen this, the practitioner reflects: "I now observe that fire, water, wind, and the element of water are all impermanent, changing and perishing in an instant."
One should contemplate the four great elements within one’s own body: fire arises without end, and earth, water, and wind are likewise so.

This characteristic of ignorance is empty and non-existent, false and inverted; it is like frost or a mirage belonging to the three realms. Conditioned by delusion and craving, thirty-three billion thoughts give rise to ninety-nine hundred cycles of dharmas. One contemplates these coarse characteristics in succession: there are ninety-eight fetters, whose branches and seeds completely cover the three realms.
Because of these various fetters, they undergo birth countless times: sometimes falling into hell, their bodies consumed by fierce flames;
sometimes becoming hungry ghosts, swallowing molten copper and devouring glowing iron balls, not hearing the sound of water or grain for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes;
or becoming animals—camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs—in numbers beyond reckoning.
In the human realm, one undergoes suffering, and the various hardships are not of a single kind.
Such a multitude [of sufferings] arises from delusion and craving.
Now, when one contemplates this delusion and craving, their nature is found to be non-existent.
While he was reflecting in this way, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted golden light and, surrounded by his retinue of śrāvakas, addressed the practitioner, saying:
"Do you know now?"
The characteristics of form are empty and quiescent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
You should now carefully contemplate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action.
Regarding the emptiness samādhi: one contemplates that form, the intrinsic nature of form, and all phenomena are empty and non-existent.
This collection of various emptinesses is called the emptiness samādhi.
The samādhi of wishlessness consists in contemplating that the nature of nirvāṇa is quiescent and signless.
One contemplates that the characteristics of saṃsāra are entirely identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
When performing this contemplation, one does not desire saṃsāra nor take pleasure in nirvāṇa.

To contemplate that the primordial limit of birth and death is empty and quiescent, and to contemplate that the nature and characteristics of nirvāṇa are likewise identical in entering emptiness, such that there is no combination or conjunction—this is called the samādhi of wishlessness.

Regarding the samādhi of non-action: one does not perceive the mind, nor the body, nor any deliberate activity within the various modes of deportment; one does not perceive the arising of any nature or characteristics within nirvāṇa, but perceives only the truth of cessation, penetrating that it is empty and devoid of anything existent.

At that time, as the practitioner heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speak of these samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, his body and mind became tranquil and still as he traversed the three gates of emptiness. In the mere interval it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he immediately, upon hearing the words, transcended ninety billion bonds of the burning cycle of birth and death, attaining arhatship. He was no longer subject to future existence; his holy life was established; he knew the truth of the Way as it is. His mind was suddenly liberated, free from all residual habits. The exhaustion of outflows and the penetration of wisdom were attained spontaneously, though the other five supernormal powers required cultivation to achieve.
"The meaning of the six supernormal powers is explained at length in the Abhidharma.

At that time, having taught Aṅgada this sphere of the mind associated with the emptiness of the noble ones and having analyzed the characteristics of the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*), the World-Honored One remained silent and peacefully entered the *araṇā-samādhi*, emitting rays of light of various colors that illuminated the entire world.
At that time, within the assembly, two hundred and fifty bhikṣus had their minds opened and liberated, attaining arhatship.
Fifty upāsakas shattered twenty koṭis of blazing fetters and attained the stage of srotāpanna.
When the great assembly of devas and humans heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were all filled with great joy.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The Tathāgata first taught the gateway of impurity to Kāṭhila-nanda; he taught the method of counting the breaths to the bhikṣu Dhyānottara; and he taught the contemplation of the four great elements to Ajita.
"How should these many subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates be received and upheld?
By what name should they be proclaimed to future generations?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This sutra is titled 'The Secret Essentials of the Dhyāna Method'; it is also titled 'The Gate of the Contemplation of White Bones,' also titled 'The Nine Successive Contemplations,' also titled 'The Method of Contemplating Mixed Images,' also titled 'The Expedient Means of Ānāpāna,' also titled 'The Contemplation of the Four Successive Fruits,' and also titled 'The Differentiation of Realms.'"
"Receive and uphold this thus;
be careful not to forget or lose it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"After my parinirvāṇa, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who wish to study the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time—to sever the seeds of birth and death, cross the river of afflictions, dry up the ocean of birth and death, eliminate the seeds of craving, cut off the flow of the various proclivities (anuśaya), grow weary of the pleasures of the five desires, and delight in nirvāṇa—they should study this contemplation."
The merit of this contemplation is like Mount Sumeru, from which various rays of light stream forth to illuminate the four continents.
One who practices this contemplation and attains the fruits of the śramaṇa is likewise so.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who wish to study this Dharma, they should distance themselves from four kinds of evil.”
What are the four?
First, to purely uphold the prohibitive precepts and not transgress the rules of decorum.
If one has committed any offense against the five groups of precepts, one should sincerely repent to restore purity.
Once the precepts are purified, this is called the adornment of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Second, one should distance oneself from clamor and dwell alone in quietude, binding the mind to a single point and delighting in the practice of speaking little.
Third, they practice the twelve profound dhūtas with a mind free from weariness or fatigue, as if their heads were on fire;
they sweep stūpas, smear the ground, provide willow branches and clean counting-sticks, and perform various menial labors to eliminate obstructing karmic offenses.

Fourth, throughout the six periods of day and night, one remains constantly seated and does not lie down; one takes no pleasure in sleep or leaning the body to one side, but delights in dwelling among cemeteries, under trees, or in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*); in eating one is like a deer, and in dying one is like a deer.
If there are members of the fourfold assembly who practice these four dharmas, you should know that such persons are practitioners of asceticism.
Through such ascetic practice, they will before long certainly attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there are members of the fourfold assembly who practice the method of mindfulness, even to the point of visualizing the appearance of a small portion of a single bone joint at the tip of a toe or a finger, making it extremely clear—whether seeing a single finger, a single nail, or all the white bones."

One should know that because this person’s mind was so beneficial, after the end of their life they will certainly be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, extinguishing all the suffering and afflictions of the three evil realms.
Although they have not yet attained liberation, they shall not fall into the evil realms.

You should know that the merit of such a person is inexhaustible; they have already escaped the sufferings and hardships of the three miserable paths, let alone those who fully possess the "white bones" (the marks of a perfected practitioner).

One who sees this skeleton, though not yet liberated from the merit of the outflows, should know that this person has already escaped the afflictions of all the three miserable realms and the eight difficult conditions; one should know that in every lifetime throughout their births, this person will never be separated from seeing the Buddha, and in a future age, upon encountering Maitreya at the first assembly under the Dragon-Flower Tree, they shall first hear the Dharma and realize liberation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās within the Buddha-dharma who, for the sake of gain and offerings, pursue them greedily without satiety; who, for the sake of a good reputation, feign and falsely commit evil deeds; who in reality do not practice dhyāna, but are negligent in body and speech and engage in heedless conduct; and who, out of greed for gain and offerings, claim themselves to be practitioners of dhyāna."
Such a bhikṣu commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
If he does not confess it when the time has passed and does not reform himself, having merely waited for a brief moment, he then commits a thirteenth saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If it lasts for one day or even two days, you should know that this bhikṣu is a thief among gods and humans, a rākṣasa executioner; he will certainly fall into the evil realms and have committed a grave and heavy offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī, being seductive, crafty, and deceitful, seeks gain and offerings like a cat watching for a mouse—greedily pursuing them without satiety—and while not actually practicing dhyāna, claims to be practicing dhyāna; if she is negligent in body and speech, engaging in negligent conduct, and out of greed for gain and offerings, claims to be practicing dhyāna.
If a bhikṣuṇī such as this commits a sthūlātyaya offense,
yet fails to confess it when the time has passed and does not reform herself, she immediately commits a thirteenth saṃghāvaśeṣa offense after a mere moment.

If it lasts for one day or even two days, you should know that this bhikṣuṇī is a thief among gods and humans, a rākṣasa executioner; she will certainly fall into the evil realms and has committed a grave and heavy offense.

If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, having not actually seen white bones, claims to have seen white bones, and so on up to *ānāpāna*, such a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī deceives the devas, nāgas, and spirits, and cheats the people of the world.
These evil persons are of the lineage of Pāpīyān; because of their false speech, they claim for themselves: "I have attained the contemplation of impurity" up to the "Summit Dharma."
After this liar’s life comes to an end, he will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell, swifter than a rain of hailstones, where his lifespan shall be one kalpa.
Emerging from that hell, he will fall among the hungry ghosts (preta), where for eight thousand years he shall devour hot iron balls.
Emerging from the realm of hungry ghosts, they fall among the animals, where they are born to carry heavy burdens constantly and, upon death, have their skins flayed.
After five hundred lifetimes, they are reborn among humans, yet they wear deafness, blindness, muteness, physical infirmities, and a hundred maladies as their clothing.
Such sufferings endured are beyond full description.
If an upāsaka, while not actually practicing meditation, claims to practice meditation, or while not actually leading the holy life (brahmacarya), claims to lead the holy life;

Such an upāsaka incurs the offense of negligence; being impure in his actions and failing to give rise to the wholesome, he falls into the foul state of a caṇḍāla, becomes a companion to evil, and as a rotten seed, he shall not produce the sprouts of goodness.
Out of greed for gain and offerings, they seek much without satiety; having passed from one day up to five days [without confession], they commit a great lie.
These great evildoers are sent by Pāpīyān; they are of the same class as caṇḍālas, butchers, and rākṣasas, and will certainly fall into the three evil realms.

When this upāsaka is about to die, the eighteen hells—with their chariots of fire, glowing coals, and various terrifying transformations—will all at once come to meet him; there is no doubt that he will certainly fall into the three evil realms.

If an upāsaka, having not actually attained anything from the contemplation of impurity up to the stage of "warmth," gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*) amidst the great assembly and proclaims these words:
"I have attained the contemplation of impurity up to the stage of warmth."
"You should know that this upāsaka is a thief among gods and humans, deceiving the world’s eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas.
After the life of this upāsaka ends, he will surely fall into the Avīci Hell, swifter than a rain of hailstones, for the duration of one full kalpa."
When their lifespan in hell is exhausted, they are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), where for eight thousand years they consume hot iron balls.
Emerging from the realm of hungry ghosts, they fall among the animals (*tiryagyoni*); there they are born to constantly carry heavy burdens, and upon death, they are flayed alive.
After five hundred lifetimes, they are reborn among humans, yet they wear deafness, blindness, muteness, and various physical infirmities as their raiment.
The suffering endured in such a manner cannot be fully described.
If an upāsikā displays eccentricities to delude the masses, falsely claiming to practice dhyāna when she is not actually practicing dhyāna, this upāsikā incurs the offense of *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*.
Her defilements remain bound and impure; she fails to arise [from the fetters] and falls into impurity, becoming a foul-smelling caṇḍāla.
This upāsikā keeps company with evil; she is a follower of Māra and will certainly fall into the three evil realms.
This upāsikā fails to speak of her transgressions and does not repent of them for a brief moment, or for one day, or even up to five days.
This upāsikā is greedily seeking without satiety; she does not truly practice the holy life yet claims to do so, and she does not truly practice meditation yet claims to do so.
This person of great evil will certainly fall into the three evil destinies, taking birth there according to her karma.

If a laywoman (upāsikā), while not having actually attained anything from the contemplation of impurity up to the stage of "warmth" (uṣmagata), should proclaim such words in the midst of the great assembly out of overweening pride (adhimāna), saying:
"I have attained the contemplation of impurity up to the stage of warmth."
"This upāsikā is a thief among gods and humans.
After her life ends, she will surely fall into the Avīci Hell, faster than a rain of hailstones, for the duration of one full kalpa."
When their lifespan in hell is exhausted, they are born among the hungry ghosts (preta), where for eight thousand years they consume glowing iron balls.
Emerging from the realm of hungry ghosts, they fall into the animal realm (tiryagyoni), where they are born to carry heavy burdens constantly and, upon death, have their skin flayed.
After five hundred lifetimes, they are reborn among humans, yet they wear deafness, blindness, muteness, and various physical infirmities as their clothing.
Such sufferings endured in this manner cannot be fully described.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās bind their mindfulness and dwell with the mind focused, without distraction, sitting upright in meditative absorption (samādhi), dwelling with the mind on a single point and closing off the sense faculties.”

Because this person has established their mind through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), although they lack a specific objective realm, upon casting off the body in another life, they will be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven and encounter Maitreya.
Together with Maitreya, they will descend to Jambudvīpa and, at the first assembly under the Dragon Flower tree, will be the very first to hear the Dharma and realize the path of liberation.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the age of turbid evil, if there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who truly practice the holy life (brahmacarya), who adorn their bodies with the twelve dhūtas, whose minds practice mindfulness and concentration, and who cultivate the contemplation of the white bones.
By contemplating impurity, they enter the profound realm; their mental eye becomes clear and sharp, and they attain mastery in the methods of dhyāna.
Thus, for the sake of increasing the Buddha-dharma and ensuring that the Dharma does not perish, these four assemblies should maintain secrecy regarding their body, speech, and mind.
It is like a person who encounters illness of body and mind; a skilled physician prescribes that they should take *sarpis* (clarified butter).

At that time, the patient goes to the king to beg for the *sarpis*. Out of compassion, the king immediately bestows the *sarpis* upon him and instructs the patient on the method for taking it: "You must drink it in a private room free from wind and dust; having drunk it, close your mouth and regulate the four great elements so that they do not fall into disorder."
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī takes this consecrated medicine of ambrosia, they must not recklessly proclaim it to others, with the sole exception of their teacher who instructs them in the Dharma.
If one speaks of this to others, one loses the meditative state and also commits the offense of the thirteenth *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Even for laypeople who wish to practice dhyāna-concentration and attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), they should not proclaim to others that they have attained such powers, nor should they speak of their mastery of immortals' spells or arts; all such matters should be kept secret.

How much more so for those who have left the household life and received full ordination (*upasampadā*): if they attain the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) or even the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*), they must not recklessly proclaim these to others.
If one were to speak of this to others, it would cause the cessation of the meditative object and lead many sentient beings to develop doubts and hesitations regarding the Buddha-dharma.

Therefore, I now decree among this assembly that all bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who attain the contemplation of impurity, up to the stage of "warmth" (ūṣmagata), shall practice it in secret to make their minds clear and sharp; they may speak of it only to a wise teacher or instructor, and must not propagate it widely by speaking of it to others.
If one speaks of this to others with a mind seeking gain and offerings, one immediately commits the thirteenth *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one fails to confess at the proper time and remains without shame or remorse, one likewise commits a grave offense as described above.
"Furthermore, Ānanda:

after the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, when no Buddha is present before them, those among the fourfold assembly of disciples who seek liberation and attain the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) should keep it hidden and secret, not letting others know of it."
It is like a person who is poor and solitary, born in a turbid and evil age under an unrighteous king.

That impoverished man digs into the earth in search of water, and by the causes and conditions of his past lives, he suddenly encounters a hidden treasure and gains a great abundance of precious jewels.

Fearing the wicked king, he concealed this treasure in secret so that others would not know of it; he would only take this precious jewel in private places to provide for his wife and children and enjoy happiness in secret.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those among the fourfold assembly of disciples who have attained the bliss of dhyāna should likewise keep this secret and not explain it extensively.
If they should explain it extensively, they commit a grave and heavy offense.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is as if an elder had an only son who fell gravely ill, such that his beard and eyebrows fell out entirely.
At that time, the elder thought to himself:
"I am now beset by misfortune;
this only son of mine has fallen gravely ill.
Where shall I seek a skilled physician?"
Having spoken these words, he distributed a great amount of wealth and treasure to seek out a skilled physician.
Due to the elder’s past merit, he suddenly encountered a physician who was well-versed in many medical scriptures and formulas.
The elder said:
"I only pray that the Great Master will give rise to great compassion.
I have an only son who has been afflicted by illness for a long time."
I only pray that the Great Master will cure this ailment.
Should I be healed, my home now possesses vast wealth and treasures, like those of the Northern Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
"If your son recovers, with the sole exception of my own person, I shall offer everything to you and dare not disobey.
Then the skilled physician said to the elder:
"If you can now construct seven-layered dark chambers, making them extremely deep and secluded, only then may your son be administered the medicine."
"Once this medicine has been taken, one must not see anyone nor speak of it to others.
After four hundred days have passed, the child may then recover.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if any disciples among the fourfold assembly of the Buddha wish to cultivate meditative concentration to seek liberation, they should—like a gravely ill person following the instructions of a skilled physician—practice the profound path of the noble ones in a quiet place, whether it be among burial mounds, beneath forest trees, or in a forest hermitage (araṇya)."

One should guard one’s body and speech, and within the inner mind cultivate the four brahma-vihāras, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the four dhyānas, and the four immeasurables; with the mind entering the profound and immeasurable gateway of the emptiness samādhi, one shall even attain the six supernormal powers.

Regarding these various kinds of supreme and wondrous merits, you should practice them in secret with single-minded devotion; be careful not to falsely claim before a multitude that you have attained superhuman states.
"If one claims to have attained superhuman states as described above, they will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the first hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this practice of the impurity contemplation shall circulate throughout Jambudvīpa, gathering in those who are heedless and causing them to contemplate the Four Noble Truths."
Those who attain liberation by practicing the contemplation of impermanence within a single day are no different from those who dwell in my presence throughout my lifetime.
Two hundred years after [my passing], one half of the fourfold assembly of disciples in this Jambudvīpa will attain the path of liberation through the practice of the contemplation of impermanence.
When [the Dharma] has lasted three hundred years, one part in four of the disciples from the fourfold assembly will cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and attain the path of liberation.
When it has lasted four hundred years, one part in five of the disciples from the fourfold assembly will cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and attain the path of liberation.
Five hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, one-tenth of the disciples among the fourfold assembly shall cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and attain the path of liberation.
When six hundred years have passed, one part in a hundred of the disciples from the four assemblies will cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and attain the path of liberation.
When seven hundred years have passed, one part in a thousand of the disciples from the four assemblies will cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and attain the path of liberation.
When [the lifespan] is eight hundred years, one part in ten thousand of the disciples of the fourfold assembly will cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and attain the path of liberation.
When it is nine hundred years, one part in ten million of the disciples of the fourfold assembly will cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and attain the path of liberation.
When one thousand years have passed, among ten billion disciples, perhaps ten or a hundred will cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and attain the path of liberation.

After those thousand years have elapsed, although this contemplation of impermanence continues to circulate within Jambudvīpa, among many hundreds of thousands of millions of disciples, only one or two will cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and attain the path of liberation.

After fifteen hundred years, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who praise and proclaim the contemplation of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, many sentient beings will harbor feelings of jealousy and will either strike those people with knives or pelt them with tiles and stones, reviling them by saying:
"You foolish person!"
Where in this world is there a contemplation of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self?
Your body’s flesh is pure white and immeasurable; how can you conversely say that the body is impure?
You are a person of great evil; you ought to be expelled.
When these signs appear,
among hundreds or thousands of people,
not a single person will practice the contemplation of impermanence.
"When these signs appear, the banner of Dharma collapses and the sun of wisdom sets; all sentient beings will be blind and without eyes.
Although Śākyamuni Buddha has disciples, the saṃghāṭī robes they wear will naturally turn white like wooden banners."
The bhikṣuṇīs are like courtesans, selling their beauty to sustain themselves;
the upāsakas are like caṇḍālas, killing living beings without restraint.
When the upāsikās engage in sexual misconduct and lack the Way, employing a hundredfold means of deception and fraud—
when these signs appear, the unsurpassed True Dharma of Śākyamuni will perish forever without remainder.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Bear my words in mind and, for the sake of the fourfold assembly of disciples in future ages, you should widely proclaim and explain their meaning in detail; be careful not to forget or lose them."
Furthermore, Ānanda!
You should proclaim these words for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages:
"The Great Dharma of the Tathāgata will surely perish before long."
"You all should apply yourselves with diligent effort within the Buddha-dharma; you must contemplate the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
When the Buddha spoke these words, eight thousand devaputras realized impermanence, became free from dust and defilement, and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Five hundred bhikṣus, while still upon their seats, did not grasp at any phenomena; their outflows were exhausted and their minds were liberated, and they became arhats.

At that time, the elder Ajita, along with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on this gate of contemplating impermanence, had their minds opened and their intentions liberated. They all thoroughly realized and understood suffering, emptiness, and impermanence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and joyfully put it into practice.
The Scripture on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna, Scroll II.
